Oṃ, salutations to Gaṇapati; salutations to the illustrious Paśupati.
Salutations to that Blessed One, Śambhu, who indeed eternally [bestows] through his grace and other qualities. 1.
The sages said:
"O Lord of Munis, through your grace we have heard the praise of Mount Meru;
now we desire to hear further the majesty of the Himavat mountain."
O Lord, tell us of the greatness of those who have performed austerities there, and especially of the gods, as well as of the sacred fords and the peaks.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Listen, O tigers among brahmins, to the account of what occurred in the past—
the dialogue between Agastya and Skanda on the mountain.
And indeed, on that family mountain, the pitcher-born Agastya questioned the great lord, the commander-in-chief who is the son of Hara, regarding the majesty of the sacred fords.
Agastya said:
Whatever has been taught by you and heard from the mouths of the two gods,
O noble one, you are indeed omniscient, since Bhava himself is born from you.
O Skanda, having drunk the nectar of speech issuing from your lotus-like mouth,
I am not so satiated as a person afflicted by heat is by water.
[1.7 This is the nectar of speech] This nectar of speech is authoritative, for it is a praise of the peaks of Mount Sumeru;
by your grace, I have heard of the abodes of the gods. 8.
O beloved of Śaṅkara, tell me of the origin of the mountains and the sacred fords within them, as well as the greatness of Himālaya and the beings born therein.
Skanda said: "O Pot-born one, everything that was told to me by the Lord himself upon the mountain of jewels—
that I shall relate to you in brief."
I shall now relate in its entirety that which occurred in the past concerning the mountains and the earth; listen to me with a concentrated mind. (11)
O wise one, if you desire your own welfare, this must never be told to one who is not a devotee, nor to a hypocrite, a slanderer, or a sinner. 12.
When all beings had perished, there was a terrible, single ocean;
Viṣvaksena, submerged in darkness, lay upon the waters in utter solitude.
Having withdrawn all the worlds, as well as the stars, the moon, and the sun,
the omnipresent Lord remains alone for a long time, covering himself with water.
O sage, that god Viṣṇu, whose form is unmanifest and whose body consists of splendor,
remains asleep for a long time, pervading the kalpa, at the end of Brahmā’s life.
Mahāmāyā resides within his gaze; her form is concealed by illusion.
Within the cosmic egg, he himself stands as the Lord of the mass of luminaries.
O Agastya, at the end of a kalpa, when the ten directions were submerged in darkness,
there arose from the navel of Brahmā a thousand-petaled lotus.
Dhātṛ, who acts for the benefit of the worlds, muttered prayers in their midst;
then, having meditated upon Śaṅkara—who is to be contemplated incessantly—as the wonderful one within his heart.
Then, O sage, the god Nārāyaṇa took the impurity from his two ears with his two little fingers and cast it into the water. (19)
Then, from that water, two terrifying Daityas were born;
known by the names Madhu and Kaiṭabha, they remained stationed in the midst of the waters.
O Sage, because they have sharp fangs and are born from impurity, they are of the nature of Daityas;
at the end of ten thousand divine years, they grow and become exceedingly wrathful.
Then those two, born from the wax of his ears—
terrible-faced, fearsome, huge-bodied, and possessed of great strength— stood at his sides.
Possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, with thick legs and excellent arms,
they were experts in all forms of combat, dark-limbed, and had eyes shaped like wheels.
Clapping their hands in preparation for battle, they struck their palms together and, looking in all directions, cried out, "Who is there? (24)
"What should we contemplate, and what indeed should we do together?
Then they beheld a lotus with a long stalk, most brilliantly radiant.
Having gone to his presence, those two wicked and wrathful Daityas climbed upon that lotus with its beautiful stalk, adorned with filaments.
There he beheld the high-souled one born from the lotus, possessed of great luster,
reciting prayers and meditating, indeed five-faced and four-armed.
He bore a rosary, was tranquil, with a slightly smiling face;
he was the primordial Hiranyagarbha, extended by his own splendors.
And [he saw] the Grandfather of the worlds, resembling molten gold,
wearing divine garments, wise, and adorned with celestial ornaments.
O Sage, those two heroes, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were by nature prone to anger, then spoke these words to their grandfather.
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"Who are you here? What is your purpose? What do you do? What is this marvel? From where have you come? Why are you so composed? To whom do you belong? Or what is it that should be told here? (31)

Tell us for certain how he indeed recited [the mantra] in that lotus which was empty, filled with water, formidable, unmanifest, and likewise situated in the quarters, and which possessed many mouths.

Brahmā said: "O heroes, remaining in meditation, I have beheld with ease that Lord of Beings, who is higher than the highest, the source of all beings, and the one who bestows compassion upon all creatures."
"O you of great strength, I am Brahmā, the creator of all beings;
for I meditate upon the Lord whose form is the bliss of the universe. (34)
"You two must not remain for a long time; go back by the same way you came.
For he who enters a secret place meets with great calamity. (35)
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"O Lord of the World, we have come here not at all to stay, but out of a desire for battle;
our hands, eager for combat, now itch. (36)
"Know that we two have come here desiring to fight;
therefore, O Great Brahmin, grant us battle now. (37)

Indeed, you grant us battle now; and if victory comes when you have appeared before us, we shall increase your glory with our own lives. But if you do not abide by this agreement, do not remain alive. 38.
If you do not grant us battle, O Lord, for we two are eager to fight, then having quickly uprooted the lotus born from the waters, we shall plunder you of that lotus. 39.
Skanda said:
Having heard those words concerning the battle and that tumultuous chatter,
O Sage, the Grandfather was pained in his mind and remained silent at that time.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can I now release Viṣṇu, who has been covered by sleep; how does the Conqueror of the Universe awaken? 41.
Having reflected thus, the Soul of the Universe (Viṣṇu) once again composed a hymn for the sake of Hari’s awakening—
a hymn dedicated to Nidrā that benefits all the worlds.
Brahmā said:
O Śivā, having withdrawn all the worlds and flooded the universe with her own waters,
she lay alone upon the eye of Hari, enchanting Hari.
Salutations to her who deludes the worlds, she who is the enchantress;
she who dwells within in the form of delusion, yet bestows happiness and possesses discernment. 44.
Obeisance be to you, O Viṣṇavī, who possess universal form; O Sovereign of the Universe, obeisance be to you!
O you who abide in the ether, whose form is the ether, whose nature is splendor, obeisance be to you! 45.
Salutations again and again to Mohinī, the deluder of the universe;
salutations again and again to Maṅgalā, to Śivā who is the very form of Śiva, and to you, Māyā. 46.
Homage be to you who take the form of clouds, drenched with moisture; homage be to you who take the form of the earth, the sower of seeds, yet yourself seedless—the medicinal one. 47.

Salutations be to You, who are the self-form of the five [elements], the enjoyer, the form of the object of enjoyment, residing in the treasury [of the heart] in the form of intellect, and whose nature is pure consciousness. 48.
Salutations be to you, who take the form of conceit, whose nature is the heart;
salutations again and again to you, the embodiment of fortitude, the one who possesses perfect composure, and the discerning one. 49.
O Mother, who are the form of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), salutations be to you in the form of the individual soul (jīva);
salutations again and again to Mātṛkā, the pure one whose form is sound.
Salutations to you who consist of one mātrā, two mātrās, and many mātrās;
salutations again and again to you whose nature is the half-mātrā and who possesses the three musical tones.
Salutations again and again to her whose form consists of the three qualities, yet who transcends the qualities;
salutations again and again to her who possesses the threefold powers of will, knowledge, and action.
O Mahāmāyā, O Mahājihvā, O Mahādaṃṣṭrā, salutations, salutations!
O Great Goddess in the form of Time, O Kālarātri, let there be salutation to you! 53.
Protect, protect me, O Mother Ambikā, who am afflicted by the sins and malevolent planets of the Daityas!
O Nidrā, O Alakṣmī, O Mother of the World, O Wrath of the World, let there be salutation unto you! 54.
Even one who is in distress should recite this praise of sleep, which yields great merit;
being liberated from all sins, he shall obtain his desired boon. 55.
By the grace of Kālarātri, one attains eternal sovereignty, the pacification of diseases arising from malevolent planets, wealth, grain, sons, and a wife. (56)
One should recite this same [hymn] for one's sons and wife during a Śrāddha ceremony; the ancestors, being satisfied, go to the Samāyuta heaven.
Through giving, one attains inexhaustible merit, and in battle, one shall obtain victory. (57)
Skanda said:
Thus praised by Brahmā of immeasurable splendor, the goddess Nidrā was then satisfied and withdrew the imperishable Viṣṇu. 58.
Having awakened, that Great Viṣṇu, having cast off his body through Māyā, beheld those two high-souled ones roaring and full of wrath. (59)
Mutually reviling each other,
the two Daityas, standing upon the lotus, were intent on uprooting it and prepared to slay Brahmā.
Viṣṇu spoke these words to the two Asuras, Madhu and Kaiṭabha:
"O you two evil-minded Daityas, having come here, what is to be said? (61)
Having heard these words spoken by Viṣṇu, the two Daityas,
possessed by rage and possessing massive bodies, [uttered] harsh and ear-piercing insults.
Then, having dismissed the Creator,
those two, deluded by great illusion, rushed toward the omnipresent Lord, itching for battle.
Their battle was great and terrifying to all living beings;
they struck one another with palms and blows of their fists.
Then, O Agastya, they engaged in a hand-to-hand wrestling match in the midst of the waters for five thousand divine years; it was truly hair-raising.
Having fought, Viṣṇu then spoke these words:
"O you two, who are great in battle, by means of your various martial exploits! (66)
"O mighty-armed ones, I am well-pleased; today I shall grant whatever you desire. Considering me as one who grants all things, do you both ask for a boon. (67)
Thinking thus, Madhu and Kaiṭabha said to him:
"O mighty-armed one, how can we two Daityas make a request of you?"
"We two shall grant you a boon; choose one from between us."
[1.68 idem °bāhau] °vāhaḥ B Skanda said:
Having heard these words, Viṣṇu indeed [spoke] for the sake of the origin of all beings.
In the past, for the sake of the world, he requested from those two the boon of their own slaughter.
O heroes, if a boon for the benefit of all the worlds has been granted to me, then grant me this certainly: the death of you two.
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"So be it, O Viṣṇu; let it be exactly as you say.
We are not to be slain in the sky, nor in the water, nor especially on dry land. (71)
Skanda said:
Having thus promised, "So be it," the Blessed One, the creator of all beings,
seized them, placed them upon his thigh, and swiftly struck them with his discus.
Having thus slain those two massive-bodied beings, each extending for many yojanas,
he cut their bodies with his discus and cast their flesh into the water.
[1.73 idem vigrahau] From that, O B, the body (*vigraha*) arose; from that, through the union of flesh, it was flooded with fat.
From that, the earth emerged when ten million divine beings had assembled. 74.
At the end of ten thousand divine years, that earth becomes exceedingly firm and heavy,
strewn with various clays and stones, and its waters and mountains are covered over.
Then she was indeed held up by the Boar, who is perpetually described by the wise as "Sthirā" (the Firm One);
and because of the spreading of his fat upon her, O twice-born one, she further acquired the name "Medinī" (the Fat One). 76.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Puṣkara," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 1 ||
Agastya said:
O Prajāpati, O Six-faced One, how was the earth produced by the Boar of immeasurable luster? That is a great marvel within my mind. (1)
This boar is indeed marvelous; tell me of its origin.
How did the Creator produce the mountains and all living beings within that [earth]? || 2 ||
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
O best of the twice-born, being thus questioned by the pot-born one,
the blessed Skanda explained to him the words concerning that cause.
Beholding that earth, which was very firm, free from depressions and elevations,
extensive, trackless, and rich in soil, that Lord of Creatures rejoiced.
How will creation come about upon this excellent earth without the grace of Maheśa, whose very self is the creation, maintenance, and destruction? (5)
Then Brahmā, the sustainer of the world and benefactor of all the worlds,
offered a hymn of praise to the wielder of the trident for the sake of restoring all the worlds.
Having bowed his head to Rudra, prostrating himself with speech, mind, and body,
he joined his palms above his head and circumambulated him again and again.
Brahmā said:
Oṃ!
Salutations be unto the one whose hair is the sky; salutations indeed unto the one known as Tāraka.
Salutation indeed to the Lord of the Tārakas, who dwells within the Tārakas.
Salutations to the one whose form is bliss, salutations indeed to eternal bliss;
salutations to the one who is perfect bliss, to Nanda, to the stainless one who wields the trident. 9.
Salutations to the one who is worthy of honor, to liberation, and to the auspicious one;
to the proud one, whose form is the heart, the intellect, and the mind; to the supreme, the self beyond all.
Salutations to Śarva, to Bhīma, to Śambhu, and salutations to Sthāṇu;
salutations to Śiva, to Śitikaṇṭha, to Śaṃkara, and to the Great Soul.
Homage to the one whose body is wind; salutations again and again to the five-limbed one.
Homage indeed to Vāmadeva, to the All-pervading, to the one whose form is space. 12.
Salutations to Yoga, to Sacrifice, to the one whose form is sacrifice, to the Yogi;
salutations again and again to the Lord of Yoga, to Yoga itself, and to the Teacher of Yoga. 13.
Salutations to Bhava, to Bhavya, salutations to the Lord of beings;
to the self of all beings, to the pervasive one, to the source of all beings, and to the source of prosperity.
Salutations to the one who has gone beyond, who is the further shore, the supreme, the Supreme Self;
to him who is perceived as both the transcendent and the immanent, and who moves through that which consists of both the transcendent and the immanent.
Salutations to the one who possesses both existent and non-existent aspects; salutations indeed to the one in the form of the *haṃsa*;
salutations again and again to the existent and the non-existent, whose nature is the essence of *saṃsāra*.
Salutations to the subtle, to the equally subtle, and to that which transcends the subtle; salutations indeed to the gross, to the one with gross limbs, and to that which transcends the gross. 17.
Salutation to the one whose nature is light, salutation to the Lord of lights;
salutation again and again to Rudra, the mass of splendor, who is beyond perception. 18.
Homage to the one whose nature is water, to the one whose form is earth, to Vāyu, to Agni, to the one whose form is space, to Sūrya, to the Lotus-born, and to the Self. 19.
Skanda said:
Having heard this great and auspicious hymn uttered by Brahmā,
the all-pervading Lord appeared in the sky with his limbs radiant and blossoming with joy.
He who is the very essence of cyclic existence and the cause of its arising,
being affectionate toward his devotees, proceeded to grant a boon to his devotee.
Jyotirūpeśvara said: O Brahman, having drunk with my ears the nectar of speech produced from the lotus of your mouth, which benefits all the worlds, I am truly satisfied.
O Brahmin, he who recites this is liberated from all sins;
by the recitation of this king of hymns, one shall accomplish everything that is otherwise unattainable. (23)
"Now I shall grant you every unsurpassed boon;
O Creator of the Universe, choose a boon, for my limbs are overwhelmed with the bliss of your praise. (24)
Brahmā said:
O Alakṣa, Lord of all worlds, embodiment of splendor, Great Pervader, Sovereign composed of all splendor, Compassionate toward all beings! 25.
If you are pleased with me, O Lord, for the sake of the continued existence of the world for the virtuous, then,
O Mahādeva, let an incarnation be granted to me as a boon.
"O Lord, having beheld this earth empty of more than ten million beings, I now desire to create the moving and unmoving creatures upon it. (27)
"I entreat you for a boon," he said, "the cause of the creation of the world:
by your grace, I shall create the beings who are to be created. (28)
Jyotirūpa said:
O best of gods, what you say is so;
let all living beings be created by yourself from this day forward.
O Viṣṇu, you shall be for the protection of living beings, both moving and unmoving; you are the destroyer of the wicked who perform evil deeds. 30.
O Creator, I shall become the very form of Time for those of short lifespan;
indeed, from time to time, I shall destroy all those who are sinful.
Skanda said: Having thus obtained the boon, the Creator (Dhātṛ) set his mind upon creating everything for the manifestation of living beings through the grace of the Lord.
Then the Creator, having meditated for a moment, remained silent toward that Imperishable One;
he indeed emitted an egg upon the earth, conjoined with the essence of the primordial waters.
Having held that [universe] for a thousand divine years, the yogi [perceives] the two— the hand and the self—
as indeed the immeasurable great egg, the source of all beings.
It was of an indescribable color, primordial, unmanifest, and the common locus of all;
it was the great cosmic egg, the source of the universe, somewhat elongated and perfectly spherical.
That [world-system], which is many yojanas in extent and many yojanas in circumference,
is submerged within a single pore of his body-hair to that same measure.
He beheld his own form as Brahmā, possessing the luster of molten gold—
the primordial support of the universe and the fundamental cause of the world's womb.
Then, at the end of a thousand yugas, Vidhi split open the upward-facing [aperture] for the sake of creating the worlds, and he split open the downward-facing one again.
Furthermore, he who benefits all beings divided the egg eightfold;
therein, he again made the division of that which is the cause of the world.
That opening above is the ether, the supreme goal of the righteous;
that which is below, which the Source of the Universe created, is Rasātala.
Furthermore, that yogin previously split the cosmic egg— the abode of the virtuous in heaven—
and subsequently created openings on all eight sides.
Furthermore, by his mere will, he likewise created intermediate and all the main directions,
as well as rivers filled with pure water and fashioned from gold and jewels.
By his grace, the clouds became bearers of many colors, possessing whatever various and beautiful hues there might be. 43.
That which was spilled within the middle of the staff became concentrated as a fluid;
it turned into gold and spread everywhere upon the surface of the earth.
O Agastya, the entire earth, which benefits all living beings, was completely covered on all sides by the flood of that ocean of moisture.
When he cast the staff upward with the desire to create the world of the gods,
the moisture that was wet there became the golden mountain.
By that water, indeed, all the cardinal and intermediate directions,
the atmosphere, the celestial vault, and whatever else exists in between were overwhelmed.
Wherever the water fell, there a mountain rose up;
with its many rocky masses, the goddess Earth became uneven.
O Sage, the earth was oppressed by many mountains and waters;
[then there appeared] that divine, golden, and effulgent form whose essence is Nārāyaṇa. 49.
Unable to support the weight, the earth sank down into the netherworld;
oppressed by the waters and the mountains, the distressed earth offered a hymn of praise to the God for her own deliverance. (50)
Medinī said: Salutations to the infallible God, to Viṣṇu of Vaikuṇṭha;
to the manifest one, to him whose form is manifest, and to the one whose majesty is both manifest and unmanifest.
To Viṣvaksena, to Kṛṣṇa, to the four-armed wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
to Nārāyaṇa, to Time (Kāla), to him who reclines upon the serpent Nāga and the Khaṭvāṅga staff.
Salutations again and again to the one with eyes like lotus petals, the enemy of the Daityas, the possessor of beautiful teeth, the transcendent Lord, and the husband of Śrī. 53.
Salutations again and again to the All, to the one of universal form, to the one of manifold forms, to the embodied one; to the one of uniform form, to the multiformed, and to the formless. 54.
Salutation to you who have one face, two faces, and many faces;
salutation to you who have one tongue, two tongues, and who lie upon the double-tongued serpent.
Salutations indeed to him whose single body has arisen from worldly existence, who is the very form of existence,
the source of the manifestation of all beings, Hari, who is adorned with prosperity.

Salutations again and again to the infinite and the immeasurable, to the master of illusion and the one who has transcended illusion, to the eternal one whose form is impermanent, and to bliss itself. 57.
Salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇa, who arises from Nārā, who is the support of Nārā, who is blissful, who is worshipped by those born from Nārā, and who is the leader. 58.
To the stainless, the peaceful, the non-conceptual, the subtle;
to the indivisible, the unceasing, the eternally blissful, the perpetual. 59.
Salutations to the Fish-form, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, the Dwarf, the Three-Rāmas, to Buddha, and to Kalki. 60.
Skanda said:
O Pot-born One, having heard this hymn—which is a delight to the ears and brings happiness—the radiant Viṣṇu was pleased with the Earth. 61.
Then the omnipresent Lord, the all-pervading one who is full bliss, being gratified by her hymns of praise,
manifested himself in his great power to grant her the boon she desired.
Viṣṇu said:
"Choose a boon, O auspicious lady, that brings benefit to the worlds;
today I shall grant whatever desire resides in your heart. (63)
Medinī said: "O Lord, if you grant me a boon first, let this one be chosen:
that all things, both moving and unmoving, may be supported by you. (64)
Without your boon being maintained, I shall undoubtedly be tormented;
yet, endowed with your power, I am capable of surpassing all things moving and unmoving. 65.
"O Lord, let the boon of lordship over the gods be granted to me;
O Protector, now further ripen for me the fruit of this hymn. (66)
Viṣṇu said:
"So be it, O Goddess Earth; let that which you desire be exactly so.
Let no mortal die before his time, and let him not be overcome by calamities. (67)
May he possess sons and power, and likewise may he not be tainted by sins;
through the recitation of this praise of the Earth, may his enemies go to their destruction. 68.
Skanda said:
Having thus granted that boon to the Earth, the Great Lord [adorned it] with meters,
syllables, mantras, and the Vedas.
Assuming the body of a boar, the all-pervading and mighty Lord raised up with his tusk the Earth, which was submerged in the ocean, she who consists of all sacrifices.
O Sage, even today the Boar sustained the earth, together with its oceans and mountains and all that is mobile and immobile,
upon his tusk.
Agastya said:
"O commander of the army, you have described to me that boar as being the form of the sacrifice;
now tell me, what is the measure of his body and what is his color? (72)
Skanda said:
He assumed the form of a boar, which brings fear to all the Daityas;
it is purified by thirty-five million hair-pores, which are themselves sacred pilgrimage sites.
That great-bodied Varāha, of divine form and praised by the Vedas, was ten million yojanas in width and twice that in height.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with a roar like the thundering of destruction,
he possessed white, blazing, and formidable fangs, and his body was like a mountain.
His eyes were as bright as lightning-fire, and his radiance was like the splendor of the sun;
he had thick, rounded, and long shoulders, and possessed the prowess of eight tigers.
His waist-region was thick and elevated; he was marked with the characteristics of a bull;
his roar was the Veda; his tusks were the sacrificial posts (yūpa); his hands were the sacrifices (kratu); and his mouth was the sacrificial altars (citī).
Fire-tongued, with Darbha grass for hair, having Brahman for his head, and possessed of great ascetic power;
having day and night for his eyes, he is eternally adorned by the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
With clarified butter for his nose and the sacrificial ladle for his snout, he possessed a great voice like the sound of Sāman chants;
he was composed of truth and righteousness, manifest as the very embodiment of true valor and honored by the virtuous;
with shadow-like power, he was a great yogi, towering like a mountain of gold.
Thus, assuming the body of a boar composed of sacrifice,
the omnipresent Lord entered the netherworld (rasātala) in order to lift up the heavy earth.
With his tusk, the one of great strength raised up the earth, which had been submerged in the waters and gone to the depths of the netherworld, as it rested upon the ocean.
Even today, the conqueror of the universe continues to hold the world, with its oceans, mountains, and all things mobile and immobile, upon his tusk for the welfare of the world. 82.
The great lord set his mind upon the differentiation of the earth;
then, O Agastya, he commanded Brahmā for the sake of its creation.
O Brahmin, in that [kalpa], the Creator constantly created all living beings through the five elements;
know that there were many hundreds of thousands of them, which became exceedingly subject to the power of illusion (māyā). 84.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Rescuing of the Earth," in the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 2 ||
Skanda said:
O Pot-born one, upon that [earth] Dhātṛ fashioned the seven continents:
Jambūdvīpa, then Plakṣa, Śālmalika, and likewise Kuśa.
The Lord further created Krauñcadvīpa, Śākadvīpa, and Puṣkaradvīpa;
then, in due order, he created Jambūdvīpa in the center of them all.
Extending fifty crores of yojanas and nine in between, this is the measure of Jambūdvīpa; I shall tell you more about them.
O Pot-born One, the Ocean of Salt Water is known to be twice the size of Jambūdvīpa;
Plakṣadvīpa is twice the size of the Salt Ocean, and likewise, Śālmalidvīpa is twice the size of Plakṣadvīpa.
Beyond that is the Ikṣu ocean, twice as large; likewise, the Śālmalī ocean is twice as large as that;
the Surā ocean is twice as large as the Śālmalī; and the Kuśa ocean is twice as large as the Surā.
Twice that amount of Kuśa grass is excellent; twice that, O Sage, is the measure for ghee;
twice that is known to be for Krauñca grass, and likewise twice that is for curd.
The Śāka continent is twice the size of Jambūdvīpa, and its milk-ocean is twice the size of that;
each subsequent continent and ocean among all the continents and oceans is double the size of the preceding one.
The extent and breadth should be known as comprising the seven islands and the lord of rivers;
in the midst of these islands, Jambūdvīpa shines forth, presided over by Agastya.
In the center of Jambūdvīpa, within a beautiful and square region,
the Soul of the Universe created Meru, the most excellent among all mountains.
The mountain is made of Jāmbūnada gold, supreme and consisting of all splendor;
it resembles ten thousand suns and is a form of light day and night.
O Sage, Mount Meru is eighty-four lakhs of yojanas in height and its width at the base is likewise the same.
And by means of which Meru was separated, with its four peaks and its vast extent, numbering sixteen hundred thousand yojanas.
Furthermore, the Creator fashioned similar ridges separately in the intermediate directions,
each measuring five hundred thousand yojanas in extent.
The eastern peak is golden, the southern peak is made of iron,
the western peak is silver, and the northern peak is likewise of copper.
The Creator fashioned one horn made of coral, another made of gems,
one of gold, and one of crystal in those intermediate directions.
The station of Mahendra is in the east, that of Śamana (Yama) in the south;
the station of Varuṇa is to be known in the west, and that of Dhanada (Kubera) in the north.
O Pot-born one, you should know that the respective abodes of the gods Vahni, Karbura, and Vāyu are located in the intermediate directions (vidiś) in their proper order. 17.
It was endowed with ten million peaks, intensely radiant with the falls of the Gaṅgā,
and it contained that fourteenth world, the abode of the gods.
It was supremely resplendent with a thousand peaks made of Jāmbūnada gold,
with peaks made of sapphire, and summits made of lapis lazuli.
[It was] with stones produced from emerald, those arising from moonstone,
those consisting of sunstone, and likewise those consisting of silver-gem.
It was adorned with divine crests made of topaz, produced from blue collyrium,
and with celestial crystals and jewels.
With peaks composed of the five precious gems and, in some places, consisting of many jewels;
with the radiant splendor of various medicinal herbs, arising from the essence of light itself.
Adorned with pearls, produced from coral sprouts,
and originating from the glorious *vajra* stone— resplendent and composed of every kind of gem.
It was endowed with a thousand peaks, featuring pavements of various jewels,
inlaid with perfected elixirs, and adorned with golden trees.
[The trees] were joined with golden canes, produced from golden lotuses,
grown from wish-fulfilling jewel-trees, and radiant with golden flowers.
It was adorned with golden rocks and caves,
with bowers filled with various flowers, and with trees that bear fruit in all seasons.
With houses made of Jāmbūnada gold, adorned with various jewels, covered in gold, brilliant, and provided with vajra-ornamented domes; || 27 ||
With ponds filled with nectar-like water, with beautiful conduits, and adorned with many variegated banners and the splendor of flagstaffs; || 28 ||
Indeed, that lord of mountains shines with four falls of the Gaṅgā, which are like beautiful waterfalls flowing from the peaks in the four directions and are utterly pure.
O Noble One, it was honored by the water arising from the eastern peak, which, falling with great speed and possessing a reddish hue, resembled a banner.
By the water falling with great speed from the peak of Yama’s mountain—
dark as collyrium— it was made beautiful, as if by a banner.
It was thus adorned by a very swift waterfall originating from a peak facing west,
with water possessing the luster of silver, appearing like a fluttering banner.
It was beautiful with the very swift waterfall originating from the northern peak,
appearing like a banner with the water of the Hiraṇyābhā.
The king of mountains shone with millions of streams of water, waterfalls, and cascades,
serving as a gathering place for all splendors.
By the river Jāmbūnadajā, which possesses whirlpools, [the city] Mahodayā is well-enclosed on all four sides by inexhaustible [waters]. 35.
In its interior, it is surrounded by other mountains composed of all kinds of minerals;
thus, O Agastya, has this mountain, the refuge of all the gods, been described.
"I shall tell you further; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Then, having gone toward the eastern direction, he created the Mountain of Sunrise."
It is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent and half that in height;
it is named Ṛṣabha, celebrated by Brahmā, and difficult to find upon the earth.
Abounding with trees of gold and silver, adorned with flowers and jewels,
it was a hundred yojanas in extent and a hundred yojanas in height.
O Sage, that Creator further adorned it with peaks made of gold and with mountain ridges abounding in many precious gems and stones.
Then [he saw] Mahendra, the lord of mountains, rising a hundred yojanas high,
with peaks made of gold that resembled the rising sun.
That great mountain shone, adorned with all kinds of minerals,
endowed with every tree and creeper, and beautified by all manner of flowers.

The Grandfather (Pitāmaha) also created there many mountains endowed with fruits of manifold flavors and inhabited by three kinds of creatures— mountains possessing peaks, containing mineral ores, and many with wings. 43.

[3.43 Just as there are mountains rich in minerals,] from the mountain clefts and slopes there arise rivers that serve as means for ascent to heaven and bestow the fruit of the desire for liberation. 44.
Having gone to the southern direction, Dhātṛ created the Vindhya mountain,
which was covered with various trees and creepers and possessed thousands of divine peaks.
Having arrived at that southern region, he created many mountains,
filled with various trees and creepers and adorned with many minerals.
And the Self-born one again created Malaya, the best of mountains,
which is always honored by rays resembling Mount Meru in form.
It was strewn with various jewels, filled with various trees,
abounding in the great splendor of divine fragrances, and possessed celestial sandalwood trees.
That supreme mountain was one thousand yojanas in length and half that in height;
it was adorned with mines of gold and silver and with jewels.
And he created many rivers of three kinds— vast, winding, and adorned with sandbanks and trees, as well as those filled with cane thickets and trees.
Furthermore, the Sānuśikhara-born Dhātā and Vaitaraṇī likewise arise there; various sacred fords (tīrthas) and diverse confluences are produced.
Having gone to the western direction, that Blessed One, the creator of beings,
created a beautiful mountain resplendent with half-gold.
One half was like the sun and the other like the moon;
it was simultaneously pervaded by two splendors, as if by those of the sun and the moon.
That best of mountains was possessed of peaks, adorned with horses, and exceedingly beautiful;
it extended for many yojanas and rose up a hundred yojanas high.
It was filled with divine trees that yield all desired fruits and are enchanting to the mind;
the entire house was made of gold, and it was surrounded on all sides by golden pedestals.
[He saw] the great mountain named Ṛṣabha, lofty and towering, rich with trees of gold and silver, and abounding in the smiles of flowers. 56.
Beyond that is Mount Mahendra, rising a hundred yojanas high,
endowed with peaks formed of gold and filled with many minerals.
Agastya made the earth as immovable as a mountain against the agitation of the subjects;
it was filled with various trees and creepers and adorned with every kind of flower.
Then he created the lord of mountains, resplendent with all splendors, endowed with minerals and rocks, and filled with many trees and creepers. (59)
It was adorned with great peaks and trees made of gold,
and with waterfalls cascading from its ridges that were beautified by many flowers.
He created Gandhamādana, which was produced from all medicinal herbs and was radiant with the splendors of those herbs and minerals.
In the west, he established sixty thousand mountains,
covered with trees that produced every kind of fruit and were unsurpassed by any flowers.
From them flowed forth navigable rivers that were indeed boundless— purifying streams that grant all desires and are joined by many confluences, O Agastya.
Having gone to the northern direction, the Creator [beheld] the most beautiful Ratnakūṭa,
endowed with many minerals and resplendent with lapis lazuli gems.
With peaks possessing the luster of gold, rich with golden trees and creepers, and with waterfalls from which flows the essence of Jāmbūnada gold; 65.
He created an excellent mountain endowed with houses of gold and silver, possessed of caves and peaks, and enriched with the splendor of various jewels.
It was a hundred yojanas in width and a hundred yojanas in height;
it was a station in the heavens that brought joy to all living beings.
And he performed austerities at Mandara, which consists of golden and silver rocks,
is endowed with many minerals, and is filled with great splendor.
Citrasānu, Susānu, and likewise Bahusānu;
Maṇisānu, Taḍidvat, and Jyotiṣsānu, the best of mountains.
It was produced from flowers, fruits, and creepers, covered with golden vines,
endowed with many trees and medicinal herbs, and adorned with all kinds of jewels.
It was twenty yojanas in width and ten yojanas in height;
likewise, it was forty, thirty, and another fifty [yojanas]. 71.
And for some, the width and height are sixty, seventy, eighty, and ninety yojanas respectively.
Likewise, he created many mountains adorned with all kinds of trees,
endowed with various mines, and produced from many different minerals.
From them flowed forth excellent rivers, radiant with golden sands,
possessing bending leaves like golden canes, and adorned with golden flowers.
The rivers have golden stones for waves and are joined with golden waters; they possess many confluences, are purifying, and are filled with great whirlpools.
Then the Creator, having gone further toward the northern quarter, fashioned mountains once again;
thus, in those wildernesses, the knower of rites established the boundary-mountains by the grace of Giriśa.
On the northern side of Meru, he created that mountain of gold,
extending for many yojanas and rising a hundred yojanas high.
It was endowed with many elements, consisting of many jewels,
abounding in blossoming golden flowers, and crowded with golden trees.
It was rich with blossoming golden lotuses, resplendent with groves made of gold, adorned with golden peaks, and endowed with mountain caves. 79.
And with conduits, ponds, and delightful ridges, with divine streams of alchemical elixirs, and with golden waterfalls; 80.
There, O Sage, having installed his own portion as Heramba with great ceremony,
the Creator, having thus performed his duty, proceeded toward the eastern direction.
Having gone to the eastern direction, the Creator fashioned an excellent mountain with variegated peaks,
further constructed from all-surpassing heights.
[It was] composed of various elements, produced from much red chalk,
endowed with all kinds of jewels, and possessing all forms of splendor.
It was adorned with lakes produced from much gold, beautified by many flowers,
and strewn with red lotuses.
It was adorned with ridges joined by beautiful altars,
and made delightful by yellow orpiment, beautiful minerals, and charming red arsenic.
It was joined with red trees and produced from red cane-creepers;
it was a mountain consisting of red splendor, with waterfalls of reddish-hued liquid.
Extending for many yojanas and rising a hundred yojanas high,
it was inaccessible to all beings, composed of every essence, and auspicious.
The Noble Lady, having arrived at the king of mountains,
joyfully entered it together with sixty-four groups and ten million yoginīs.
Having fashioned Citrasānu, the Creator, the Ordainer and sustainer of the worlds, went toward the southern direction once again in order to create another mountain. || 89 ||
Then Brahmā, having arrived there,
created the supreme mountain Kailāsa, which possessed massive peaks, was composed of all splendor, and was auspicious.
The mountain shone with a silver luster, abounding in various minerals and splendid stones,
and was adorned with great trees that possessed a silvery brilliance.
It was resplendent with auspicious ridges, with canes growing from silver,
with rows of silver-grown reeds, and likewise with silver flowers.
With lakes filled with water possessing the luster of silver, produced from royal sources, and with groves of white blossoms formed by silver-grown creepers; 93.
With auspicious streams produced from silver-like water, consisting entirely of splendor,
and with the falling of torrents of the Gaṅgā that had become like silver-colored earth.
It was endowed with delightful fruits of various flavors produced in all six seasons,
possessed the three qualities of wind, and was compassionate toward all living beings.
Extending for many yojanas and rising a hundred yojanas high,
it had chambers made of silver and copper, was rich in caves, and was filled with jewels.
He placed the Pārijāta tree, which was born from the essence of Jāmbūnada gold and brings happiness, upon the summit of the great mountain; it was a smile of flowers. || 97 ||
One yojana in width and one yojana in height,
it is endowed with the essence of the juices of accomplishment and bestows the fruits desired by the mind.
Abounding in crystal, with great splendor, made of jewels, and enchanting; eternally blissful, a great mountain that captivates all splendors. 99.
The adorable god Śaṅkara, the Lord, established himself continuously upon the king of mountains together with his sixty-four attendants. 100.
Having likewise fashioned Trikūṭa, which resembled a heap of crushed collyrium,
the Creator then proceeded toward the southern direction as he pleased.
Then, having meditated upon Maheśāna, the great lord of all the gods,
he who was skilled in ritual procedure acted toward Himavān, the lord of mountains.
The wondrous mountain Himavat, possessing a thousand peaks, most exalted, abundant, and beautiful, shines forth with an essence that surpasses all others. 103.
Having quickly and joyfully created dharma in the form of snow, the Creator adorned that mountain with those snowy forms of dharma. 104.
The great-peaked Mahāśṛṅga is a sacred place, the most excellent among all mountains;
it has the luster of silver, possesses various forms, touches the clouds, and is the lord of the gods.
It is attended by thousands of peaks composed of various jewels,
and it shines brilliantly with peaks adorned with snow that resemble silver.
It is endowed with thousands of holy pilgrimage sites, with millions of excellent waterfalls,
and with thousands of peaks joined by thousands of mountain ridges.
In some places it shone, rich with corals, adorned with peaks formed of gold, produced from lapis lazuli gems, and born of coral sprouts.
It was rich with crystal peaks that were exceedingly pure,
made of topaz in some places and composed of sapphires in others.
In some places with peaks made of diamond, and likewise of moonstone, of sunstone, and of divine substances resembling heaps of blue collyrium; 110.
With great horns made of copper, as well as others made of iron, with horns made of tin and lead, and likewise those composed of many minerals; 111.
With peaks composed of yellow orpiment, enchanting with realgar,
and formed from red chalk, they were as dark as mountains of collyrium.
The ornament of mountains is eternally adorned with various ridges,
and with most beautiful, elevated pavements made of refined gold.
[The city] was resplendent with moon-chambers (candraśālā) made of silver and gold, shining with great brilliance,
and adorned with moon-chambers rich in highly radiant diamonds.
Adorned with moon-chambers fashioned from lapis lazuli, and made beautiful by radiant pavements produced from sapphire; 115.
With courtyards made of emerald that possessed a white luster, and with moon-chambers constructed of emerald that shone with a green radiance; 116.
With the dark luster of pavements fashioned from blocks of blue collyrium stone, and radiant with white moon-chambers constructed from moonstones; 117.
With floors made of sun-stones (sūryakānta) that emitted red luster, and with moon-chambers (candraśālā) constructed of crystal stones that radiated white light; 118.
With floors made of ruby that were beautiful in their crimson splendor, and with moon-chambers of exquisite construction rich in coral, glowing with a reddish luster; 119.
Thus did he behold the Himalaya, resplendent with great peaks that shone with paved courtyards fashioned from various jewels and were radiant with many-colored minerals.
With trees made of Jāmbūnada gold, with trees produced from silver, with trees produced from tin and lead, and with branches originating from silver; 121.
With creepers arising from gold, with those produced from pure silver, with excellent golden flowers, and with blossoms born of many colors; 122.
With groves arising in great abundance and with such sprouts of darbha grass, as well as divine golden lotuses and silver-grown lilies; 123.
With various ponds, excavated pools, caves, and mountain clefts;
with precipices, waterfalls, peaks, and most wonderful boulders.
O Sage, the king of mountains then shone with its many-named peaks,
its precipices from which sages leapt, its rivers, and its numerous sacred bathing places.
Furthermore, by means of Kedāra, Badrikāśrama, Triśīrṣa, Śikhara, as well as Viṣṇvāśrama, Mahākūṭa, and the peak of Kūrmādri; 126.
With the peaks of the silver mountain, Jambū-dri, and Brahma-śikhara;
likewise with the peaks of Agni-śṛṅga, Eka-śṛṅga, and the Umā mountain.
Wherever the Blessed One’s Dharma has become fluid by means of its cause, even such unrighteousness (adharma) is likewise [overcome] by the ford of Dharma; what then [remains]? 128.
With clouds licking the peaks of the Dharmakūṭa mountain, with the excellent cities of the Siddhas' hermitages, and likewise with the dark summits of the Gaṇḍa, Mukti, and Pāṇḍu mountains; 129.
Furthermore, with the peaks of Mount Vṛtta, Āhārya, Triśūla, Adrimuñja, and Uñjava, as well as the excellent summits of Mount Buddhaśrama, Mount Viṣṇu, and Mount Gaurī; 130.
With the excellent peaks of Mount Kuśa, Mount Parvataka, Mount Kāmādri, and Mount Nīla; with Mount Agniśekhara, Mount Bhasmādri, Mount Kāmādri, and Mount Sundarādri.
Having beheld Himālaya, the king of mountains, shining with these primary causes, Acyuta looked toward the eastern and southern peaks.
Viṣṇu, together with the hosts of Badarikāśrama, established his joy upon that mountain which was ten million yojanas in extent and one hundred thousand yojanas in height.
It pervades the eastern and western oceans, and likewise extends beneath them;
it is joined with ten million peaks and honored by hundreds of millions upon millions.
The Himalaya mountain shines with its millions of sons who are worthy recipients,
resembling Mount Meru and adorned with its snowy ornaments.
As many as there are rivers that flow forth, so many are the purifiers of all worlds that grant desires incessantly and indeed liberate one from sins. 136.
By the flow of the Brahmaputra, by the Gaṅgā of the Himalayas, by the Bhadrā, the Alakanandā, the Revā, and the Śatarudrī; 137.
The wise Himavat shines perpetually with the Kauśikī, Gaṇḍakī, and Vāgmatī rivers, as well as the Śiprā, Vāta, and others. || 138 ||
Having fashioned various winged mountains that moved like arrows,
the Creator again created many sacred lands.
Then Brahmā, whose nature is the welfare of all worlds, set his mind upon creating living beings in the netherworld for the stability of all creatures.

Then, desiring to see the mountains whose power was haughty for the sake of obstructing mortals, Śakra cut off their wings with his thunderbolt; they had long since attained the state of being immobile.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Origin of All Mountains," in the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 3 ||
Skanda said:
Then the righteous Dhātṛ, having meditated for a moment upon the three-eyed, all-pervading Lord Śaṅkara,
the source of all beings, offered him praise.
Placing his joined palms upon his head in salutation, the venerable Lord bowed down.
Brahmā said:
Oṃ!
Salutations be to the God of gods, the source of all beings, the progenitor of existence.
Salutation to the source of all beings, to that which is yet to be, and to the Lord of all beings. || 2 ||
To the Great Lord, whose nature is the creation and maintenance of the universe, who is omniscient, discerning, the soul of the universe, and whose form pervades all things. || 3 ||
To the one who is indefinable, partless, changeless, and blissful;
to the immeasurable, the measure itself, who is accessible yet possesses a body that is inaccessible.
Salutations to the one who maintains honor and dishonor, to the illusory and the non-illusory;
to the essence, to the god of autumn, and to the self that has destroyed the cycle of worldly existence.
To the one who is unperceivable, whose limbs are imperishable, whose form is the moment, and who wields the trident;
to the life-force born from within, who dwells within, and who is eternal.
Salutations again and again to the one whose form is splendor, to the burner, to the three-eyed one;
salutations to the giver of boons, the creator of the world, and the eye of the worlds. 7.

Salutation to the Lord who arises from the fivefold nature, to the one whose glory consists of the fivefold nature; to the one who abides in the elements, to the Ordainer, to the fashioner of the entire world; to Rudra, the giver of worldly existence, who has the form of worldly existence. 8.
Skanda said:
Having heard this hymn of praise, the all-pervading Lord in the form of light was well-pleased and proceeded to grant a boon to the Creator.
Having manifested his own self, the all-pervading Lord, composed of all splendor, joyfully illuminated the cardinal and intermediate directions with his own radiance. 10.
Jyotirūpa said:
"O noble one, I am pleased with your hymn of praise which benefits all living beings.
O Lord of the World, choose a boon—whatever you desire at this time. (11)
"O Creator, knowing me to be the granter of desires for the benefit of all living beings, I shall give you all this, consisting of both the moving and the unmoving. (12)
Whoever in this world recites this hymn that has issued from your mouth shall be liberated from all sins and obtain the fruit of all desires.
Brahmā said:
"O God, by your grace I have fashioned the mountains that support the earth;
now, O Śaṅkara, I desire to create all living beings."
The entire world has become blinded; how shall living beings survive?
O Lord, if you have love for me, you must illuminate it with your equal light. 15.
Skanda said:
Having heard these words of the Creator, which were intended for the benefit of the worlds,
that god then reflected for a moment, O Pot-born One.
Then, taking a portion from the eye of Dakṣa with his hand,
the omnipresent Lord first created in ancient times a god who was the form of light and possessed great power.
The primordial, eternal God, whose form is splendor, who is the eye of the world, immeasurable, beyond the reach of the senses, the witness of the universe, and rich in radiance.
Two cubits in height, joined with a lotus, having one face and sharp rays, three-eyed, with a red body, and saluted by all the gods. 19.
Furthermore, the Lord of Beings, the Imperishable Master of Creatures, having taken a portion of the Left Eye, created [him] who is devoted to the welfare of all the worlds. 20.
He who is the delighter, possessed of great luster, the moon, cool yet invincible,
of divine form, of great majesty, and whose very nature is the support of all.
And Soma, with a gentle form, the luster of silver, a beautiful body, three eyes, two arms, peaceful, solitary, and beneficent. 22.
The radiant one again created a god composed of all splendor,
taking hold of him by his upward-turned eye with his divine hand.
He had seven faces, was exceedingly fierce, possessed an Aurva-like body,
was endowed with twenty-one eyes, and likewise had fourteen arms.
Having united the three gods, O lord of brahmins, Rudra then spoke these words to the Grandfather regarding the cause of his manifestation.
Īśvara said: "Hari is to be known as my form, and likewise I am the form of Viṣṇu;
O Brahman, Hari is your form, and you are the form of Viṣṇu, who is the Self."
My form is you, and likewise, my form is you; yet again, I am your form.
Therefore, there is no difference between us; I tell you this truth, the absolute truth.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, our forms are the deities of the sun, moon, fire, and water; the goddesses of earth, space, and wind; and likewise the sacrificer.
"O wise one, I have given you this command: you must not create any distinction between yourself and my forms, nor between them and all beings, by means of your entire being and prosperity. (29)
Skanda said:
Having thus manifested himself and addressed the Grandfather (Brahmā),
the Lord, illuminating the quarters with his splendors, departed for Kailāsa.
Having heard these words of Rudra, the Supreme Soul,
the Grandfather (Brahmā) then once again offered praise to Agastya.
Brahmā said:
Oṃ!
To Śiva who has the form of Viṣṇu, and to Viṣṇu who has the form of Śiva.
Homage to the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, the source of prosperity! 32.
Salutations to the one whose forehead is marked by the moon; salutations to the one who adorns himself with a tilaka mark;
to the three-eyed and the two-eyed; to the two-armed and the many-armed.
Homage to the one whose neck is like that of the lord of serpents; homage to the one whose neck bears the Kaustubha gem;
to the one who shines with the application of ashes as unguent; to the one who is fond of the application of camphor as unguent.
Salutations to Bharga, who wears tiger-skins; to Viṣṇu, who wears yellow garments;
to the unborn one who dwells on Kailāsa; salutations to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha.
To him who possesses various bodily forms, who assumes manifold bodies, who is beyond time, who is Time itself, who is the beloved of Kāma, and who is Śauri; 36.
Salutations to the Noble Lord of All, and salutations to the Sustainer of the Universe;
O Vāmadeva, homage to you; O Vāsudeva, let there be salutation to you. 37.
To Śiva, who is the form of water; to Viṣṇu, who is the form of the earth;
to Rudra, who is the form of space; and to Hari, whose form is wind. || 38 ||
Salutations to Īśa in the form of the Sun, to Kṛṣṇa in the form of the Moon, to Ugra in the form of the Sacrifice, and to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow in the form of Fire. || 39 ||
Salutations to Bhava, to the Mantra, and salutations again and again to the Vedāṅga;
salutations indeed to him who is the very form of the sacrificer and the form of the sacrificial ladle.
Salutations to the one whose essence is clarified butter, to the Unborn; salutations to the one whose nature is the sacrificial oblation;
salutations to the enjoyer and the enjoyed, to bliss, to eternal joy. 41.
Salutations indeed to the one who is satisfaction for the sake of satisfaction, who is the form of contentment;
salutations again and again to Rudra, the Lord of living beings, who is pure consciousness. 42.
Skanda said: Having heard this divine hymn consisting of both Hari and Hara, Viṣṇu, who was born from Brahmā, then became greatly delighted with that Brahmā. 43.
Then, O Sage, having manifested a physical body in order to grant a boon, Hari was pleased with him and spoke these words.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Brahmin, I am pleased by these hymns of praise issued from your mouth.
I shall now grant you a boon; listen to me with a concentrated mind. (45)

[4.45 idem viniḥsṛtaiḥ] O Grandfather, O many-eyed one, when those who have emerged from you by their own will create all the worlds in the netherworld (rasātala), I too shall create them along with you.
O Brahmin, whichever mortal shall recite this hymn consisting of Hari and Hara, which is dear to us, shall be liberated from all sins. 47.
Having obtained wealth, grain, fame, and long life, and being freed from affliction, may he quickly accomplish what is difficult to achieve and crush all his enemies. 48.
Having become a Brahmin learned in the Vedas and having enjoyed pleasures as he desired,
he attains the fruit of the four aims of life and, at the end, shall be dissolved into me.
Skanda said:
Then, having heard the words spoken by Viṣṇu, the Creator (Brahmā) considered himself the doer; his hair stood on end and he was filled with joy.
Then the Soul of All emitted the supreme single syllable "Om";
from that the vowels were produced, and after that the prosodic measures and the consonants. 51.
The Great Goddess, consisting of the twenty-four syllables of the Vyāhṛtis, gives birth to that divine state endowed with four feet. 52.
From that, the primordial sounds (nādas), the meters (chandās), and the exclamation vaṣaṭ are produced;
likewise, the Ṛg, Sāman, Atharva, and Yajus Vedas, as well as the sacred scriptures (śruti), come into being. 53.
O Sage, in ancient times, Nārāyaṇa, whose essence is Nara, created the divine sages by his mere will for the sake of maintaining the order of the world. (54)
The Blessed One Sanat, the primordial Sanaka, the all-pervading Mahāvibhu, Sanātana the soul of the universe, and Sanandaka the bestower of boons; || 55 ||
Sanatkumāra, the noble Brahmā, and likewise Kapila—
these are the primordial yogins, born from the mind of Viṣṇu.
These sages, established in righteousness and observance of vows, are teachers of dharma;
for these lords of yoga sustain the entire universe, both moving and unmoving.
Then, O Agastya, Brahmā first created the seven sages, the best of the twice-born,
by his mind alone for the sake of the origin of all beings.
O sage, [he created] Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Bhṛgu, and likewise Aṅgiras— these foremost of sages.
Jaigīṣavya, Manu, Asita, and likewise Devala, as well as the ancestors of all beings—including men, gods, asuras, and rakshasas. (60)
And from those seven sages were indeed born all beings, both moving and stationary:
the gods, asuras, along with gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
The Kinnaras, Guhyakas, Vidyādharas, hosts of Apsarases,
Sādhyas, Anilas, and Piśācas— these, O Agastya, are born from the gods.
Agastya said: O omniscient one, how does the birth of embodied beings— of all creatures whose bodies are the essence of worldly existence— come to be without [the prior existence of] Śakti?
"The universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, is said to consist of Śiva and Śakti;
thus a doubt has arisen in us, and great wonder would be felt in this regard. (64)
Skanda said: "The beneficial conduct of the gods regarding their maintenance, origin, and destruction must not be doubted, especially since it is extraordinary."
I shall recount the deeds of the God, which are praised by Brahmā and the Vedas for their benefit to all living beings; listen to me as I speak them.
At the end of the kalpa of Brahmā, when the enemies of the gods were utterly destroyed,
Hari meditated upon the supreme Śiva for the sake of creating the world once more.
Formerly, as Viṣṇu was contemplating creation, a person emerged from his mouth; indeed, that portion of a god stood before him and asked, "What shall I do? (68)
Having said, "Unite with yourself," Acyuta vanished;
thereafter, that Puruṣa meditated upon the embodied beings to be created. 69.
Then, O Agastya, from that man who was thus absorbed in meditation, water was produced; and from that water, the earth was produced once again.
From that, the mountains were born, and likewise the medicinal herbs;
the moon was born from his mind, and from his eyes the sun was produced.
From his two ears he generated wind, and from his mouth fire was born;
from his two nostrils space was born, and his head became the imperishable heaven.
O Pot-born One, from the big toe of the Unborn One's right foot, the ten directions and the Prajāpati named Dakṣa were indeed born.
From the left thumb of his hand, Dākṣāyaṇī was born;
know her to be the wife of Dakṣa, and from her were born daughters. (74)
From his head indeed came the Brāhmaṇas, from his two arms the Kṣatriyas,
from his two thighs the Vaiśyas, and likewise from his two feet the Śūdras.
All clays from rivers and other sources become pure upon the earth; likewise, all their waters are undoubtedly sacred fords (tīrthas). 76.
Then, O wise one, Dākṣāyaṇī gave birth to sixty daughters;
she gave ten to Dharma and thirteen to Kaśyapa. (77)
Dakṣa gave twenty-seven daughters to Soma and thirteen to Manu;
he gave Satī alone to the high-souled Śaṅkara.
Indeed, from his wife Aditi, the gods were born to Kaśyapa;
these included Indra, Upendra, and other deities by the thousands of millions upon millions.
And from the second wife of the high-souled Kaśyapa,
Diti, were born the Daityas, who were great heroes and possessed of great strength.
Hiraṇyakaśipu by name, and likewise Hiraṇyākṣa; Śumbha and Niśumbha, and the great asura Andhaka. 81.
O one of great wisdom, from these gods and daityas were born sons of intense prowess, numbering in the tens of millions of millions of suras and asuras.
And at the end of time, there was a great mutual conflict between the gods and the asuras, as they fiercely sought victory over one another.
O twice-born one, from that time forward, due to the curse of the noble Durvāsas, there arose hostility among them because of their offenses. 84.

On the Himavat, the excellent mountain that grants desired objects, those gods and daityas who have obtained incomparable fruits through the grace of the God of Gods shall attain worlds of extreme beauty, O best of the twice-born; for this creation has been described by me out of affection for you. 85.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Creation of the World," in the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 4 ||
Agastya said:
What is the measurement of the netherworlds (pātālas), and how was the Golden Mountain (Sumeru) supported? Who among the seven are powerful, and who are their inhabitants and sustainers? || 1 ||
By what boon was Himavat, the lord of mountains, gratified?
How was the maiden married, and whose daughter was she? Tell me, O Lord. (2)
Skanda said:
Listen, for I shall relate to you in its entirety everything that was told to me by the Lord of the City on this supreme mountain composed of jewels. 3.
He assumed a tortoise-like body, ten million yojanas in width and half that in height,
covered with skin and bone.
O Pot-born One, upon him stands that Great Boar with his massive body,
for the support of the fourteen worlds.
Upon its back, on a great, brilliant, and radiant lotus measuring ten million yojanas across,
complete with filaments and a shining pericarp, [he sat].
O Sage, the Self-born Lord established Mount Meru, extending as far as the world of Brahmā,
together with the elephants of the quarters and measuring thousands of yojanas.
Furthermore, it was immensely radiant, supporting fourteen worlds in the four directions in succession, each measuring four of those same units.
Situated in their midst is Jambūdvīpa, together with its mountains, firmly established; its measurement has been stated previously, and now I shall declare that of the remaining continents.
And at the edge of the continent, situated below and adorned with the circular form of the remaining serpent,
is the seventh region named Pātāla, which exists eternally.
Shaped like a lotus with its filaments, blazing with the great splendor of jewels in the darkness,
it stood beautifully pervading the four directions upon the jeweled peak.
The extent of Pātāla is fifty crores of yojanas,
and its height is one million [yojanas].
There, the lord of the Nāgas, Vāsuki, dwelling eternally with his attendants and worshipping Maheśāna, shines forth incessantly.
With his white body, he shines eternally, his noble neck adorned with strings of excellent jewels;
he is Vāsuki, the lord of serpents, enriched by a thousand hoods, his lotus-like hand intent upon the worship of Śiva.

The Lord of Serpents, ring-shaped, supports the earth from its very edge with his thousand hoods, which possess flickering tongues and sharp fangs; his head rises up, heaving with the weight of great merit and sin.
And while supporting the entire earth, he shines resplendent in the midst of the assembly;
yet when men do not honor the gods, the twice-born, and the cows. (16)
The earth becomes heavy and exceedingly burdened by sin;
oppressed by that weight, Vāsuki sighs deeply,
and from his sighing, an earthquake occurs along with the mountains.
At that time, a trembling of men portends a short life;
conversely, if mortals feel no such trembling, they will undoubtedly be long-lived. 18.
And there the lord of the Daityas, the exceedingly powerful Vairocana,
shines eternally together with Viṣṇu and the Dānavas.
The powerful one seizes all that which is given by men to the ancestors at a śrāddha through defects in the Brahmins, defects in speech, or due to impurity. || 20 ||
And having obtained the most excellent boon from Śaṅkara’s grace on the Himavat mountain, he worshipped Mahādeva with joy.
Beyond that, O Sage, is the region named Rasātala, whose ground consists of masses of stone; it is endowed with a white luster due to the rays of its jewels.
That aforementioned extent, in measure, is ten million yojanas;
the expansion of Rasātala is one hundred thousand leagues in height.
And Mahāpadma, the lord of the nāgas, well-served by many nāgas,
dwelt continuously in a palace made of white jewels.
His supreme body possesses the luster of Mount Hemādri, and he is beautiful with the radiant splendor of his necklace;
his head is marked with a trident, a lotus, and a conch, and he shines brilliantly with three-headed women. 25.
The lordly serpent Valaya, in the form of a bracelet, supported the earth with his hoods;
the great naga Mahapadma, devoted to the worship of Hara’s feet,
supports Patala there and worships Maheśvara.
When people on the surface of the earth no longer observe religious fasts,
the heaviness of the earth will arise incessantly due to their deep-seated sins.
Greatly oppressed by that burden, the king of serpents hisses;
from the wind arising from the serpent’s hiss, an earthquake is produced. || 28 ||
The trembling of those [limbs] indicates various diseases for men;
furthermore, when men perform those [specific actions], they are indicative of the destruction of disease. || 29 ||
There, in the auspicious city of Suvarṇābhā, the lord of the Daityas named Suloma shone resplendent together with the asuras, worshipping the Lord at that time.
Food defiled by hair, food served past its proper time,
and that which is given without faith— all such things the Asuras consume.
On a sacred peak of the Himalayas, that great asura, having obtained a boon,
performed penance for a thousand divine years through the grace of the Lord.
Beneath that is the region named Sutala, yellow in luster, adorned with serpents,
divine, composed of yellow jewels, and possessing the brilliant splendor of yellow gems.
Furthermore, measuring fifty crores of yojanas in sequence,
its height is likewise one hundred thousand yojanas.
Together with a great multitude of nāgas, the nāga Takṣaka shines in that beautiful abode, supporting the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Takṣaka, shining with his exceedingly beautiful body and enjoying magnificent pleasures, is indeed resplendent among the hosts [of serpents];
resembling a crest-jewel with a beautiful svastika-marked head, he is constantly accompanied by a multitude of daughters of the serpent-king.
The glorious Takṣaka, king of the nāgas, accompanied by ten million nāgas,
constantly celebrates Mahādeva there with great festivals.
When men on the surface of the earth do not perform acts of charity, the earth becomes excessively burdened by the touch of those evil-minded ones. 38.
Completely oppressed by that weight, Takṣaka gasps for breath;
and from the wind exhaled by his breathing, an earthquake is produced. (39)
The trembling of those [limbs] indicates poverty for men at that time;
however, if men perform those [auspicious rites], they are indicated to be prosperous.
And his sovereign, the Daitya Kālanemi of great strength,
shines resplendent in a palace that resembles molten gold.
Accompanied by many millions of asuras and well-served by tens of millions upon tens of millions,
he shines resplendently in that divine assembly hall composed of various jewels.
If a mortal performs the act of eating without having washed his hands and feet, Kālanemi certainly takes all of that away from him. (43)
After a thousand divine years, having obtained a boon through the grace of Īśa by means of his ascetic penance,
the great Daitya continued to worship Maheśvara.
Beyond that is the world named Talātala, its ground strewn with gravel,
illuminated by the quarters of the sky with the greenish luster of emerald gems.
The extent of Talātala is fifty crores [yojanas], with a height of one million, and it is filled with divine cities and nectar. 46.
In that world illuminated by great emeralds and possessing divine splendor,
Karkoṭaka shines resplendent together with ten million hosts of nāgas.
Having received a boon from Lord Hemādrīśa, he of great strength and prowess bore the earth, including Sutala,
upon his head, carrying its immense weight.
Resplendent with a body dark as a cloud, this two-tongued Karkoṭaka was licking [his lips];
adorned with three lines upon his neck, he had a Naga maiden marked by fearsome fangs clinging to his throat. 49.
The great Naga Karkoṭaka, endowed with the power of poison and pride,
indeed worships Sadāśiva there at all times.
If human beings were devoid of ritual baths, sacrifices, festivals, and gifts, the earth would be heavily burdened and smeared with their sins. (51)
Indeed, Karkoṭaka, the king of the Nāgas, overcome by that burden,
hisses with a great hiss that strikes fear into all living beings.
From the wind arising from his breath, an earthquake is produced; and the trembling portends the auspicious and inauspicious destinies of living beings. (53)
Thus he praises those who have not rained for years past, as well as famines, provided that mortals are their authors and are entirely perverse in every way. (54)
Indeed, in that divine palace, resplendent with manifold beauty and filled with many jewels,
Hiraṇyākṣa shines forth together with the asuras.
And Hiraṇyakaśipu, the grandfather of all the Daityas,
shone together with the asuras in a palace made of various jewels.
Whatever dharma is performed by men with wealth acquired through unrighteousness,
all of that the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa seizes.
Having obtained boons from Mahādeva at the best of mountains, Himālaya,
he worshipped Hara for a thousand divine years through ascetic penance.
Beneath that is the netherworld named Nitala, with a ground of blood-red hue;
it shines with many mines of jewels, is shaped like a lotus, and is perpetually festive.
O Ghaṭasambhava, the width of Nitala itself extends for fifty yojanas,
and its interior height is one million [yojanas].
With houses of various jewels and the finest, manifold light-givers, the darkness has indeed been driven far away; for it shines brightly both day and night.
The great naga Śaṅkhapāla, accompanied by many servants,
shines there constantly, illuminating the quarters with his own jewels.
The Lord shone with a deep black luster, marked by a single streak on his neck from the brilliance of excellent jewels;
he who, like a double-tongued serpent, devours the pride and prowess of poison, has his left form adorned by the daughter of the King of Serpents.
Śaṅkhapāla, radiant with splendor and a worshiper of the lotus feet of Śiva, who supports the earth as the fourth [serpent], is worthy of Maheśvara. 64.
When those of noble lineage, devoid of the duty of giving, lick the kings and the twice-born— depriving them of their cattle and land— then [the end has come].
The earth would have been unable to bear those sins;
therefore, it sank even further down into the netherworld (pātāla) along with the exceedingly heavy Agastya. 66.
Firmly oppressed by that burden, Śaṅkhapāla, the lord of serpents,
hisses with a great sound arising from the pain of the heavy weight.
And from the wind arising from his breath, an earthquake is produced, which, having split the fourth stage, brings fear to all living beings. (68)

The trembling of that [wind] constantly portends calamities, the depletion of cattle and milk products, sparse crops upon the earth, the growth of shrubs, and the decline of the intellect of living beings. (69)
If men seeking great happiness honor those venerable ones,
there will indeed be abundance of milk, great harvests, and the prosperity of well-being.
Right there, the lord of the Daityas, the exceedingly powerful Anuhlāda,
shone resplendent in the midst of the assembly hall together with many crores of asuras.
Those lowest of men who eat food, drink, and all such things without first offering them to the gods, the twice-born, and the cows, are truly devouring excrement. (72)
Having gathered all that from the surface of the earth onto the Nitala level,
the great asura Anuhlāda enjoys happiness there.
Having obtained a boon on the Himalayas through the grace of the Lord,
the Daitya worshipped the Lord for a thousand divine years with ascetic penance.
And beneath that is the level named Tala, a brilliantly radiant white ground that shines eternally with the luster of gems as bright as the moon and the sun.
And fifty crores of yojanas [deep], it gradually descends into the earth;
this is the measurement of its base, being one million [yojanas] in height.
In a palace made of white gems and furnished with divine utensils,
this Naga king named Padma shines resplendent with many attendants.
His body shone like a beautiful white lotus, with trembling lips like those of a lovely lotus-eyed woman;
adorned with the five-faced [Śiva] and the moon as his ornaments, he was formidable with his body marked by serpent maidens. 78.
The great nāga Padma, renowned for his devotion to the worship of Hara’s feet, shines resplendent in the center of the base, supporting five stories. (79)
When the Brahmins weep out of fear of a king who has seized their wealth and heart, and their tears fall upon the earth, by that the earth becomes burdened. (80)
And when kings punish their subjects unjustly without due deliberation, the earth, along with its mountains, becomes exceedingly heavy because of that sin. 81.
By insulting her father, mother, and high-souled preceptor, she would cause that earth to become exceedingly burdened with sin on all sides. (82)
The lord of serpents named Padma, firmly oppressed by that burden, hisses with a great sound arising from the pain of the intense weight. (83)
From the wind that has arisen from the upward breath (udghāta), an earthquake is produced; having forcefully pierced the five elements, it causes all living beings to tremble. 84.
Its trembling constantly foretells for kings the loss of their position, the destruction of their subjects, the ruin of their kingdom, and great suffering. (85)
Prahlāda, the king of the Daityas, shall be its eternal lord in happiness;
together with many millions of asuras, he shines resplendent in that abode of jewels.
Whatever deeds that lowest of men performs without forming a mental resolve, Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas, takes all of that upon himself. || 87 ||
Having obtained the boon, he indeed propitiated Śiva through his great asceticism,
remaining intent on the worship of Rudra for a thousand divine years.
Beyond that is the one named Mahātala, situated at the very bottom and shaped like a lotus;
it indeed shines eternally with the luster of five-colored jewels.
And fifty crores of yojanas [below], the height of Mahātala, according to its measurement, is one million [yojanas]. 90.
There, the lord Ananta, the king of serpents, resplendent along with the *pannagas*, dwells in a palace composed of every kind of jewel, saluted by both gods and asuras. (91)
With his supreme body anointed by the luster of jewels, his face beautiful with deep red eyes and lips,
and his lovely head marked by the brilliance of great blue lotuses, the thousand-headed one shone, beloved by his consorts.
Ananta, the lord of the serpent kings, devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet, supported the sixth underworld while worshipping the imperishable Śiva. 93.
When mortals are marked by sin and devoid of the practice of giving and righteousness, they become partakers of falsehood, and the earth becomes most heavy. 94.

Those who reach the culmination of approaching women who should not be approached, those who violate the wives of others, and those who are backbiters—these shall become the earth's most heavy burdens. 95.
When cows, brahmins, gods, mortals, scriptures, and virtuous people are reviled, and when mantras, dharma, fasting, and the teacher are always disregarded, the earth will surely sink. 96.
When kings are most unrighteous, devoid of policy and dharma,
and do not protect the dharmas of their subjects, then the earth itself becomes the preceptor.
Subjects do not properly serve cows, the twice-born, the gods, or kings;
therefore, the earth becomes their preceptor, and they are deprived of their respective duties. 98.

When the Brahmins do not perform [their duties], being devoid of rites such as ritual bathing, and turning their backs on the dharma of the gods through recitation, fire-oblations, worship, and charity; 99.
Those who persist in accepting what is improper become brahmarākṣasas;
because they consume what is unfit for consumption, the earth becomes exceedingly heavy for them. 100.
Local rulers beat the twice-born and the cattle, and they plunder their property; they shall become denizens of hell, and therefore the earth becomes heavy with sin. 101.
For that sinner by whom gods, brahmins, the Vedas, or land are stolen goes to a terrible hell; for the earth is a great weight of sin upon them. 102.
The earth would be unable to bear those sins, and consequently, the world would become increasingly burdened more and more. (103)
Those who steal the crops on the earth, deceiving the owner of the land—even the cultivators of that field shall indeed have but meager harvests. 104.
O Sage, Ananta, the king of serpents, being firmly oppressed by that burden,
sighs deeply, arising from the pain caused by the weight of everything.
From the wind rising with a great many exhalations, an earthquake is produced, which, having pierced the sixth netherworld (pātāla), brings fear to many living beings. 106.
Trembling constantly portends a great pestilence and a supreme terror;
O Pot-born One, the great-formed Saṃvartaka swallows the world. 107.
Kings devoted to the duty of giving will honor the gods, cows, and Brahmins;
and the subjects shall remain perpetually happy in the subterranean realm (Rasātala). 108.
And if the Brahmins, devoted to austerity and intent upon the study of the Vedas,
remain constantly engaged in recitation and fasting, then the earth will always be auspicious; thus did that trembling of the ground foretell for all upon the surface of the earth.
And his sovereign was the great Daitya Hayagrīva;
accompanied by millions upon millions of Asuras, he worshipped Śaṅkara.
