He shone in the assembly hall together with Nikumbha, Andhaka, Suhlāda, Kāla, Madhu, Niśumbha, and others.
The highly fortunate wives of the Daityas, the auspicious daughters of the Daityas, and the sons of the Daityas likewise shone resplendently together with one another. 112.
Whatever wealth base men accumulate through dishonest conduct, the Asura seizes all of that—including their actions, merit, and gifts. (113)
Having obtained a boon from Śaṅkara on Himālaya, the best of mountains,
she gratified Hara with ascetic penance for a thousand divine years.
And in the darkness below the seven netherworlds (pātālas),
there exist the pits of hell, which are the abodes of those whose nature is sinful.
There are exactly twenty-eight crores of hells beneath the earth,
situated at the end of the seventh layer in most terrible darkness.
The first category is called Ghorā; below that is Sughorā;
then Atighorā, Mahāghorā, and the fifth is Ghorarūpā. 117.
The sixth is named Taralatārā, the seventh is Bhayānakā, the eighth is Kālarātri, and the ninth is Bhayotkaṭā. || 118 ||
The tenth is Caṇḍā below that, and Mahācaṇḍā below even that;
then Caṇḍakolāhalā, Caṇḍā, and Pracaṇḍā—these are the nine leaders. 119.
Padmā, Padmavatī, Bhīmā, the terrifying leader Bhīṣabhīṣaṇā,
Karālā, Vikarālā, and Vajrā— these are remembered as the twenty.
The triangular, the pentagonal, the very long, the perfectly circular,
the seven-storied, the earthly, the radiant, and the eighth is called Māyā.
These twenty-eight terrible hells have been enumerated by name; they consist of torments for the sinful.
For each of these, five heroines are to be known in sequence; learn their names according to every category. (123)
Raurava is the first of them, where embodied beings wail;
indeed, even the great wail there due to the torments of Mahāraurava. 124.
Tamas, Śīta, and likewise Uṣṇa—these five are remembered as the primary leaders. A hundred hells are recorded, beginning with Raurava and ending with Avīci. 125.
The circle of the great hells consists of forty-one;
therein sinful men are cooked according to their respective sins. (126)
Through various tortures, men endure intensely until their karma is exhausted,
just as smiths heat iron in a fire until its impurities are completely consumed.
Likewise, through the destruction of their sins, the wicked are purified in the fires of hell—
men who are bound very tightly by the hands with the chains of austerity.
They are suspended from the high branches of great trees by the servants of Yama;
swinging with extreme velocity, they lose consciousness for a distance of a yojana.
But for those situated in the intermediate space, two loads of iron are bound to their feet by the mighty messengers of Yama.
Bowed down deeply by that great burden, men stand motionless and silent, reflecting upon their own past deeds.
Then, those evildoers are struck on all sides by the terrible henchmen with hair like fire and iron rods covered in thorns. || 132 ||
Then, their limbs mangled and wounded, they are smeared on all sides with blazing caustic lye, even more so than with fire.
Furthermore, having been split open again in their limbs, starting from the head and proceeding in order,
they are cooked like eggplants in cauldrons of boiling oil.
Then they throw them into a pit of excrement and powder, then into a heap of worms, and again into a pond filled with fat, blood, and pus.
They are devoured by sharp worms and by crows with iron beaks;
they are attacked by dogs, gadflies, wolves, tigers, and fierce beings with distorted faces;
and they are cooked like fish in a pond within various hells.
I have described to you this subtle vessel of Pātāla, the abode;
now listen to me as I further proclaim the renown of Rasātala and the other six worlds of the sevenfold universe.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Pātāla," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 5 ||
Skanda said:

The earth is situated above the seven netherworlds (pātālas). I shall describe its dimensions in detail; listen. 1. The earth is situated above the seven netherworlds (pātālas). I shall describe its dimensions in detail; listen.
It is ten thousand yojanas in height and extends for many millions of yojanas in every direction.
It is renowned as Bhūrloka, the most excellent among all worlds,
and is frequented by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas.
By humans and animals, by beasts, birds, and reptiles, and by stationary beings of various forms—by these six kinds of living entities. || 4 ||
O Sage, among the seven continents situated in the middle of the world of earth (bhūrloka),
that which is known as Jambūdvīpa is sometimes described as being shaped like a half-moon.
On the delightful Hemavat peak, the most lofty of summits,
there stood a great Jambu tree, radiant with all living beings.
Extending one yojana in width and likewise in height,
that auspicious tree bears many jambu fruits throughout the six seasons.
O Noble One, from whatever ripe fruits fell upon the mountain peak, and from that which was moistened by the sage’s essence, this excellent river indeed came into being. (8)
Once, when Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun, came to that place desiring to bathe, she was cursed by Durvāsas, saying: "Become liquid! (9)
Because she was constantly drawn out by their union and became liquefied,
that river is known as Yamunā, owing to the confluence of those two.
Purified by Brahmā, by the Ṛṣis, and by the Sun after they had bathed there,
the salt-water ocean (Kṣāroda) thus lies at the edge of the land named after the Jambū tree.
Renowned as Jambūdvīpa, it stands firm amidst all other islands,
shining with an extent of fifty koṭis of yojanas.
Jambūdvīpa is the great continent, the most excellent among all continents;
there, men endowed with both happiness and suffering are born according to their actions.
Whatever is done in Jambūdvīpa, one experiences that very thing oneself;
it is known as the Island of Karma, for it is a land of merit that bestows the fruits of action.
Whatever a mortal performs, that very thing bears fruit for him therein;
O Sage, whatever great deeds of merit or demerit have been committed by living beings, all of that is surely obtained in Jambūdvīpa, for it is the land of action. 15.
In the midst of that, the Himālaya, the king of mountains, shines forth;
and on the southern side of Meru, there is another known as Meru.
Where a Plakṣa tree stood, from that it became Plakṣadvīpa;
and Śālmalīdvīpa is renowned for shining with the Śālmalī tree.
Because it shines with Kuśa, it is known as Kuśadvīpa;
that which shines with the Krauñca mountain is heard of as Krauñcadvīpa; and that which shines with the Śāka tree, O Sage, becomes Śākadvīpa. (18)
Because that island shone like a lotus (puṣkara) due to its identity with Acyuta, it was named Puṣkaradvīpa, the most excellent among all islands. 19.
From the Bhūrloka up to the Bhuvarloka as far as the solar orb—
within that distance, there reside in this world the Vasus and Rudras together with the Sun.
Above the solar orb and extending up to the pole star (Dhruva), the heavenly world (Svarloka) is said to exist;
twenty-eight crores of celestial chariots reside therein.
Dhruva stands as the central pivot above all celestial mansions;
there, they are bound in sequence to the circle of wind and move along with it.
Fifteen yojanas above the surface of the earth is the Pole Star (Dhruva);
and seven fixed layers of wind are situated there in the region to its north.
On the earth, the first layer extends up to the circle of clouds;
it is named Āvaha, which performs the gathering and bringing forth of the clouds.
The second is named Pravaha, which is fixed within the solar orb;
the third is Udvaha, a mass of wind situated toward the moon.
The fourth wind-sphere, Saṃvaha, is situated within the circle of the constellations;
the fifth among the planets is likewise proclaimed to be Vivaha.
The sixth wind, Parāvaha, is situated in the circle of the seven ṛṣis;
the seventh wind, named Parivaha, is bound to Dhruva.
The wind Āvaha performs the acts of leaping and so forth, as well as raining and so forth;
situated above the other six, it carries out the function of supporting the celestial chariots.
Maharloka is situated ten million yojanas above the Pole Star;
it is the abode of the great-souled ones whose offices have ceased.
Twenty-eight crores of gods who hold office, having come to the heavenly world by the command of the Lotus-born One, [remained there]. (30)
Having remained there for a manvantara until their own duties are completed,
some ascend to Maharloka, while other people return.
In this manner, having performed their duties over the course of a day of Brahmā, the fourteen classes of gods dwell in turn in Maharloka.
Janaloka is elevated two koṭis above Maharloka;
in it dwell the gods named Sādhyas, always happy.
In the world of Tapas, it is four crores of yojanas;
there dwell the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), the mind-born sons of Brahmā.
Satyaloka rises six crores of yojanas above Tapoloka;
it resembles sapphire and is adorned with great enjoyments.
O Pot-born One, my world is beyond the world of Viṣṇu;
it resembles clear pearls and is endowed with excellent enjoyments. (36)
Beyond my station, the station of the goddess Umā is celebrated;
it resembles molten gold and is endowed with every excellence. 37.
Beyond the station of Umā lies the primordial station of the Lord of Umā;
and beyond the world of Viṣṇu is the great and glorious city of Śiva.
It was thirty-two crores in extent and half that in height, endowed with great majesty and possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns. || 39 ||
The place was inhabited by countless hosts devoted to yoga,
crowded with throngs of Apsarases and provided with all kinds of musical instruments.
They were accompanied by countless retinues endowed with immeasurable virtues, possessed of the delights of song and dance, and as swift as thought.
It was pervaded on all sides by celestial chariots, like the sky by stars;
in some places, there were delightful swing-houses adorned with networks of tiny bells.
He was unapproachable for all the gods, meditated upon by the deities and asuras,
and was free from the sixfold group of the fluctuating senses as well as from all illusions.
For this is not the sphere of the wicked in thought or deed, nor of those embodied beings who are evil-minded, from which words turn back. 44.
In that supreme abode of light, composed of every kind of jewel,
Mahādeva shines eternally together with Umā.
The primordial Lord of unbroken bliss, the unborn Śiva who is the bliss of reality,
the Self that is innate bliss, and the Sovereign who is the bliss of absolute liberation.
O Sage, he is the full bliss, the unborn bliss, the all-pervading bliss who is worshipped by the hosts, the eternal bliss always adored with the three kinds of devotion.
By all the hosts seeking liberation who had obtained boons on Himālaya, that state was indeed joyfully attained through the grace of Mahādeva. 48.
O Sage, those who abide there in the world of Rudra as embodiments of the Lord are neither born again in a womb nor do they perish. 49.
Even those mortals who are practitioners of Āpeśa-yoga are undoubtedly liberated while living;
having abandoned their births, they go there to the abode of Yoga. 50.
By that very self which was purified through the worship of Rudra on the Himavat mountain, one attains the incomparable world of the Lord of Mountains, which is endowed with every happiness. 51.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Worlds," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 6 ||
Skanda said: Having thus created the mountains, O Pot-born one,
the Creator set his mind at that time upon the marriage of Himālaya.
O Sage, Brahmā first addressed these words to the eternal assembly of the Pitṛs regarding the marriage of his own sons on Mount Meru and the Himavat.
"You are the daughters of the host of Pitṛs, and you two maidens possess auspicious marks;
let them unite with divine bodies, being mind-born, ageless, and immortal."
Having heard the word of the Creator, the hosts of Pitṛs,
having assented with "Om" in their minds, created excellent daughters.
And among them, in former times, there were two— the father and the daughter— Divyaṅga and Divyāmanā, who possessed auspicious marks and were endowed with every perfect characteristic.
After some time, O Agastya, those two maidens grew up;
playing with birds, they reached the age of seven years.
Then, at the word of Brahmā, Nārada went to his grandson and delivered the message, speaking these reasoned words to his ancestors. (7)
Nārada said:
"O ancestors, let there be salutation to you; may there be auspiciousness and stability in your bodies. To those whose souls and bodies are imperishable, let my own body bow down in prostration. (8)
O Lord, hear now the seed of this body which has come here;
it is that word by which I have been sent by the Supreme Lord.
"O Lord, you indeed have two daughters who are the eldest among all;
let them be immediately united with two suitors named Divya and Ena. (10)
"Let the divine Menā be given to Meru, and let Himavat indeed receive her.
"Thus, O blessed ones, this is my agreeable opinion," so was it said by Brahmā to you. 11.
Skanda said: Having heard those words of the sage who was filled with indignation, the Pitṛs,
their anger subsided and their resentment gone, bowed down and spoke respectfully to him.
The ancestors said:
"Welcome, O best of sages! Is all well with your bodies?
Salutations again and again to that Creator by whom this entire world was emitted."
"Alas! A great calamity has arisen for us by the word of the Creator.
O Lord of Sages, how shall I give my daughter to those two immobile beings? (14)
He was stationary and motionless, afflicted with leprosy, one-eyed, lame, and possessed of pain;
he was deaf, devoid of virtues, mute, and likewise impotent. || 15 ||

One with reddish-brown eyes, one who is squint-eyed, one who is foolish, one with deficient or extra limbs, one of a different caste, one of no caste, one of the same lineage, and likewise a slanderer; || 16 ||
A wise man desiring his own welfare should not give a daughter to these;
for by not refusing, he would violate the great word and even the command of Brahmā. || 17 ||
"I will certainly not give my daughter to those two; let her return, O Lord of Sages.
Forgive my offenses today, and let the Creator be praised for his joy. (18)
Skanda said: Having heard the words of the ancestors and having returned to the abode of Brahmā, Nārada, bowing down, related that news to Brahmā. (19)
Then, having heard from the mouth of Nārada that account concerning the ancestors, the Lord Brahmā became enraged toward them.
Restraining his inner anger as he proceeded toward Śaila,
Brahmā suddenly and wrathfully produced wings for the unborn mountains.
Having joined the Himalaya, he went to the vicinity of Sumeru;
while the rite was being performed, the gods arrived there on the side of Meru.
The gods said:
"O Lord, you must never at any time break off a wing of the mountain;
for if it were to move along with its wings, the worlds would fall away from it. (23)
O Lord, when that mountain of jewels moves here and there upon it, these flavors produced by effort will once again submerge.
Skanda said: O Sage, having heard the words of the gods and the ṛṣis, the Creator, whose nature is truth, was filled with joy and then turned back from Meru to create wings.
O dear one, beholding such a sight brought about by the creation of wings,
Ratnasānu, his soul overwhelmed with grief, quickly descended and spoke to Aja.
Meru said:
"O dear one, how has this [world] been deceived by those wicked-souled celestial sages, who, disregarding us who abide on my wings, have now accepted their words as the truth?"
"If it be so, I shall utterly overthrow all those who are my adversaries;
by my own strength and vigor, I swear this to you today, O Unborn One."
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Mountains, do not ever cause such grief on account of your wings.
Indeed, O dear one, you shall remain as an immobile being with this gross body. (29)
O Meru, because you always wander with your subtle body,
your gross body has been prohibited for fear of causing the destruction of the worlds.
For this reason, listen, O Jewel-peaked Mountain, for I shall grant you a boon:
those who treat you with contempt shall indeed be possessed of sin. (31)
"O son, there is never any difference between us two in our embodied forms; whoever makes a distinction between us shall be a destroyer of my own body. (32)
Knowing you to be the principal mountain and the support of the world,
they bow down to you, whose body is composed of jewels, thinking, "I shall lift her up from you."
The ascetics were worshippers of Rudra, devoted to charity, righteousness, and fasting;
they were not lacking in devotion, were most virtuous, and had their sins washed away by bathing at sacred fords.
Devoted to truth and righteousness, peaceful, and always eager for compassion and charity,
they were devotees of the Goddess, of Viṣṇu, and especially of Rudra.
Let them remain with you, enjoying their pleasures;
protect them constantly, bringing forth various forms of happiness for them.
O son, cast down those very ones who have exhausted their merit and whose bodies are marked by sin from the mountain peak with utter mercilessness. 37.
"O sinless son, go now; for you shall surely travel to the world of the ancestors with this body bearing the *liṅga*, and there you must marry that maiden."
Skanda said:
Having heard the word of the Creator, Meru considered his purpose fulfilled;
assuming a human body, he went to marry the daughter of Pitṛ.
Having heard that Sumeru had obtained a boon from the Creator, Himālaya propitiated Brahmā with devotion; consequently, he too received a boon from him.
Himavat said:

Salutations to you, the God who transcends the qualities (guṇas), salutations to you whose self consists of the three qualities. Salutations to you who are firmly rooted within the phenomenal world and who are the creator of the phenomenal world. 41.
Sprinkle me with the showers of nectar from those excellent boons of yours,
so that our physical form as a linga may be bestowed upon us like Mount Meru.
Brahmā said:
"So be it, my son; let it be exactly as you say.
May you be able to assume any form at will and move wherever you desire. (43)
"O son, marry a maiden born of a noble family of ancestors;
they too will give you their daughter, so go to that world with certainty. (44)
Skanda said:
Having heard the words of the Creator, Himavat was filled with joy;
he then summoned the sages and the mountains who had assumed human forms.
Accompanied by the worlds headed by Nārada and by the Himavat mountains,
he went swiftly to the realm of the ancestors, filled with joy, in order to perform the wedding.

On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, when Jupiter is in conjunction with the Sun, and while the auspicious yoga is present and the ancestors are under the influence of benefic planets— 47.
They gave the divine maiden named Sulakṣaṇā to the Mountain of Gold;
taking her, his soul filled with joy, he returned to his own abode. 48.

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Rādha, on a Thursday, under the auspicious constellation Revatī and in a favorable yoga, with Jupiter situated in its exaltation. || 49 ||
O Agastya, in ancient times, having performed the ritual according to rule, the ancestors gave their daughter named Menā to Himavat, with cows and gold as the sacrificial fee.
The donor gave one hundred beautiful maidens of his retinue, well-adorned, as well as ten thousand palas of gold, to his own daughter.
The ancestors again bestowed their blessings upon Agastya’s son-in-law;
having touched his head with their hands in the assembly, they uttered the threefold benediction.
The ancestors said:
"May you live long and happily, my son, as long as the earth exists! O mighty-armed one, may you become a treasury of compassion for the two worlds, like the king of mountains. (53)
"O child, may you become the refuge of all the world and honored by all the world;
as long as water flows forth from you, let it be a sacred ford. (54)
For as long as living beings of the four classes shall abide in you,
they, liberated from all sins, will at the end attain the supreme goal.
Those men who abide in you, even if they are devoid of [other] forms of knowledge,
shall attain supreme liberation in the hereafter, which is difficult to obtain through yoga.
"O noble lady, may you not become a widow; may you be very dear to your husband.
May you have many sons, and may you be free from old age and immortal. (57)
Worshipped by the divine sages and worthy of honor, you are saluted by Bhava, the Lord;
you whose very soul is compassion for all the worlds, may you protect them constantly. 58.
Skanda said:
Having thus bestowed blessings upon the two of them, the Pitṛs honored them greatly and sent them back to their own world,
providing them with food along with their attendants.
Taking his wife with him and gladdening his attendants, Himavān returned to his own abode, Vyomakūṭa, accompanied by auspicious portents.
O Sage, those two, the bride and bridegroom, repeatedly experienced the happiness born of their union; endowed with the essence of amorous play, they remained as husband and wife. 61.
At the end of fifteen divine years, she returned to her father's house;
Menā spoke these words to her parents concerning her beloved deeds.
Menā said:
"O ancestors, protect me who am repeatedly deprived of my husband;
having served your lotus feet, I shall indeed remain there. (63)
"O dear father, you do not remain even for a moment in private with me;
filled with fear, you do not look upon my face even with joy. (64)
He would have been the beloved of those female slaves, for they were indeed dear to him;
he did not leave them for even a moment, day and night, in succession. 65.
Skanda said:
Having heard these words of Agastya’s daughter, her fathers were then immediately filled with indignation and began to curse the mountain.
The Pitṛs said: "Since those daughters of yours, having become slave-girls, have treated you with contempt, their offspring as well as their progeny shall remain stationary. (67)
And let your female slaves be crowded with their own offspring;
may they not obtain even a moment's happiness, even from their beloved. 68.
"Even though those rivers were born as daughters,
they shall become your female slaves, since they have been shattered by your daughters."
"You shall give birth to an excellent son, and likewise others;
may these three slender-waisted daughters become honored by the world. (70)
"Return home, daughter, just as you came;
for women should not remain in their own homes even when beaten by their husbands. (71)
Enduring her husband’s constant transgressions, she should remain in his house;
for she will undoubtedly obtain [his] lineage, wealth, fame, and renown. 72.
"O daughter, worship Rudra together with Śivā incessantly;
by observing vows and fasting on those specific lunar days, you will certainly obtain good fortune. (73)
Skanda said:
Having heard these words of instruction spoken for her welfare by her father Mena,
she quickly returned home to her husband along with her female companions.
At her father's command, Menā observed a vow while fasting;
having worshipped Śaṅkara with devotion, she passed some time.
Thus, by the power of her merit, she rejoiced with her husband;
having enjoyed the kingdom and its pleasures, she spent some time in happiness. (76)
And she gave birth to Maināka, the most excellent of sons, who was renowned;
and at the end of that time, three daughters were also born to her.
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā;
she is Tyaktaparṇā, and indeed Aparṇā, while the other is Ekaparṇāśanā.
Another is known as Ekapuṣpāśanā, and likewise Ekapāṭalā;
endowed with most formidable asceticism, they observe such rules in their vows.
Long ago, Himavat indeed gave my mother to Śūlin;
he gave Asitā to Ekaparṇā, and another to Jaigīṣavya.
Those female slaves gave birth in succession to hundreds of thousands of sons;
established by their mothers in various places, they attained stability right there. || 81 ||
And at the end of time, those daughters gave birth repeatedly in due order;
all the rivers, overflowing with water, flowed from the mountain like currents.
O sage,
by the command of Brahmā, all those rivers— bestowing the fruits of the four goals of life— constantly beat, threatened, and censured him again and again throughout the night, as did the Pitṛs.
Marked by the inner pain of their hearts, the female slaves repeatedly spoke to their sons, striking them, threatening them, and reproaching them again and again. (84)
"O sons, move about constantly; do not remain in one place.
Through movement, one obtains everything—excellence, honor, and even daring. (85)
Thus addressed, the sons did not utter them;
nevertheless, those mothers said, "There is no power in us to speak them. (86)
Beholding such sons, the daughters became distressed and the female slaves were overcome with grief; they reported that matter to their husband. (87)
Having heard the words of his beloved, the wise Himavat then consoled his bride with wise words of sweet expression.
Then, at the end of a hundred yugas, there occurred a battle between the gods and the asuras;
Kaśipu, having summoned the mountain, fought together with the gods.
Then that Himavat, as a bird, covered [the sky] with his two wings;
with his wings obscuring the heavens, he sought to strike down the army of the gods.
Beholding that mountain-like being, the army of the gods was overcome with fear;
crying out, "Save us! Save us!", they sought refuge in Viṣṇu. (91)
O Creator, Protector, Viṣṇu, Lord, Creator, Infallible One, Destroyer!
O Lord of protection, O All-pervading One, protect us from sin, from Kaśipu, and from the mountain. 92.
Having heard their words, Hari, having emerged from the Ocean of Milk and raised his discus belonging to Pūṣan, spoke to the gods.
Viṣṇu said: "O gods, do not fear; there shall be a remedy for this.
For this wicked one will be pacified, just as a leader is subdued by his own followers. (94)
For the sake of punishing the wicked and protecting the virtuous, I take various incarnations in separate bodies. (95)
Skanda said:
Having spoken thus, O Pot-born One, Nārāyaṇa quickly set out together with the immortals to cut off the wings, to where that Kaśipu was.
Beholding Viṣṇu arrived with the gods, the mountain Kaśipu and his son fled from him who was armed with the discus, like living beings fleeing from Death himself. || 97 ||
Out of fear, Himavat placed Kaśipu in his own abode;
and having cried out "Save me! Save me! to the Lord, the Grandfather, the Creator, [spoke]. 98.
"O Agastya, having said, 'Whatever hardship has been caused by the enemy faction and whatever has been done by oneself, let that go to the Himavat,' Viṣṇu became enraged. (99)
Rushing toward the Ocean of Milk and aiming at the mountain’s wings,
Viṣṇu, intensely filled with rage, suddenly hurled his discus.
Sudarśana swiftly cut off the two wings of Himavat;
having done so completely, he returned to the hand of Viṣṇu. || 101 ||
Being praised by the immortals, Viṣṇu went to his supreme abode;
and the gods, leaving the battlefield, returned once more to their respective worlds. 102.
With his wings lopped off and his body in a state of great distress, Himavat went to Brahmā;
showing him his mangled form, he related all of that to Brahmā.
Having heard his words and seeing the mountain marked by distress,
the Creator consoled him and spoke to him with sweet words.
Quickly propitiate Him alone, who is affectionate toward devotion, on the Himalayas;
He will grant His devotees their heart's desire, of this there is no doubt. (105)
Having heard the words of the Creator, that embodied being departed for where Hari was stationed,
taking with him the perfected jewel along with those standing at his side.
O Sage, having presented an offering before Viṣṇu, Himavat circumambulated him and bowed at his feet with devotion, praising him again and again.
Homage to the one born from Nārāyaṇa; homage to the Lord of the divine ones!
Homage to you, O Leader of the World, the source of men, the source of joy! 108.
"O Father, because I lack wings, I am reviled by mobile beings as 'immobile. Since I have been made capable of changing form at will by the Creator, you should grant me this boon. (109)
Beholding the mountain filled with devotion, bowing down, and desiring his petition,
the Blessed One spoke to him in order to grant a boon to his devotee.
Viṣṇu said:
"O child, this gross body of yours shall remain as an immobile being for a long time, constantly causing fear to the worlds wherever it may wander. (111)
"Therefore, let not your heart grieve; become the protector of the worlds.
O child, by means of this limb, you shall be able to assume any form at will at all times. (112)
Listen, I shall grant you a boon—the most excellent of all boons. From this day forward, O king of the lords of mountains, become one who is honored by the world. 113.
I abide in you eternally along with my own hosts and the thirty gods;
likewise, Vidhātṛ, Śaṅkara, the Siddhas, and the celestial rishis abide there.
Indeed, the lords of the quarters, the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Dānavas serve you;
and the Apsarases, following their own nature, dwell with you constantly and with joy.
O Mountain, you have always been adorned with righteousness by the Lord;
you have never experienced unrighteousness, since you are the hermitage for all the gods.
Seeing you is seeing me; there is never any difference between us.
He who creates a distinction between us is indeed a fool and a destroyer of my own body.
The mountain is the abode of all stages of life, and I am indeed composed of all the gods;
he who honors them as equal attains the supreme state.
"Go, O king of mountains, to perform penance on your own auspicious peak;
propitiate Maheśāna, and he will grant whatever is desired by your heart. (119)
Skanda said:
O Pot-born one, having thus granted the boon to Himavat, Viṣṇu disappeared;
yet he continued to dwell there without interruption.
On Mount Hiraṇyaśekhara, Mahāviṣṇu stands with his neck severed,
eternally worshipped by gods and asuras, and especially by the ancestors.
Having obtained his boon, that lord of mountains, Himālaya, returned;
all the worlds frequented his peaks, dwelling there repeatedly.
And at the end of a hundred divine years, having obtained boons through the grace of Paśupati, he became a great being, devoted to the divine hermitage on Mount Parācala.
Then he became the primordial, infinite, and supreme ornament, composed of ascetic power and bestowing the fruits of the world;
he was indeed the Himālaya mountain, the hermitage of all the gods, the noble one who attained his majesty through the grace of Aśutoṣa.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Bestowal of Boons upon Himālaya," in the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.

Skanda said: O sage, a boon was granted to Himavat by the Lord in the past;
I shall describe all of that—listen with a concentrated mind. 2.

Paśupati said:
"O Himavat, become inexhaustible as long as Brahmā exists; there is no doubt.
Remain firm for a long time, O immovable mountain, and be equal to Mount Meru. (4)
As long as people do not perform penance upon you, O Golden Mountain,
so many sinless ones shall not remain even on Mount Meru.
"O bearer of gold, I abide within you as the individual self in the form of the *liṅga*;
likewise, the Creator, the gods, Viṣṇu, and the guardians of the quarters remain there perpetually. (6)
My beloveds, who are worthy of worship, possess many forms, and bestow boons upon all the worlds; they stand upon your peaks, having become distinct from one another, together with their hosts.
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, celestial rishis,
and ascetics dwell upon your peaks, as do Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Dānavas.
O Himālaya, humans shall dwell eternally upon your peaks;
you shall nourish them with fruits, roots, and grains, and thus protect them. 9.
Those mortals who, possessing the vigor of householders, constantly take refuge in you—
whether in the valleys, on the ridges, on the peaks, or on the summits.
They shall dwell in the bliss of the third heaven, accompanied by their retinues,
for as long as you remain in the state of a renunciant, according to that same number.
And those who ascend its ridges, though devoid of [higher] knowledge, obtain at every step the fruits of the Vājapeya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. || 12 ||
Those who, dwelling repeatedly upon your peaks, perform austerities,
are not dissolved even by the wise, having abandoned the miserable cycle of worldly existence.
O wise ones, do not look toward us who are devoted to recitation and worship;
for I shall deliver you by casting off this cycle of worldly existence.
O Himavat, whatever mortal bathes even once in the streams produced from you, having cast off the sins accumulated since birth, shall go to the third heaven. || 15 ||
Whichever women give birth even in the valleys near you, they, having bathed on the sacred festival days, are freed from the sins accumulated over seven lifetimes. (16)
Those who behold you from afar, adorned with snow and gold, are undoubtedly liberated from the sins accumulated over a single year. 17.
"O Mountain, while we are traveling, those who are even once devoid of devotion toward you on your peaks deserve [punishment]; I shall uproot them. (18)
The Śaityā, the Ālakanandā, the Bhadrā, the Haimavatī, the Gaṇḍakī, the Śatarudrā, the Bhāgīrathī, and the Vāgmatī. || 19 ||
Haimavatī, Bhadrā, Satyagaṅgā, Kauśikī,
Śatarudrā, and Śaityā were likewise bestowers of boons during the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age she was the Bhāgīrathī, and in the beginning of the Kali age, the Alakanandā; in the middle of the Kali age, the Vāgvatī, and at its conclusion, once again the Gaṇḍakī.
And those rivers shall become bestowers of desired boons upon the world; they will grant whatever is in the minds of those who depend on them within the realm of mortals.
Adorned by these eight powers of manifestation, which are my own descents, you are constantly sanctified.
"Go, O king of mountains; may you be possessed of many sons.
Furthermore, our lineage shall find a cause for alliance with you. (24)
Thus, having obtained this boon from Rudra, that Himavat,
the lord of mountains, was always to be worshipped with a disciplined mind by all beings, including the gods.
Agastya said: This Himavat, the lord of mountains, is presided over by the gods and is perfectly endowed with boons by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.

O Skanda, tell me: which men on this earth, having been liberated from the cycles of worldly existence, have attained their fruit—those who reside on the Himavat mountain or those whose vigor is like that of its peaks? 27.
Skanda said: Listen, O Pot-born one; in former times, humans were liberated.
I shall relate that account concerning Himavat, whose strength is like that of a mountain. 28.
A certain Mleccha named Karaṅga, a famous inhabitant of the mines, wandered toward the mountain accompanied by his retinue. || 29 ||
Constantly searching for minerals, he arrived at the Himalayas;
from birth his soul was defiled by sin, and he was utterly devoid of the virtue of giving.
Where the stream of fame had arisen from Nīlakaṇṭha in the west,
he went three yojanas further away to Mount Hemakūṭa.
There, the Liṅga of the Lord of Wealth shines in the midst of the pool;
it is the Lord of Liṅgas made of pure crystal, bathed in the liquid flowing from his body moistened by heat.
Formerly, he performed austerities out of envy toward me, which were propitiated by his host;
therefore, he obtained the office of leader of the Gaṇas, and is honored by gods, sages, and Daityas.
The Mleccha, afflicted by thirst, repeatedly drank the water from the stream;
having washed his hands, face, and feet, he quickly sprinkled that water upon his head. 34.
Ceasing his blows upon the earth, his fierce exertion exhausted,
he rested for a moment on the riverbank while striking at the waterfall.
Beholding that golden mountain, his limbs rendered motionless by the numbness born of joy, he spoke quickly to his servants with words of faltering utterance.
O Pot-born One, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa,
in the forenoon, I was afflicted by hunger and distressed by the suffering of cold due to the lack of food.
Karaṅga said:
"O brother, O dear son, behold before you, bowing down, the golden lord of mountains, the most excellent benefactor of others. (38)
"Oh, what fortune for us who were once protectorless, since he has been revealed this very day!
Indeed, our birth, though burdened with many sins, has become fruitful this very day! (39)
O beloved, in former times we once gave wealth to a Brahmin;
because of that, we have been tormented by those who are destitute and led astray here by their greed.
In many previous births, that which was attained by me was difficult and most hard to endure;
indeed, having seen him wandering in distress, it was through the grace of the Lord that we [attained this]. 41.
And by its power, I was cleansed of my sins by the waters;
having had a small remnant of dharma remaining from before, I have come here to this place.
And whatever we may desire—whether sovereignty, the state of the yogins, or the earth girt by the oceans—as shown by the Lord; 43.
"Behold, my son, this mountain, a treasury of splendor, dear brother;
such is it to its west, east, and likewise to its north. (44)
Behold those peaks from which formerly arose the Kauśikī rivers honored by the gods, and from which the Gaṇḍakīs also originated. 45.
Behold, bowing before you, this entire mountain made of gold, possessing a thousand peaks and born of Jātavedas, blazing indeed with various jewels. 46.
The servants said:
"O Lord, we have certainly not seen that king of mountains made of gold;
the lord of mountains is adorned with cool trees, shrubs, and stones. (47)
Karaṅga said:
"O son, bowing down, let your eyes be cleansed with these pure waters;
then, having drunk the water, you shall behold the Mountain of Gold."
Skanda said:
Having drunk the ocean with devotion using those hands produced from the Gaṇa-vessels, O Agastya, they beheld mountains before them. 49.
Before him was a mountain consisting entirely of gold, with a thousand peaks,
shining with the rays of jewels and adorned with wonders.
On the shore of the stream of water, the Mlecchas repeatedly prostrated themselves like a staff with great devotion toward the mountain; they considered themselves fulfilled in their hearts. 51.
Abandoning his attendants and his litters, he ascended all alone that mountain which had arisen before him; being exhausted, he rested upon its ridges.
Having thus placed this thought in my heart and taken these juices with these golden vessels,
I shall become a sovereign emperor on earth, swiftly conquering the kṣatriyas.
O Sage, having ascended the mountain peak, he reached Gaṇakuṇḍa;
there he beheld the Lord, crystalline like Brahmā, situated within the water of the pool.
Then he beheld there the host of immortals attending upon the Lord of Waters, making them dance with great festivals of song and instrumental music.
He saw Lambodara dancing together with the gods in great festivities, while Vṛṣaketu was being praised in song by the Apsarases and the lotus-born Brahmā.
When that Mleccha reached the edge of the pure sacrificial pit at the riverbank,
a rain of flowers fell from the sky and a roar resounded in the heavens.
Then the devotees of Śiva arrived there from the sky,
holding celestial chariots and illuminating the four quarters with those sun-bright aerial vehicles.
Having ascended that celestial chariot belonging to Śiva,
those devotees of Śiva traveled through the sky while it was fanned with chowries waved by the hands of the Rudra-maidens.
O Sage, they were immediately led to the city of Śiva amidst great festivals of song and instrumental music,
illuminating the quarters with the splendor of their celestial chariots while still in their physical bodies.
His attendants led such servants from the sky to their respective cities;
having spent a hundred yugas in happiness, they indeed enjoyed the state of Śiva.
Thus he became a sovereign king;
by the power of the Gaṇakuṇḍa, he brought all the kings under his own control and ruled over the entire earth.
Remaining there, that river, seeing her attendants in such a state out of fear and being unable to move her feet, wept bitterly in her solitude.
Hearing her wailing and crying, the sage of the Gaṇas arrived there;
approaching, that gentle one with matted hair spoke to that Brāhmaṇī. (64)
Jaigīṣavya said:

"Do not weep, daughter; you were afflicted by poverty due to sins committed in the past. For that reason, O woman of sinful character, you have become utterly destitute through your former lack of charity. (65)
"Why do you weep, O most sinful one, now tormented by your own deeds?
Even now, indeed, practice righteousness, which carries one across the cycle of existence."
Śilā said:
"Alone and powerless, abandoned by my husband and sons, where shall I go here? Alas, what misery! Where have they gone, leaving me behind? (67)
O Lord, we have fallen into a deserted wilderness on the bank of a river resounding with the splashing of water, inhabited by creatures and birds, and devoid of human beings. 68.
"O twice-born one, tell me truly: by what many sins committed in the past, or perhaps by faults arising from my servants, have I been so tormented? (69)
Jagīṣavya said:
"You were dear to a farmer, yet you were devoid of the merit of giving;
therefore, you became both unfortunate and poor in birth after birth. (70)
Previously, she had given no vegetables, roots, or fruits to anyone;
she filled only her own belly, not even a single grain of food for others. (71)
Having become a field-guardian on a stone plot during the Kali age, she protected it from being fruitless;
moreover, she drove away birds and living creatures with a staff. 72.
While you were guarding it, a crow seized a single sheath;
you quickly struck him with a fruit, saying, "Let him be filled with impurities! (73)
That crow gave his hoard to Citragupta to accumulate;
for he had properly accumulated it so that he might give it back again at the end. 74.
When you had passed away and I was led to Saṃyamanī by the followers of Yama, I wept most bitterly, crying, "I am afflicted by thirst! I am afflicted by hunger! (75)
Saying "Eat!", Yama first gave those treasures to you;
having increased them ten millionfold, they were then taken away by his servants.
"Eat them! Look at them! Break them apart with your claws!"—thus she spoke;
yet she beheld them filled with impurities and was deeply distressed.
With their limbs scorched by hunger and thirst, they sink into the abodes of hell;
at the end of a hundred thousand years, they take birth again, separately in all species.
At the end of a hundred thousand years, this body was born again in human form on the bank of the Gaṅgā due to merit; those very same people are indeed your servants. (79)
Having obtained that boon through the power of my holy ford and the mountain,
they too abandoned you, who were ungenerous, and ascended to the Himalayas.
"Having certainly bathed at this Mātṛtīrtha, ascend this mountain;
O Śilā, you shall then reach that path, free from sin, and regain those servants. (81)
Skanda said:
O Brahmin, having thus enlightened her and shown her the path of merit, Jaigīṣavya went to the Varāhārṣi lake to perform austerities. 82.
Where in ancient times Varāha indeed performed austerities on Muniśṛṅga,
even today the Siddhas and celestial rishis do not leave that place for a moment.
Having ascended Siddhakūṭa, one who goes there is liberated from sins;
merely by beholding the lake, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. 84.
If a person performs a bath at Kacā through the power of destiny, he is liberated from the sins committed during seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt. (85)
Having heard the words of Śilā, Agastya, and Jaigīṣavya,
and having taken them to heart as truth, he proceeded slowly to that sacred ford.
Jaigīṣavya bathed in the water mixed with the juice of jambu fruits;
he then ascended the peak of Mount Gaṇḍatīrthaśilāgastya.
She too, along with her attendants, departed by means of a vehicle possessing the brilliance of the sun;
and in this way, many were liberated through the power of that sacred mountain.
Ten million human beings always go [to their respective realms], likewise twenty million animals; thirty million proceed [as such], while four are at most mere worms. (89)
O Sage, those beings of the three modes of birth who were devoid of knowledge did not ascend that mountain, which was adorned with the splendor of golden-peaked crests.
O Agastya, in former times, living there with vital energy for a thousand years,
he remained in heaven, pervaded by joy and enjoying great happiness.
Formerly, one hundred thousand pearls were offered at Abdhīśa, and likewise at Bhasmapaṅkeśvara;
one hundred thousand were offered at Kāleśvara, and one hundred thousand at Aiśānakeśvara.
One hundred thousand [recitations] at Abhratuṅgeśvara, likewise at Ratnakoṭīśvara;
one hundred thousand at Kāmeśvara, and again one hundred thousand at Vāgmatīśa. (93)
O Sage, at Kāmarūpa, Bhasmeśa, and Saundaryādri,
as well as at the great Liṅga Jaleśvara and Hayagrīva, one should perform a hundred thousand recitations.
Likewise, one hundred thousand [recitations] at Bahurūpeśvara, at Pretāsana, and again at Vidyāliṅga, Mahākūṭa, and Viśvambhareśvara. || 95 ||
O Sage, one should likewise perform a hundred thousand repetitions at Vārāha, Śaṃkara, Mleccharūpeśvara,
Svarṇaliṅga, and Ratnaliṅga.
When Mahāviṣṇu had his neck severed, one hundred thousand [offerings] were made to Devapureśvara;
likewise, one hundred thousand were made to Pārvatīśa, and again one hundred thousand to Dugdhasteyeśvara.
At Nīlakaṇṭheśvara there is one hundred thousand [recitations], at Pāśupata one hundred thousand;
at Paśupati there should be two hundred thousand, and they become liberated while still possessing their bodies.
One hundred thousand [offerings] at Cakratīrtha, Śūleśa, and Harikṣetra;
likewise one hundred thousand at Devaghaṭṭa and one hundred thousand at Prabhātīrtha. (99)
Likewise, at Dharmakūṭa, a hundred thousand [were sacrificed] where the Dharmanadī originates;
for in ancient times, Aja cursed Dharma, saying, "Become liquid from this day forward. (100)
At Abhrakūṭa, on the mountain of the Lord of Beings (Śiva), there are three hundred thousand;
likewise, at Halotkhāta there are one hundred thousand, and again at Keśava there are one hundred thousand.
There are three [lakhs] on the great peak of Svarṇanābha and on the mountain Svarṇagarbha;
two lakhs on Badrikāśaila, and two lakhs at Kedāra. (102)
There are three distinct [sites] at Viśvakūṭa, Mahāpatha, and Svarṇadvāra;
there are two hundred thousand [verses] at Bhairavīśaila and two hundred thousand at Triyugīśvara.
Three hundred thousand at Mānassara, three hundred thousand at Bhadrā,
one hundred thousand at Alakanandā, and likewise three hundred thousand at Bhāgirathī.
One hundred thousand at Karṇaprayāga, two hundred thousand at Viṣṇuprayāga, one hundred thousand at Rudraprayāga, and two hundred thousand at Brahmaprayāga. (105)
There are two at Lakṣa and Devaprayāga, as well as the one called Vyāsasaṅga;
there is one at Lomāśraya Mahāliṅga, and three on the Jvālāmukhī mountain.
One hundred thousand [recitations] at Viśvaṃbhareśvara, likewise at Gaṅgākānteśvara;
one hundred thousand at Vimale Trikūṭa, and one hundred thousand at Viśvaketu.
Likewise, there are one hundred thousand [yojanas] on Jambūśaila, and one hundred thousand on Śrīśekhara;
two hundred thousand on Sūryādri and Candraśaila, and one hundred thousand on Agnidīpta.
At Maṇibhūmi there are two hundred thousand; at Candraśekhara, two hundred thousand;
at Abdhikūṭeśvara, one hundred thousand; at Ratnakūṭeśvara, three hundred thousand;
at Taptācala, three hundred thousand; and at Bhuvanaśekhara, one hundred thousand. (109)
O Pot-born One, the earth realm (bhūrloka) was pervaded by tens of millions upon tens of millions of men,
as were the atmospheric realm (bhuvarloka), heaven (svarga), the world of the sages (muniloka), and the realm of Death (kṛtāntaka).
The region of Nirṛti was pervaded by mortals, as were the abode of Varuṇa, the temple of Vāyu, that of Kubera, and likewise those of Īśāna, Sūrya, and Himāṃśu. || 111 ||
And [he saw] the Nākṣatra world, Maharloka, Janaloka, and likewise Tapas; furthermore, Satyaloka, the realm of Brahmā, and also that which is the realm of Viṣṇu.
Beholding their respective worlds pervaded by mortals, the gods,
beginning with Brahmā, gathered together and out of distress went to Paśupati.
Brahmā said: "O Lord, that which was previously given by you to us has become a futile effort here; for Janaka is the progenitor of living beings, and I am their protector. (114)
The abodes of the gods were filled on all sides with mortals possessing bodies,
yet devoid of bathing, giving gifts, and worship, as well as with beasts, birds, wild animals, and the like.
"May we become mountains composed of mortals this very day, lasting for a hundred thousand years!
May the wise be liberated, and may these [mountains] be filled with common folk. (116)
Paśupati said:
"O gods, whatever fruit is necessarily obtained by ascetics,
you shall obtain those abodes through the touch of the immovable mountain, for you have received boons."
Therefore, O Hari, do not grieve; a remedy will come about.
People on the peak of the Himalayas will certainly provide it for you. 118.

Having quickly cast off their bodies upon the peaks of the snowy mountain, even common folk and those who have completed their Vedic studies, as well as ascetics— once they have reached you, I shall deliver them, along with their very bodies, through liberation, provided there is no strife.
Skanda said:
Having heard the words of Paśupati, the gods, filled with joy, bowed with devotion to the jyotirliṅga, circumambulated it, and departed for their own abodes. 120.
From that time forward, O Pot-born One, those who lived upon that mountain abandoned their bodies and went to heaven in a state of liberation, even without performing ritual acts.
The wise who hear of the majesty of Himavat attain great renown and follow after excellent fame;
whatever merit one performs on the Golden Mountain quickly results in grain, wealth, and long life upon the earth. (122)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Himālaya," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Skanda said:
O Sage, in former times the eighteenth world was agitated by the sons of Mlecchas;
[it was pacified] indeed through the grace of Badrikeśa and likewise through the favor of Kedāra.
Through the instruction of Nārada, they attained liberation in the Gaṅgā; O Sage, this majesty of Nirvāṇa was obtained by them on the Himavat. 2.
Agastya said:
O Lord of the Army, how was the realm of the gods agitated by the Mlecchas,
and how were the two deities Kedāra and Badrikeśvara propitiated?
Tell me how even the barbarians attained perfect liberation in the Gaṅgā through the instruction of Nārada; speak of that origin.
Lomaharṣaṇa said:
Having heard the words of the Pitcher-born Sage (Agastya), the sages and the son of Pārvatī spoke these words to him as a reply to the story previously related. 5.
Skanda said:
O dear one, while Cyavana was established in ascetic penance at the sacred ford of Cyavana’s hermitage,
a fisherman named Vaṅgu, carrying his net, went there.
He cast his net aiming at the fish for the sake of slaughter;
he killed some of the fish, disregarding both men and sages.
Having repeatedly disregarded those words forbidden by the sage, you, O evildoer, were overcome with anger and quickly cursed him: "Become a boar! (8)
That boar wandered from forest to forest until only a remnant of his lifespan remained;
at the end of a hundred years, he reached a mountain beautiful with the slopes of the Himavat.
There, at a distance of five yojanas to the north of Devaghaṭṭa, Kolī lived happily in the treasure-chamber of Tāmrakūṭa.
On the full moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, joined with the constellation Pūrvābhādrapadā,
he beheld the supreme lake of Agastya on a pleasant morning.
On the mountain peak, at the lake, a boar drank water for sustenance but once;
indeed, at the end of a month, by the turn of fate, it was eating roots and fruits.
Having drunk that water, the Mleccha did not abandon his kola-body;
indeed, for some time he dwelt on that mountain together with his kinsmen.
A certain matted-haired mendicant came from Badarikā to his house seeking alms;
that fisherman, having given him wild rice, touched his feet with reverence.
"His feet have been purified by ascending Badarikā; my sins have been cast far away by the touch of them.
Today, today indeed, I shall follow in his footsteps"—thus he made his first resolve within his heart. (15)
"O sons, you must protect all your servants and the household;
I, being old, am going to practice asceticism out of fear of suffering. (16)
Many living beings have been slain by me with utter mercilessness;
my body smeared with their sins, I shall certainly go to the realm of Yama. (17)
Skanda said:
Having thus instructed his sons and abandoned those twenty at night,
he departed for the Himavat mountain in the direction north of Varuṇa.
O gentle one, having transcended the mountains, he, who was composed of the essence of Udaśīka and Keśava, proceeded alone to Badarikāśrama. || 19 ||
The Mleccha, who was in essence Siddheśvara, ascended Badarikācala;
having joyfully bathed in Taptakuṇḍa, he drank the water of Udakuṇḍa.
And on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, O Sage, he beheld the Supreme Lord; having prostrated himself like a staff, he bowed with devotion in the three ways.
O Lord, this people, deluded by Your Māyā, is submerged in the deep ocean of saṃsāra;
yet even though they do not serve You, the supreme elixir, You still protect them out of Your compassion for the ignorant. 22.
Salutations again and again to the god Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Lord of Siddhas, the supreme sovereign, Nanda, and the highest one.

I am forever bowed down before that Supreme Lord, the supreme form of Brahman, the supreme Lord Śaṅkara, in whom the state of duality shines forth as rooted in His very body; I worship that Supreme Ruler with my mind, my speech, and my body. 24.
Thus being praised, the hosts led him in a celestial vehicle to the world of Viṣṇu, while he remained in his own body, wielding his four weapons.
For his sons immediately followed their father to comply with his will;
crying out "Alas, O Father! together on the road, they went along.
The eighteen brothers, having crossed over the mountains, departed from the forest;
they reached Rudraprayāga and dwelt at that sacred ford day and night.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, they bathed in that supreme water and, having drunk its waters,
they also took leave of the householders as they returned to their own abodes.
For having reached Kedāra, they proceeded very slowly;
and by touching the water of Rudrakuṇḍa, they cast off their former sins.
Beholding that supreme, most wonderful linga in the form of light, the Mlecchas then said to one another, "O brothers, we have abandoned Śaṃkara;
we will not go home, but shall indeed serve Him here in peace. (30)
Having prostrated like a staff out of devotion before Kedāreśa, the fishermen,
filled with joy, praised the Lord with voices faltering with emotion.
The fishermen said:
"We bow to the Great Lord, the three-eyed one of triple form, whose limbs are adorned with a multitude of serpents, the Supreme Sovereign.
I worship that embodiment who is smeared with abundant ashes and whose head is radiant with a mass of matted locks. (32)

I worship Maṇḍu, whose limbs are radiant with waves of movement through the three worlds, whose forehead is marked by a crescent moon as his ornament, who wears a tiger skin and a necklace of lordly serpents, and who holds a trident. 33.
Resplendent with twelve eyes like the sun and moon, bearing the emblem of the bull, possessing a gentle form and a smiling face;
with one half of his body in the embrace of the daughter of the Himālaya, he is the embodiment of eternal bliss and the supreme light. (34)

May that [Lord] who shines in the hearts of the virtuous yogins, who blazes forth from the eye on the face of the Daughter of the Mountain King, whose form is the very pinnacle of the moon’s luster, and whose mental fluctuations shine within the midst of the phenomenal world—[grant us peace]. 35.
Sadānanda said:
[I bow to] the Lord whose form is consciousness and bliss, who is free from all modifications, who has cast out the ocean of blinding sins and rescued those submerged within it;
whose nature as the individual soul (jīva) shines forth in the lotuses of the six bases (ādhāras), and whose mind manifests the emergence of creation within the interior of the body. (36)

I joyfully worship that Lord, who is unstained, who has destroyed all sin, whose activity resides in the midst of the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumṇā* channels, and who shines forth as the fourfold limbs of the phenomenal world; "I worship Him! I worship Him! (37).

I always meditate upon the Lord of Liberation, the Great Lord and Sovereign of the gods, who is the very embodiment of yoga for the virtuous; he dwells within the lotus of the mind, and his radiance consists of the eye, the moon, the sun, fire, and other luminaries, manifesting as the essence of all the lords of the divine.

Salutations to you, O ocean of compassion, O Lord of the eight forms, who protects the heavenly world as its sovereign portion, whose manifest splendor dispels darkness, and who is the master of liberation for the dull-witted, the ignorant, the foolish, and the unenlightened. 39.
Skanda said:
Having thus praised Mahādeva and circumambulated him again and again,
they worshipped him with devotion by means of the five [offerings] on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
Abiding by the command of Rudra, Nandin went before him and joyfully spoke these words to them for the purpose of granting a boon. 41.
Nandin said:
"Entreat me with devotion for whatever is truly desired by your hearts;
by the sight of Rudra, you shall indeed become free from sin this very day."
In this world, the preeminent position of kings is very difficult to attain;
likewise, even in the world of the gods, supreme prosperity is exceedingly hard to obtain.
The fishermen said:
"We do not beg for you here in this world while you remain;
we desire [a place] in the heavenly worlds. Grant us a separate station. (44)
Skanda said:
Having heard their words, the god gave his consent;
those fierce Gaṇas then placed him upon a celestial chariot that fulfills all desires. 45.
And the Pramathas, stationed in their vehicles, led them through the sky to the abodes of the gods;
those [beings] were established separately by the fierce Gaṇas in the worlds of the deities.
"Do not stay here; go quickly to that place which you desire, even from Śakra.
If you do not depart, I shall expel you today, for I will strike you in battle. (47)
Thus being struck by those sword-like words, the inhabitants of heaven,
suddenly filled with indignation, rose up for battle.
The fishermen, arrogant because of their boon, fought together with the gods;
having completely conquered those places, they remained in the abodes of the gods.
Having made those leaders of Śakra’s world their own, O noble one, they enjoyed pleasures therein by the grace of Rudra. 50.
O Pot-born One, at the end of a thousand years, all the gods, including Śakra and the others who oversee the worlds of the guardians of the quarters, assembled and departed. 51.
Having heard their words, he immediately went to the world of Viṣṇu along with the gods in the cosmic egg and reported that calamity.
Having heard those words, Viṣṇu, together with Brahmā and the others,
went once more to the world of Rudra and then related that calamity.
The gods said:
"Protect, protect us, O Lord, your servants who have been shaken from our positions and afflicted by the calamity of the fisherman! Salutations to you, the remover of all distress! (54)
Rudra said:
"The gods must necessarily experience the fruit of actions performed that are declared auspicious;
for they have been thoroughly gratified by those fishermen, who were free from sin through the power of their asceticism. (55)
Therefore, with my mind uplifted by their devotion and satisfaction, I granted them a boon:
"They shall enjoy me for a hundred thousand years, not through my being requested. (56)
Skanda said:
Having heard the words of Rudra, the gods returned to their own world;
there they enjoyed happiness for one thousand lakhs of years.
The worlds of Bhuvaḥ, Svar, Jana, Maha, Tapa, and Hari are mine;
these are the eight divine worlds belonging to the sun, the moon, and the host of stars. 58.
Once, while wandering the earth as an envoy of Viṣṇu, Nārada was honored with devotion by a fisherman,
who bowed down to him, addressing him as "the son of Brahmā."
Vaṅgu said:
"Oh, what great fortune is mine today that you have come here!
O Lord, knower of events, tell me the news of the worlds."
Nārada said:
"O child, having become a guardian of this world, why do you not remain vigilant?
A lifespan of one hundred and ten thousand years has been granted to you by Rudra for your stability."
At the end of that period, you will undoubtedly fall from your equanimity, once again performing your own worldly duties on earth as before. 62.
Vaṅgu said:
"O Goddess, I shall perform austerities here, propitiating the all-pervading Śiva;
for in liberation, such brothers as those will not exist for me again for a long time. (63)
Nārada said:
O wise one, you should never even mentally speak thus regarding a mortal;
for the tree of austerity that has grown here bears no fruit there.
"O child, formerly on the holy Himalaya, this tree of asceticism arose; it was produced by those who performed penance there at that time. (65)
Vaṅgu said:
"O Lord, O Knower of All, tell me again how many years I must remain in this place, especially in relation to my brothers. (66)
Nārada said: "Indeed, there remains only one year of the enjoyment of heaven for you;
yet all your brothers and you yourself will surely fall from heaven."
For as long as there is pleasure, so long indeed will there be suffering; since prosperity is accompanied by both pleasure and pain, it is abandoned by the wise. 68.
Nirvāṇa alone is true happiness, being entirely free from all sufferings;
for this very reason, liberation should be sought by the noble and the wise, since it is auspicious. 69.
Vaṅgu said:
"O Nārada, knower of dharma, we certainly and steadfastly desire nirvāṇa;
therefore, quickly sprinkle me with those nectars of instruction. (70)
"In the presence of our brothers, let this truth and news be related;
we shall certainly go there once again to that place of asceticism. (71)
Nārada said:
"Go quickly with your brothers to the Tapaḥsānu peak of the Himālayas;
there you should perform penance, having received instruction from Lomaśa. (72)
Skanda said:
Having thus instructed him, O Sage, the self-controlled Nārada went to the fishermen;
having traveled through all the worlds, he related that news to them.
Having heard the words of Nārada, they then consulted together and,
abandoning all the worlds, departed for the Himavat mountain.
Beholding Lomaśa, who was self-controlled and established in austerity, they went to his hermitage;
having bowed down according to the rules with devotion, they spoke from all sides.
The fishermen said:
"We should be known as those devoid of dharma, fallen from heaven;
having enjoyed much happiness among them, we have been impelled here by fate. (76)
"Where shall we go? Where shall we stay, we who desire nirvāṇa?
Therefore, please instruct us, for you are all-knowing and a knower of the self. (77)
Skanda said:
O sage, having heard these words of theirs, Lomaśa, filled with joy,
then spoke these words to those well-come ones who were established in yoga.
Lomaśa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O best of men, since you have maintained such an intellect!
Turning your backs on great suffering, you regard heaven as a trivial dream-like pleasure."
Having bathed three times at the confluence of the river worshipped by the head of Hara with the Alakanandā at Dharmakūṭa, proceed to the hermitage of Rudra.
Meditating upon the five-syllabled [mantra] with the heart, worship Śaṅkara;
that form of Śiva, which bestows liberation, consists of "Namaḥ" at the beginning and the fourth [case-ending] at the end. 81.
The fishermen said:
"O Lord, we wish to ask you something regarding your master:
for how many years has that religious student been performing penance here? (82)
Skanda said: Having heard those words, the self-controlled and noble one, whose face was smiling, laughed and spoke these words to them, he who is the very essence of long life.
Lomaśa said:
"Since my life is short, let this chest of mine be seen by you two while it is still hairless;
for that original state, inferred from its seal, was certainly devoid of hair."
At the end of each manvantara, this single hair will certainly fall out;
by this measure, O fishermen, the manvantaras have passed away.
Skanda said:
Having heard his words, the fishermen were struck with wonder;
censuring themselves, they indeed bowed down to that mountain-dweller. 86.
At the end of the bright fortnight of the month of Śukra, they joyfully bathed according to the prescribed rites three times at Devaprayāgaka, during the transit of the sun and on the full moon day.
Having ascended the Rudrāśrama mountain, they practiced austerities for a long time;
with their minds fixed on Him alone, they worshipped Him day and night continuously for one year. 88.
Then, having swiftly abandoned their bodies, those wise ones entered Śaṅkara, who is the embodiment of light—the fruit of their austerities performed on the Himālaya mountains. 89.

The wise man, endowed with devotion and excellent mental disposition, who hears the majesty of Himavat, shall obtain that fruit which one gains from bathing in the waters at Devaprayāga, as well as pure fame and the celestial realm. 90.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Himālaya," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 9 ||
Agastya said:
O best among the knowers of Brahman, I desire to hear from you once more about the penance performed by the gods, the asuras, and others. (1)
O Lord, in what manner did he perform penance? Who was he? When did he do so?
By what rite? Who was he? And in what place upon the Himālayas was the object of meditation? || 2 ||
Skanda said:
Listen, O sage, for I shall indeed explain to you that which was asked of me by you—
concerning the rite of Brahma, austerity, and knowledge— at the outset, with your mind composed.
Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should first remember the Lord;
then, having paid homage to the Earth, one should perform the placement of the syllables (nyāsa) according to the sequence of one's own seat. 4.
O Goddess, whose girdle is the ocean and whose breasts are the mountain ranges;
O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch of your feet.
Having thus offered praise and placed his foot [on the threshold], the wise man should go outside;
proceeding toward the south-western direction, he should perform the evacuation of waste.
One should void urine and excrement facing north during the day;
at night, one should face south; but during the two twilights, one should face as one does during the day.
Having placed the sacrificial thread around his neck and becoming silent, the wise man,
having thus performed these acts for the sake of purification, should approach a body of water.
Having taken up water and earth, one who is restrained in speech should perform the rite facing north during the day, or facing south if it is at night. (9)

One application [of clay] should be made on the penis, three on the anus, ten on the left hand, and likewise ten on both hands; thus, seven applications of clay for purification must be performed by a noble, wise, and pure person. 10.
O Brahmin, having thus performed purification three times for each hand and three times for the feet, one should take pure water and sip it again and again. 11.
Thereafter, O Agastya, that wise man should indeed look upon the sun, a cow, or a twice-born brahmin;
for by looking at them, he shall attain complete purification.
Having washed his face and both hands, he should perform the cleansing of the teeth;
taking a pure twig from a milky tree that possesses a knotty joint. (13)
The entire meritorious thorny branch should be twelve finger-breadths in length;
having consecrated it with the mantra, he should face either the east or the north.
O Lord of the Forest, grant us longevity, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and mental retentiveness. 15.
Having washed his face, hands, and feet,
being composed and observing silence, O best of the twice-born, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again and again.
With his hand at the *brahmatīrtha*, the wise man, mindful of the mantra with his intellect, should sit with an upright body, facing either east or north. (17)
Then, O Agastya, one should perform the binding of the ears with the thumb and ring finger;
likewise, one should touch the mouth, the nostrils, the sense of smell, the eyes, the ears,
the arms, and the thighs, and thereafter all the limbs.
May *oṃ* be in my mouth; may *oṃ* be in my two nostrils; may *oṃ* be in my breath; may *oṃ* be in my eyes as sight; may *oṃ* be in my ears as hearing;
may *oṃ* be in my arms as strength; may *oṃ* be in my thighs as vigor.
"May my limbs be free from harm; may my body possess strength through its own form.
(19) Recalling this mantra, the wise Brahmin should touch all his limbs.
Then, having arrived at the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), he should perform the ritual bath again according to the rules. (20)
Having washed his hands, feet, and tongue, and performed the sipping of water (ācamana) together [with the mantra],
he should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) and bind the topknot with the mantra.
Then, having invoked the sacred ford and remembering the mantra with his mind, [he should say]:
"Today, in this very sacred ford, for the sake of joy or whatever is desired in the heart... (22)
"Or I shall perform my bath according to my desire;
thus, O knower of sacred fords, one who holds kusha grass in his hand should emerge from the water with the realization that he is the Ganges itself. (23)
O river, free from fault, with pure waters, the crest of Hara—salutations be to you!
First, the wise man should offer a handful of water (añjali) to the divine Sun.
Reciting the mantra, the wise man should give it and perform a bath with clay:
"O Clay, remove my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me. (25)
"By the sin removed by you, one is liberated from all sins";
reciting this once, the wise man should perform the smearing of his entire body. (26)
Then, with the Praṇava, the practitioner of mantras should cause the water to circulate three times;
thereafter, in a very pure, auspicious, and merit-bestowing sacred ford that removes all sins.
The wise one, recollecting the mantra with a mind free from impurity,
should rub all his limbs and rinse himself again and again.
One should perform three immersions; this is considered the supreme bathing for the deity.
The wise man should purify himself while reciting the Drupadā verse and other hymns. (29)
Taking water with kusa grass, facing the east, and joining his palms together, he should repeatedly recite the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā. (30)
One should again place water on the head twenty-one times, or fifteen times;
having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one should recite the Gāyatrī ten times.
Having sprinkled water three times on his hands and head with a water-pot,
and having thus performed the ritual of bathing, he should emerge from the water,
put on two garments including an upper cloth, and then perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
Whether standing in water or on dry land, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
indeed, one may offer them as one desires, for everything is established in water.
All the hosts of gods are water, and the hosts of ancestors are remembered as water;
therefore, water should be offered in water, for what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
One should offer handfuls of water to the thirty gods and the ancestors in the water; one should offer handfuls of water to those who died without the funeral rites on dry land.
A twice-born Snātaka, being pure, should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) every day, in due order, for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. 36.
Both the gods and the ancestors long for water;
but if it is not given, they return in despair just as they came. (37)
Therefore, with every effort, one should satisfy the ancestors and the deities; through such satisfaction one attains success, while failure to satisfy them leads to transgression. 38.
Having performed that rite of libation (tarpaṇa) and wearing his lower garment,
the ascetic, being wise and observing silence, should perform the twilight devotions (sandhyā) after sipping water three times.

With his body straight, sitting with his face turned either toward the east or the north, the wise man, mindful with his intellect, should remember the Manu [Mantra] at the Brahmatīrtha of the hand. || 40 ||
Having arrived at a pure place, one should consider the purification of the site:
a ritual performed at home is said to have a single-fold merit, while that performed by a river is remembered as having a ten-fold merit.
In a cow-pen it is a hundredfold; in a fire-sanctuary it is more than a hundredfold;
and in perfected fields, at sacred fords, and in the presence of deities, it is likewise.
In the presence of Śiva, on a mountain peak that was exceedingly lofty, there were likewise hundreds of thousands of millions of kiṃśuka trees, infinite in number.
There, one obtains merit multiplied by ten million times ten million;
on the ridges of the snowy mountain, the merit of asceticism is increased a hundred millionfold.
On a peak where snow is visible, ten times the fruit is obtained;
on a peak marked by icicles, one shall obtain a hundredfold fruit. 45.
In the valleys of the Snowy Mountain it is a nikharva, but in the middle,
on the peaks of the massed snow, it is progressively a mahāpadma-fold greater.
Then the wise one should prepare a seat according to the prescribed rule:
tiger skin for the attainment of all siddhis, and the skin of a deer for the attainment of knowledge.
Know that clothing made of reeds removes disease and increases prosperity;
silk is known to be nourishing, and woolen cloth is the liberator from suffering. 48.
On the seat as described, the wise one, with body straight, should enter; the discerning one, having adopted either the svastika or the lotus posture. (49)
Having properly placed the soles of the auspicious feet between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body straight, one assumes the Svastika, the great posture.
Having thus performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the one of great wisdom, first recollecting the sages, remained silent with eyes closed. (51)
Having performed inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbha), and exhalation (recaka), one should then meditate upon [the syllables] as dark, red, and white in the three locations. 52.
O twice-born one, the wise man should know the sequence step by step at the navel, the heart, and the forehead, during inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka). 53.
The knower of mantras should perform the touching of the limbs upon six locations;
he should place [the mantra] on the heart, the forehead, the head, the shoulders, the eyes, and the hands. (54)
The wise man should first offer the *arghya*—accompanied by flowers—to the Sun, while recollecting the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā" and remembering the Manu in his mind. 55.

Then, having taken up the rosary made of the gems as previously described, the practitioner of mantra, established in meditation and with senses well-controlled, should perform the recitation with a focused mind. (56)
A rosary fashioned from rudrākṣa beads accomplishes all desires; a rosary fashioned from crystal beads bestows all supernatural attainments (siddhis). 57.
A garland made of pearls brings about good fortune and is an ornament of auspicious splendor;
another, likewise produced from rubies, bestows the direct realization of mantras;
and a golden or silver garland grants all desires.
One should keep count; then that which is recited becomes fruitful.
Whatever is recited without counting, all of that becomes fruitless. 59.
Therefore, the wise person should diligently keep count of the recitation;
then, having offered the recitation, the knower of mantras should present the arghya offering to the deity.
Then the practitioner of mantra should perform a hymn of praise for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims.
This is the duty prescribed for householders; for yogins, another is said to be required. (61)
That which has been proclaimed by the very steadfast as the practice of dharma within the home is indeed the duty of the householder;
and that which is practiced on a seat, at a sacred ford, or on a mountain peak by the foremost yogis is the duty of yoga.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Duties of the Householder," in the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 10 ||
Skanda said:
Now I shall proclaim the Dharma, especially for yogins;
having risen at the hour of Brahmā, the lord of yogins should indeed remember his guru and the Lord.
Having performed purification, the yogi should then sit upon a firm seat in a sacred field of accomplishment,
with his body straight, facing either the east or the north.
Placing one foot upon one thigh and likewise [the other] upon the other thigh—this is declared to be the yogic posture (yogāsana). || 3 ||
Having taken up the ritual ingredients and reciting the mantra, the wise knower of mantras should satisfy the deity and the Guru, and indeed smear himself [with the remains]. || 4 ||

One should always first apply the Tripuṇḍra on the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), then on the forehead, the throat, the region of the waist, the heart, and likewise on the two shoulders. || 5 ||
The yogi [should place his hands] at the navel, on the back, as well as on the elbows, on the other two [elbows],
on the wrists, and on the hips and the region of the waist.
The immersion of yogins is considered to extend from the crown of the head (brahmarandhra) down to the soles of the feet;
for householders and ascetics, it is specifically limited to the area above the navel.
Having bathed in this manner, the great yogi should then wear rudrākṣas;
the yogi should then meditate upon himself by means of the self as that supreme Lord.
