In the heart-lotus with eight petals, within the pericarp and its beautiful filaments,
one should meditate upon the Lord, whose form is the Praṇava, devoid of beginning or end, and the size of a thumb.
Then the yogi, remaining perfectly steady, should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas):
he should fill the air through the iḍā and retain it (kumbhaka) through the piṅgalā. 10.
And by means of that Suṣumṇā, he should surely cause [the breath] to enter the Brahmarandhra;
then, being without support, the yogi shall attain the supreme yoga. 11.

One should bathe the Lord with mental [offerings], one should worship Him with mental [offerings], and with silken garments produced from the mind, and with sandalwood pastes originating from the mind and so forth. 12.
With mentally blossomed flowers, with mental incense and lamps, with food offerings produced from the mind, and with excellent recitations born of the mind; || 13 ||

O Sage, the wise knower of mantras should mentally recite the mantra with the syllables arising from the six locations, along with the groups of protective deities, using both the sequential and reverse orders. 14.
One desiring liberation should recite the mantra "Tāra-pūrva-namaś-cānta-śivāya," which delivers one from the suffering of saṃsāra. 15.
The wise one should mutter the supreme six-syllabled mantra, joined with Śiva and Śakti, the seed-syllable conjoined with the six vowels, together with the Tāraka. || 16 ||
Thus, know this to be the supreme yoga of the yogis who are one with the Supreme Self;
the yogi who practices in this way is liberated while living, without a doubt. || 17 ||
O Sage, one should worship him at the appropriate times with offerings produced from the mind, according to the six seasons, as they arise.
Agastya said:
"What you have told me is wonderful for all living beings;
indeed, for yogis, bathing with sacred ashes while bearing spiritual power is highly commended. (19)
From what does that arise, and what would its fruit be like?
And who is the one liberated by bathing in ashes? O Skanda, tell me that now.
Skanda said:
Listen, O Pot-born one; I shall speak that which you have indeed asked me of.
By the mere hearing of it, one obtains the fruit of the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna). || 21 ||
When the three worlds were consumed by the fire of the eye of Bhīmarudra at the end of the eon (kalpa),
they therefore call it "ashes" (bhasma).
Having taken that ash, Rudra smeared his limbs with it;
bathing in water was set aside by him. Therefore, ash is praised.
The celestial sages, yogins, and perfected ones, having been sprinkled with the ashes produced from Rudra’s glance, quickly attain the supreme state, purified.
There is no bath superior to ash, and there is no liberation superior to ash;
there is no firm standing superior to the seat of ash, and there is no worship superior to the worship of ash.
The wise man, who bathes in ashes and whose nature is Śiva, is not defiled by sins,
nor even by the five great crimes beginning with the killing of a Brahmin.
If a mortal who eats forbidden food bathes with ashes,
he is not tainted by those sins, nor even by the act of approaching a woman who should not be approached.
He is not tainted by the sins arising from false speech, nor by the verbal censures arising from slander, nor by untruths that strike at the vital points, nor by denials. || 28 ||
There was a certain best of the twice-born, who had reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge and was renowned as a devotee of Viṣṇu, residing in the excellent city of Antarvedī.
The Brahmin was devoted to the six duties and intent upon the recitation of the Vedas; he was truthful in character, disciplined by austerity, and self-controlled toward all living beings. (30)
Devoted to the performance of rites for the gods and ancestors, he was intent on worship;
he was constant in his habit of giving and always acted kindly toward his guests.
His son, the best of the twice-born, known as Viṣṇudāsa, was devoid of learning and suffered great misery; he passed away when his father was still alive.
His conduct was always contrary to worldly norms; he was a consumer of all things, a mere mockery, constantly fond of the wives of others, and a thief of others' property.
O Pot-born One, he wanders by night and sleeps by day, is intent on visiting courtesans,
and is shunned by all people as well as his own kinsmen.
O sage, that deceitful Mleccha had previously died on the bank of the Vāgmatī;
by the merit of that [death], O Brahmin, he was reborn as a learned Śrotriya who reviled sacred rites. (35)
Once, during the day, a brahmin, severely afflicted by hunger,
failed to obtain any food anywhere, even by means of theft, while in a foreign land.
Then, having wandered through regions, villages, and houses during the night, that twice-born man requested his wife for a meal. || 37 ||
Viṣṇudāsa said:
"O dear one, O virtuous Suta, give me food now;
for I am afflicted by the fire of intense hunger, so that I may sustain my life. (38)
O beloved, we wandered through many kingdoms within the house of the wind-god,
yet nowhere could food be found, and I was overcome with exhaustion.
Sumukhī said:
"What has been spoken by my beloved today is true; O Lord, you have surely been afflicted by the fires of hunger and are distressed by wandering in exhaustion—of this there is no doubt. (40)
"O beloved, I swear that even though I rose at the same time as you, I have not eaten food today.
Is there no food in the house? What shall I give you? Forgive me. (41)
Skanda said:
Having heard these words, though they were truthful, the Brahmin perceived them as false;
and because of his wife’s sweet speech, he was utterly overwhelmed with anger.
Afflicted by hunger and filled with rage, he struck his sweet-speaking wife with his foot, threatening her for the sake of his belly.
Having now abandoned his wife, who was pregnant and deceased, within the house,
that most sinful man departed from the city gate and went outside.
Having fallen from there, he wandered from country to country for a long time; adopting the life of a thief, he spent some years in that manner.
Once, that wicked man committed a theft in the city;
having been seized, the people quickly bound him and beat him severely. 46.
Then, having quickly released the rope from his teeth in secret during the night,
the wicked one fled outside and sought out a place in the forest.
Then that most wicked man lived continuously in the forests;
having slain certain travelers there, he spent several months.
Having failed to obtain [the meat] on one day, that sinful man killed a cow and, moreover, ate its flesh without having first offered it to the ancestors. 49.
Then that sinner wandered from forest to forest like one insane, his body emaciated by the fire of hunger, afflicted by thirst, and suffering from leprosy. (50)
Then he saw a brahmin walking alone on the road, seeking alms, extremely dejected, destitute, and clad in but a single garment. || 51 ||
From afar, the most wicked man struck a traveler in the forest with an arrow;
having killed him, he then searched that arrow-head for treasures.
Having fallen from his state and wondering what might remain, he searched for whatever wealth he had displayed;
then he beheld an eleven-faced Rudrākṣa upon his head.
Taking that rudrākṣa, he bound it upon his own head;
though possessed of the five great sins, he wandered the earth like a madman.
Then, having crossed over mountain passes, he went to the ridge of Mount Himādri;
there stands the self-manifested Linga Kuśeśvara, supreme in its splendor.
There flows the clear Kauśikī, the best of rivers;
and at its confluence with the Indravatī, the Linga of Ādi shines resplendent.
Having wandered from forest to forest, he reached the bank of the Kauśikī;
his soul restrained by the five sins, he was afflicted with leprosy sores and trembling all over.
He beheld that great Liṅga, joyfully worshipped by the sage with offerings of fruits and roots, along with the five types of ritual services (pañcopacāra). || 58 ||
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, at the dead of night,
it was indeed worshipped by the seer named Kuśa while he remained sleepless during his ascetic penance.
Thereupon that thief reflected upon his attendant:
"How shall I take those foods there for my own meal? (60)
If that Snātaka, being alone there, should strike me while I am likewise alone in anger, I shall endure it and eat those [fruits] by force. (61)
If he should strike me severely while I am afflicted by hunger, or if he sees me in such a wretched state, I shall not release them. || 62 ||
Skanda said:
O Pot-born one, as he reflected thus, he became despondent in his heart;
trembling and with emaciated limbs, he approached his presence.
While the Sage was meditating at night, intent upon his prayers and reflections,
[the demon] went quietly to the vicinity of the Linga and forcibly carried off the offerings.
Then, out of fear of the sage, the twice-born one, trembling and agitated, struck his forehead against the top of the linga; thus he rubbed it at that time.
Touched on his forehead by the touch of the linga and smeared with its sacred ash,
he slowly rose up, trembling, overwhelmed by fear, and deeply agitated.
Having touched his hands, which were marked with ash, to the base of the linga with both wrists,
that most wicked man brought the offerings, went outside, and ate them.
The five great sins, having observed that he was stationed in a sacred region of Śiva, approached him in order to deceive him. (68)
Then, by means of their illusory power, they displayed divine food of many flavors before him in order to entice him, and having approached him, they strove [to seduce him].
The wicked ones said: "O fallen one! Behold this excellent divine food brought here by us out of affection for you. (70)
"O Brahmin, we are afflicted by hunger, emaciated in body, and likewise wounded;
once we know for certain that [the food] has been brought, we shall surely become your companions. (71)
"O Brahmin, perform your bath in the water, smear ashes upon your forehead, and now cast the Rudrākṣa residing on your head into the water. (72)
"O Brahmin, having thus performed your purification, though devoid of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, eat the food as you desire; indeed, O dear friend, take it. (73)
The fallen one said:
"O friends, even though you have brought this fourfold choice of food out of affection for me, I shall not eat it today. (74)
I have brought this fruit-offering of various excellent flavors;
it is a grace from the Lord of Beings, as well as through the favor of the sage.
Wounded, trembling, and with emaciated limbs, I was unable even to bathe;
yet I did not abandon my rudrākṣa beads, nor was I able to wash away the sacred ash. || 76 ||
"What was eaten last night was pleasant and complete; therefore, I am satiated by those fruits.
Whatever the Lord of Beings shall give tomorrow, that I shall eat—of this there is no doubt. (77)
Skanda said:

Indeed, through contact with the ash, the rudrākṣa, and the Śiva-liṅga, he became free from sin, possessed of knowledge, and, having fallen away from [worldly existence], his soul became one with Śaṃkara. 78.
Then, having heard his words, they set out in despair;
O Sage, once he had slipped away, they were unable to remain there nor could they touch him.
Seeing the ashes and the rosary on his limbs, the sins of the fallen one became overwhelmed with fear and dissolved right there upon the ground.
Then that brahmin also, having fallen from his state, met his death at night;
having reached the bank of the Kauśikī, he was tormented by its many cold waters. || 81 ||
At that very moment, those messengers of Yama arrived in the cave of the Himalaya mountain to bring him away, and they bound him with ropes. 82.
At that very moment, the messengers of Śiva arrived there,
seated upon a celestial chariot (vimāna) resplendent like ten thousand suns.
Reproaching those messengers of Yama, they quickly cast up the rope and joyfully placed him upon a vehicle accompanied by the daughters of Rudra.
Having been placed upon a celestial chariot by the messengers of Śiva,
he was certainly led by the Gaṇas in a vehicle possessing the splendor of the sun to the abode of Śiva.
Having immediately cast off his body, he attained supreme liberation;
and beholding their actions, they reflected, filled with sorrow.
Then, O Brahmin, that Kāla, having first deliberated among themselves and recognized that they were endowed with the power of Śiva, spoke to those servants of Yama.
Kāla said:
"O you devotees devoted to Śiva, how is it that you have so thoughtlessly placed this hell-bound brāhmaṇa upon the vehicle? (88)

Seized by the five great sins and fallen from his own conduct and caste—namely, the killer of a cow, the killer of a Brahmin, the killer of a woman, the killer of a child, and likewise the killer of a man. (89)
O Lord, by this [person] no bathing has been performed, nor likewise recitation, worship, charity, purification, meditation, virtuous deeds, or ritual action. (90)
O Lord, having abandoned that hellish state of unbearable torment for one who is thus marked by sin and fallen from the auspicious vehicle to which he had been elevated, [he attains liberation]. 91.
"Commanded by Citragupta, we have come here;
having brought that fallen twice-born man, let him be cast into the hells. 92.
"O auspicious-souled one, having received this command and being sent by our Lord, we have come here; what shall we do as your servants? (93)
The messengers of Śiva said: "You must not speak of his despicable conduct; for by the Lord, his sins have been removed from every side. (94)
"Even if many and manifold sins have been committed by him at all times, he has become sinless; O messengers of Yama, hear the reason for this. (95)
O child, he who has touched this supreme Liṅga Kuśeśvara with his two hands or his head, even if unintentionally, is purified. 96.
Those who behold him constantly wearing a rudrākṣa on his head and sacred ash (vibhūti) upon his forehead, [perceive that very reality] within his body. 97.
"An order was swiftly given to me by Śiva: 'Let him who has certainly fallen from his status in this world be brought back. For that reason, we have come here. (98)
"Now this twice-born man is being led by us to the world of Śiva; you go to the realm of Yama, so that those who have come here shall not suffer. (99)
Skanda said:
Having spoken thus, those messengers of Śiva now [departed] from the followers of Yama;
indeed, having mounted that celestial chariot, they urged on the vehicles and mounts. 100.
Resplendent in a vehicle that shines like ten thousand suns, adorned with networks of tinkling bells and filled with the sounds of song and musical instruments, he glows as he descends.
He is attended by yak-tail whisks shaken by the hands of Rudra’s daughters,
and, having fallen from his former state, he is honored with offerings by Gandharva servants.
Then, having cleansed his evil deeds, he departed by means of a celestial chariot;
and after surveying all the worlds of the gods, he reached the world of Śiva.
Uttering "Excellent! Excellent! to all the gods dwelling in every world, he approached Śiva filled with joy, like a second Śaṅkara himself. || 104 ||
There, in that divine Śivapura, which is supreme and endowed with every happiness,
he who has fallen [from his former state] is honored by the Gaṇas for thousands of millions of Yugas.
Then, having fallen from there, that lord of the earth was born upon the earth;
O best of the twice-born, he became a sovereign ruler in Jambūdvīpa.
Then, having fallen from there to the earth and enjoyed pleasures as he desired,
he became once again the king of the gods after casting off his own body.
On the excellent Himavat mountain, the highest fruit of ascetic power;
this is what has been told, O wise one, by Viṣṇudāsa regarding that which was performed. 108.

O Brahmin, I shall further describe specifically the supreme fruit of the various manifestations [of power]: the merit of performing the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) ten million times, which supersedes the ritual bath with water.
A bath with water and a bath with ashes—the latter is far superior;
for ashes consist of all sacred fords, and Śiva consists of all gods.

One who bathes in ashes, wears rudrākṣas, and especially recites the Rudra-mantra—that person is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. Thus, such a person does not see the realm of Yama and, through his sincere devotion, attains the supreme state.

Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices— that fruit, indeed, the mantra-practitioner obtains by wearing Rudrākṣa beads while being joined with the Śiva-mantra and performing the ash-bath. 112.

Whatever merit is found in all acts of giving and whatever fruit exists in all religious duties, that is attained by one who, concentrated in meditation on Śiva, has applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) upon his forehead. || 113 ||
The wise and discerning man should wear rudrākṣas in various places:
on the crest-lock, amidst the mass of hair, on the neck, and likewise on the two hands. 114.
The wise one was Rudra himself—of this there is no doubt—present in his forearms, his two elbows, his wrists, as well as his chest and ears;
he was inaccessible to all beings to behold, let alone to harm. (115)

O pot-born Brahmin, O scorcher of enemies, you have described the most wonderful fruit that arises from the wearing of ashes and the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads; what further, supreme matter do you wish to hear? 116.

O twice-born one, I have indeed described to you that which was done by me through ignorance regarding the wearing of ashes; do you now wish to hear further of the excellent fruits obtained by Nami? (117)
Agastya said: "O Lord, O scorcher of foes, you have described to me the great merit of the rudrākṣas; I am delighted by hearing of that most wonderful thing. (118)
Who is the deity? What is its form? And what is the fruit from wearing it?
O Lord, tell me how Rudra was satisfied by the rudrākṣa. (119)
Skanda said: "O Agastya, that which was previously told to me by Śaṅkara on Mount Acala— namely,
the fruit of the rudrākṣas and their form according to the prescribed rule— " (120)
For the rudrākṣas are my very forms, bestowing the fruits of the four aims of human life;
I shall tell you all that was indeed spoken by Rudra—listen. 121.
And among all trees, the Nameru is the most excellent;
know that its fruits are the Rudrākṣas, which are the very forms of Rudra. 122.
The Lord of the tree of saṃsāra bears fruit and the essences of the earth;
likewise, the world consists of those very things which are the causes for the upliftment of the world.
O Agastya, all beings, beginning with the gods and including humans, become the very forms of Rudra through this dhāraṇā; whatever they desire, they attain it—of this there is no doubt.
Know that the rudrākṣa bestows liberation, is a means for attaining prosperity, and grants all desires;
the rudrākṣa burns away sins and destroys suffering and poverty. 125.
By binding Rudrākṣas on the hand according to the prescribed measurement, one attains liberation;
he directly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation—he is Rudra himself, of this there is no doubt. 126.
By wearing it on the head, the wise man obtains a fruit ten million times greater;
on the ears, it would be ten million-fold; and on the neck, a thousand million-fold. (127)
It should be infinite at the crest-lock and likewise at the two armpits;
it should be ten lakhs on the chest. By wearing [the mantra] upon the limbs, such is the fruit. 128.
Even if devoid of recitation and meditation, a twice-born who wears the rudrākṣa is worthy of salutation by gods and asuras alike, just like the Lord himself. 129.
Completely liberated from all sins, he attains the supreme goal;
moreover, he obtains ten times the merit of other garlands through the recitation [of this]. 130.
By moving [the beads] with the hand, one attains a thousand [mantras] joined with the human [count];
by three zeros [i.e., ten thousand] moved by the human [hand], one attains a hundred thousand by that very thousand. || 131 ||
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, it becomes ten million; by reciting it ten million times, one becomes all-seeing.
Therefore, through a rosary of Rudrākṣa beads, the merit is multiplied by ten billion.

O twice-born one, O highly wise one, by means of the whispered recitation (upāṃśu) as well as the mental recitation (cetas), one obtains merit ten million times ten millionfold more than that of the vocal recitation (vācika). || 133 ||
Through the mind engaged in the yoga of meditation, one shall obtain infinite fruit.
Now I shall describe the fruit of each of the faces of the rudrākṣas individually. 134.
Śiva with one face directly removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
this God of gods with two faces certainly destroys the sin of killing a cow. 135.
One with three faces, having the form of fire, removes the sin of killing a woman in an instant;
one with four faces is Brahmā himself, who dispels the sin of killing a human being.
Likewise, Rudra is five-faced, known by the name Kālāgni, and terrifying;
O sage, listen with a concentrated mind to the majesty of the Five-faced One. 137.
By avoiding those who should not be approached, by abstaining from what should not be eaten,
by not looking at what should not be seen, and by not speaking what should not be spoken—
one is liberated from all sins through the wearing of the five-faced [linga]. || 138 ||
O Sage, by constantly wearing [this mantra] at the base of the right hand, my six-faced form shall belong to me, and one is liberated from all sins. (139)
One attains victory in battle and is liberated from sins and fears;
hear now the fruit of wearing [this] six-faced [mantra] on the hands and the neck:
one becomes incapable of being slain by any beings and may wander upon the earth like Rudra. 140.
The seven-faced rudrākṣa is indeed the serpent king named Ananta;
by wearing it, one becomes fortunate, enriched with gold, and happy.
Furthermore, there is the destruction of enemies, as well as freedom from disease, strength, and the absence of all distress. 141.
The Rudrākṣa is the eight-faced deity, known by the name Śūlapāṇi.
O Pot-born one, comprehend the greatness of this eight-faced one:
by wearing it, one lives for more than a hundred years, becoming equal to the Lord himself. 142.
O Sage, this nine-faced Rudrākṣa is the god Bhairava;
by wearing it on the left hand, one becomes possessed of incomparable strength.
He is never at any time afflicted by the nine planets, nor by spirits, piśācas, hosts of ḍākinīs, or by various other deities. || 144 ||
Whoever commits five thousand million killings—all that indeed perishes through the wearing of the nine-faced [mantra]. 145.
This ten-faced rudrākṣa is Lord Janārdana himself;
O highly wise one, I shall describe the fruit resulting from its wearing—listen to that. (146)
All the planets, piśācas, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas,
and pannagas perish through the recitation of the ten-faced one.
O Sage, the Rudrākṣa with eleven faces is joined with the eleven parts of Īśvara; it is the great pervasive lord named Śambhu. 148.
One should always wear it on the crest-lock; hear now the fruit of its merit:
by wearing that rudrākṣa, one constantly obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of vājapeya sacrifices. (149)
O Pot-born One, the twelve-faced Rudrākṣa is named Sūrya; it possesses the great splendor of the Sun and is endowed with the twelve rays of Āditya.
By wearing it, one becomes possessed of great splendor continuously;
by wearing it constantly at the hairline, one becomes equal to the sun—of this there is no doubt. (151)
One is not afflicted by the nine planets, beginning with the Sun, even when they are most terrible; such is the fruit proclaimed for the Gomedha sacrifice and for its vows. 152.
One certainly obtains that fruit which is the reward of fasting;
the sick man is freed from afflictions, and the unfortunate gains good fortune. 153.
This rudrākṣa with thirteen faces is indeed named Kāmadeva;
he by whom it is worn around the neck is Rudra himself—of this there is no doubt. (154)
This second [form] is Kāmadeva himself; he becomes the agitator of women.
One attains all desires and the perfection of all good fortune;
even one devoid of luck shall obtain success in every undertaking. 155.
On the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, one should constantly wear upon one's head this rudrākṣa, which is the eternal Supreme Brahman, all-pervading, and composed of all splendor. 156.
He is undoubtedly the embodiment of the fourteen worlds;
therefore, he is remembered as the fourteenth face, the most excellent of all. 157.
And by those who wear the fourteen-faced rudrākṣa upon their head, all fourteen worlds are held there. || 158 ||

As many forms as there are of the inhabitants of the netherworld and the heavens, and as many as there are among stationary beings and those endowed with life— so many are the forms of Rudra; all these forms abide throughout the worlds.
O Sage, he by whom an udumbara fruit is worn has indeed worn me;
for he who always bears the four-faced Lord on his head has borne me as well. 160.
Out of affection for you, I shall declare the fruit of its merit; listen!
All success rests eternally in his hand.
That is obtained with great hardship; likewise, another becomes a perfected one (siddha).
It constantly removes all sins and is attained through great merit. 162.
He by whom that rudrākṣa is worn is not defiled by sins; it is as if all the great gifts (mahādāna) that exist on earth have been bestowed in their entirety. 163.
A mortal obtains that fruit by wearing this rudrākṣa;
whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, [he attains it]. 164.
Through the dharma of worship and fasting, one obtains that fruit incessantly;
having become a human like a god, one enjoys every happiness, and after enjoying all desires for a long time, one goes to the supreme state. || 165 ||
By wearing Rudrākṣas with fifteen faces and so forth, the common fruit should be known to arise from the garland worn upon the chest, just as described. 166.
Thus, O Noble One, have been told to you those fruits of the rudrākṣas, which enable one to cross over the cycle of existence, as they were described to me by Giriśa.
In former times, the gods indeed performed most rigorous and meritorious austerities on the Himavat mountain;
having applied Rudrākṣa beads and ashes to their bodies, they obtained the status of chief guardians of the quarters from Maheśa.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Vibhūti and Rudrākṣa," in the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 11.
Agastya said: O Skanda, son of the God of gods, by your grace I have heard the ritual practice for the twice-born regarding the *bhūti* and the rudrākṣa beads. || 1 ||
Now I desire to hear from you, the best among the knowers of Brahman,
concerning the very great peaks of the great mountain Himavat.
"O benefactor of the world, tell me which gods performed penance there;
and also the names of the peaks and the specific characteristics of the sacred fords. (3)
O Lord, tell me in their entirety the names of those sacred fords (tīrthas) wherein the best of gods, having bathed, quickly obtained their fruits.
Skanda said: In former times, there was one of great splendor named Kaśyapa, who was truthful in speech and the grandfather of the three classes—gods, asuras, and humans. || 5 ||
He was always truthful, self-controlled, intelligent, and highly discerning;
he maintained an equal vision toward all beings and had mastered all the scriptures.
He was constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva, dedicated to the mantras of Śiva,
free from all transformations, eternally blissful, and intent upon the meditation on Śiva.
Wearing Rudrākṣas on the aforementioned limbs and smearing his body with holy ash,
he indeed constantly wore the Tripuṇḍra mark upon his foreheads.
O Pot-born One, his son was named Śakra, possessed of great splendor,
sharp intellect, and profound wisdom, and learned in all the scriptures.
At a certain time, in a great field, the most excellent of all holy places, between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, which is purifying and sanctifies the world— 10.
Śakra indeed performed a hundred horse-sacrifices, complete with all their constituent parts,
accompanied by sages who were knowers of the truth of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, together with his family priests.
Together with various sacrificial components, offerings to the gods and ancestors, and acts of worship,
he constantly fed the Brahmins and gave them golden gifts along with ritual fees.
Then the Brahmins and the gods likewise were satisfied;
consequently, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the deities indeed bestowed upon him the consecration.
Then those perfected ones and the seers made that great-souled one the king of Amarāvatī, and they consecrated Śakra as such.
The gods said:
"O Lord, from this day forward, let your sovereignty belong to us;
you are the destroyer and the creator in heaven, you are our giver and indeed our protector."
He is the slayer and the teacher of our enemies, our lord who is ever-evil.
Śakra said: "A great favor has been bestowed upon me by you, the best of the gods, as well as by the sages; therefore, today I honor you who are worthy of reverence."
Skanda said:
Then Śakra honored the sages and gods with various offerings; he honored the brahmins with manifold hymns and the guests with circumambulations. 17.
Then the wise Bṛhaspati spoke to them with certainty:
"Having accepted the worship according to the rules, he shall appear in the midst of the assembly. (18)
Bṛhaspati said:
"O gods, listen to my words, which speak the truth:
O dwellers of heaven, you must not remain here for long after abandoning your celestial realm."
In this world, there are always many calamities for those who are not immortal;
moreover, out of a desire for the state of heaven, the world will inevitably encounter further afflictions.
Devala said:
"Aha! The word of the preceptor is truth, spoken for the welfare of all beings;
what was spoken by the preceptor is indeed true, especially for you."
"Go, O Thirty [Gods], for indeed heaven must not be abandoned;
let not those words spoken even at that moment become false. (22)
Skanda said:
Then the immortals, accepting the words of Jīva and Devala as true,
set out for heaven, quickly placing Kāśyapa at their head.
At that time, as they were setting out toward the third heaven, a mass of splendor spoke from the atmosphere, observing their actions.
Jyotirūpa said:
"O gods, let Śakra not be led to a heaven devoid of austerity;
for that which is worthy of worship in heaven cannot be obtained without rigorous austerities. (25)
O Śakra, if you wish to perform the supreme austerity while enjoying the highest happiness in your kingdom in Amarāvatī, then perform it upon the excellent peak of the Himavat.
Skanda said:
Having heard these great words of the Lord, who is the embodiment of supreme splendor,
Śakra gazed upon the face of his preceptor with a mind full of wonder.
When the Guru had spoken these words, Śakra paid homage to the auspicious Guru and went to the supreme peak of the Himavat mountains to perform ascetic penance.
Having arrived at the eastern direction upon a mountain abounding in darbha grass,
Śakra indeed performed austerities, being perfectly composed in three ways.
Agastya said: Having drunk the incomparable nectar issuing from the lotus of your mouth, I have become eager; impelled by its sweetness, I am moved to drink it once again. (30)
O Viśākha, tell me according to the rules how Śakra then performed penance on the Himālaya mountain; describe that to me exactly as it was done.
Skanda said:
O Sage, there is an excellent river named Āryā, the daughter of Brahmā;
at the confluence of those two, a sacred ford (tīrtha) belonging to Śakra is proclaimed.
He who bathes there even once, having already bathed a hundred times in the Gaṅgā and likewise given gifts, is Śakra himself; of this there is no doubt.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, conjoined with the Pūrvabhādra constellation,
he, to whom the mantra of the Guru had been imparted, joyfully set out for the Himālaya mountain.
Having taken up water with kusa grass and having indeed washed his mouth, feet, and hands,
he performs the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) with sentences consisting of collections of verbal and nominal stems, preceded by the word "today" (*adya*).
Śakra bathed in that great, auspicious tirtha which fulfills one's heart's desires;
having smeared his body with ashes from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head.
Wearing such Rudrākṣa beads on his limbs in the appropriate places,
and having applied the Tripuṇḍra mark upon his forehead, Śakra, the best of gods, [proceeded].
With a single-minded and concentrated focus, he gave gifts to the brahmins;
then Śakra ascended the Himālaya mountain, which was like a crore of jewels.
On the peak adorned with snow, he respectfully assumed his seat;
having installed a linga made of ruby according to the prescribed rites, the bull [Nandin] stood by.
Seated upon a divine throne, he worshipped with devotion through offerings;
then, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and excellent oblations. (40)
Having become perfectly secluded during the eight festival days (parvan), Śakra,
with a serene countenance and purified, having cast off the six groups [of enemies] and discarded the cloak of delusion, was clothed in the cloak of knowledge.
Adopting the yoga previously described and relying upon the dharma of yoga, the lord of yogis performed all manner of asceticism originating from the mind.
Having meditated upon Rudra, the supreme light, as the Liṅga within his own self by means of his own mind,
Śakra indeed recited the mantra for more than a hundred divine years.
Then, at the end of those hundred years, the Lord of Gods, the all-pervading master who brings beings into existence and is composed of all splendor, manifested himself.
Then, in order to grant a boon, he manifested his body from that linga;
having seen him clearly as he joyfully muttered prayers in solitude, [the sage] gazed upon him with delight. 45.
He beheld the Blessed One, the god who is the lord of the three worlds,
Mahādeva in manifest form, Śiva composed entirely of splendor.
O Sage, [he saw] the all-pervading Lord, who has three eyes and two hands, who is peaceful, adorned with a garland of severed heads, and holding a khaṭvāṅga staff and a trident.
The unborn Lord, whose lotus-hand embraces the Goddess, who is worshipped by the secret ones,
who is richly adorned with ornaments of serpents, and whose face is slightly smiling.
Śiva, whose head is crowned with matted locks as radiant as the Gaṅgā, adorned with the crescent moon, moon-faced, gentle, and his body decorated with sacred ash. 49.
Having circumambulated him, he, being thrilled, bowed down like a staff before the wielder of the trident and then offered praise with devotion, joyfully through speech, body, and mind. (50)
Śakra said:
Oṃ!
Salutations to Rudra, the Supreme Self, who holds a trident in his hand.
Salutations again and again to the bearer of the skull, for the sake of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Obeisance be to you, O Three-eyed One, the Great Soul, the sustainer of the world, whose form is the vessel of the cosmic egg, and whose limbs are adorned with divine manifestations. 52.
Obeisance be to you, the bearer of the skull-topped staff, who wears a garland of skulls; O Mṛḍa, Śipiviṣṭa, Bhīma, Vyomakeśa, let there be salutation unto you. 53.
Salutations be to You, who are compassionate toward Your devotees, who are peaceful and whose very form is peace;
salutations to You, the Self appearing in the form of a body, and whose form is the eye. 54.
Salutations be unto you who abide in the nose as the sense of smell, who abide in the ear as the vital air, who are the tongue in the form of taste, and who are the throat itself. 55.
Salutation to the wind residing in the navel, who is the very nature of prāṇa and apāna, who takes the form of samāna and udāna, who is all-pervading, and who is the source of birth.
Salutations again and again to the one who is the fire within the stomach, to Śambhu whose form is fire, to the enjoyer,
to the one whose form is the object of enjoyment, and to the nourisher.
O Supreme Lord, salutations be unto You, who are wisdom, whose form is the mind, who are the mental faculty, and fear; who are wrath, the eater of flesh, and the unborn. 58.
Salutations to you, O Hara, who are consciousness and the individual soul, whose nature is *māyā*, who are the form of both the supreme and the non-supreme self, and who transcend the supreme. 59.
To the one who is without marks and yet possesses all marks, whose nature is existence and who is the future itself;
you are the mother, compassionate toward devotees, and you, O Lord, are the father of the eightfold sovereign powers.
O Lord of my protectors, you who are devoted to the welfare of all beings, please forgive my thousands of offenses, for I was ignorant and possessed of a wicked nature. 61.
Skanda said:
Having heard this divine hymn of praise, Maheśvara was greatly delighted;
indeed, he had been praised by Śakra with threefold devotion.
O Sage, having observed that fierce austerity of Śakra as he remained engaged in penance,
Rudra then spoke these words in order to grant him a boon.
Śrīśvara said:
"O child, a most difficult and great penance has been performed by you;
this superhuman deed was undertaken for the sake of your own liberation."
Therefore, you have manifested your visible form upon the Himālaya;
I am pleased solely because of that fruit which they know resides on the snowy mountain.
"Choose a boon, O knower of dharma, whatever you now desire;
for you, devoted to asceticism, know me to be the cow of plenty. (66)
O Maghavan, that man who shall recite this divine hymn of praise to you will be liberated from all sins and shall go to your city.
His enemies go to destruction at the mere sight of his face;
O Śakra, he shall recite this hymn which removes disease, grief, and fear. (68)
The wise person who recites your hymn shall accomplish even that task which is impossible to achieve;
when he is born upon this earth, he becomes your equal—of this there is no doubt. (69)
Then Śakra, filled with joy upon hearing those cooling words,
entreated Mahādeva with a voice faltering with emotion.
Placing his joined palms upon his head and circumambulating him again and again,
he then bowed down to the Lord of Gods, who had arrived to grant him a boon.
Śakra said: "O giver of boons, I do not seek any other boon;
O Lord, I beg of you that which has been granted to me by the gods. (72)
Īśvara said: "O child, from this day forward, you shall be Indra, the worshiper of the gods;
you shall be the first enjoyer of sacrifices and the lord of the deities in due order. (73)
The gods devoted to your teaching shall prevail; it cannot be otherwise.
As the sovereign in Amarāvatī, I grant you lordship.
"O Śakra, I grant you further the protection of the eastern quarter;
your abode shall be upon the peak on the eastern side of Mount Meru. (75)
A world named Prācīnabarhis shall be yours;
therefore, you will always be the ruler, the creator, and the destroyer of the eastern regions.
Go, O Śakra, toward that direction from which Amarāvatī fled;
having taken the consecration of the gods, you shall surely be with them.
Skanda said:
Having granted the desired boon, the unsurpassed boon of all,
he departed, gladdened by his asceticism, and vanished into the heavens.
Then the gods, having assembled and beheld Śakra from the sky as he was engaged in ascetic penance, felt great joy;
they touched him with their hands, which trembled with intense delight, after having obtained an excellent boon from the Lord of the Mountains.
Then all the hosts of gods, with the Brahmins headed by Bṛhaspati placing Śakra at their front, went to the eastern ridge of the mountain.
Marīci, as well as Atri, Pulastya the best of sages, Pulaha, Kratu, Bhṛgu, and likewise Aṅgiras; || 81 ||
Brahmā and Nārada, the Siddhas, and the best of sages;
Mārkaṇḍeya of long life, and Dadhīci, the best of sages. || 82 ||
Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanandaka, the most virtuous Sanatkumāra, Brahmā, and likewise Kapila. 83.
The Gandharvas and others, the Vasus and hosts of Apsaras, the Sun and the Moon, the stars, Viṣṇu, and likewise others [were there]. 84.
Having bestowed upon him the consecration with waters drawn from the sacred fords of the noble ones, they were filled with reverence as he was established upon the eastern peak of Mount Sumeru.
Agastya said: O Skanda, how did the gods, the celestial sages, the Gandharvas, and the hosts of Apsarases perform the consecration for that great-souled one? 86.
"In what place on Mahāśṛṅga do the perfected ones and the best of sages dwell?
I truly wish to hear this; tell it to me, O all-knowing Lord. (87)
Skanda said:
O Sage, having then brought him from the Himalaya mountain to the Ratnakoṭi peak according to the prescribed rites, he seated him facing north upon a divine jeweled throne. 88.
Having brought the sacred water of the Śakra-tīrtha according to the prescribed rites,
they performed his consecration with water drawn from golden jars.
Brahmā gave [the consecration] while reciting the Vedas, as did Bṛhaspati and Vidhi;
and the Seven Sages repeatedly bestowed the consecration with Vedic hymns.
The gods and other perfected beings (siddhas) likewise praised him with collections of mantras;
the gandharvas did so with songs and instrumental music, and the hosts of apsarases with dances.
Afterwards, honored by the Guru with various kinds of sandalwood paste with joy,
Brahmā further bestowed upon him the sovereignty over all and the lordship of the gods.
The Sun-god again bestowed upon him that most excellent boon of consecration,
which produced heat unbearable to his enemies and possessed a thousand rays of his own splendor.
And Candramas bestowed upon him another boon:
a divine consecration that grants happiness to the gods, cooling yet intensely radiant.
And Viṣṇu further bestowed upon him the most excellent consecration, which instills fear in enemies and crushes the foes of the Daityas. 95.
And Pulomā gave her daughter, the great chaste lady named Śacī;
he married her according to the prescribed rites by the best of the twice-born. 96.
Then those dwelling in heaven joyfully played musical instruments and blew conchs,
as well as kettledrums, war-drums, cymbals, and other mṛdaṅga drums.
There the celestial maidens sang, showers of flowers rained down,
throngs of Apsarases danced, and the sages bestowed their blessings.
Then the cry of "Victory! arose once more on all sides;
and then Agastya, as well as other celestial rishis, offered him worship. 99.
Then Śakra, seated in his celestial chariot, went joyfully to Amarāvatī together with the hosts of gods, Gandharvas, and Apsarases.
Thereafter, he protected Amarāvatī and the gods;
from that time until the present day, he has remained the guardian of that quarter, Vṛṣa.
Therefore, one who is firmly resolved should ascend the mountain Ratnakoṭi;
having bathed in the waters of the noble Tīrtha, he shall dwell for a long time in the world of Śakra.
Thereafter, Vahni, possessing innate and great splendor, surely performed severe penance on the Himālaya;
and having heard that Śakra had obtained the fruit [of his merit], he became once again the noble guardian of a cardinal direction. 103.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Coronation of Śakra," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 12 ||
Lomaharṣaṇa said: O noble Brahmins, having heard that ancient account issued from the mouth of Skanda, the pot-born one rejoiced greatly and became desirous of hearing it again.
Listen, O tigers among sages, to that which was asked with devotion by the pot-born Agastya concerning the life-story of the Son of Pārvatī, the consumer of oblations.
Agastya said:
O Lord, son of Śaṅkara, these people here desire to hear further from you,
the omniscient one, that news concerning the origin of Kṛśānu and Tapana.

O Lord Skanda, leader of the divine army, on which peak of the Himalayas did Agni bathe in what sacred ford, and how did he perform his penance? By whom was he instructed, O All-pervading One, and from where did he obtain that fruit?
Skanda said: In ancient times, there was a brahmin named Aṅgiras who was the mind-born son of Brahmā; his son was the highly resplendent one known as Agni, renowned throughout the three worlds. (5)
He was of great strength and great wisdom, proficient in all the scriptures;
he was constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra and permeated by the constant remembrance of Rudra.
O Sage, at one time that learned Dahanas heard from the seers about the conduct of Indra and how he attained the lordship of the three heavens.
Once during the day, Vahni joyfully questioned Janaka,
repeatedly bowing before his father regarding the news brought by Śakra.
Agni said:
"Salutations again and again to the worshipful father-god, the giver of birth.
Father, how was such extremely difficult penance performed by Śakra?"
"Such is my desire to perform penance;
O highly wise one, please instruct me with compassion as to which place would be suitable for it. (10)
Aṅgiras said:
"The son of Brahmā is the best of rivers, and the river Brahmajvālā is the most excellent;
at the holy ford (tīrtha) where those two meet, O son, the state of Brahman is attained."
On a great peak of the Himavat mountain, which bestows the fruit of all merit,
strewn with various jewels and adorned with much snow.
Between the east and the south, upon the summit of Jyotikūṭa, and to the north, on the mountain of radiant stone named Tejas, which is a mass of ashes; || 13 ||
O son, having bathed at that sacred ford and having duly installed the Liṅga on Mount Tejovacchekhara, you should perform recitation with a one-pointed mind.
One should practice this mantra, which begins with "Tāra" (Om) and ends with "Namaḥ," followed by the name of the recipient; it is the savior from saṃsāra and bestows the desired enjoyments. 15.
Skanda said: Then the brahmin Vaiśvānara, having heard the words of his father,
concentrated his mind with single-mindedness and went joyfully to the Himavat.
Having bathed at that sacred ford and smeared his body with sacred ash,
he should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) on his forehead and then wear rudrākṣa beads.
Then, having ascended that radiant mountain with its beautiful peaks,
one should indeed enter the pure, jewel-flaming summit.
Seated in the yogic posture with the body straight and facing north,
he should meditate according to the prescribed rule upon the Lord who dwells within the cave of the heart of all bodies.
Having installed a linga made of jewels according to the prescribed rite, the best of the twice-born should then worship it with devotion through the three kinds of mental offerings. 20.
For more than a full hundred divine years he recited the supreme mantra;
then the God appeared from the sky, his body composed of radiant light.
Then Rudra revealed his own body to that solitary ascetic, assuming a manifest form for the sake of his devotee.
He too beheld the Lord of gods, the Great Sovereign of all beings,
descending from the sky into the place of his ascetic penance to grant him a boon.
Having beheld Mahādeva in his manifest form, with a smiling face,
two arms, and mounted upon his bull, he was then filled with joy and became pure.
Having circumambulated the god, he then prostrated himself before Rudra with his eight limbs,
addressing him with sweet words faltering with joy.
With his hair standing on end and his palms joined above his head,
he, endowed with the threefold internal state, offered praise to the wielder of the trident.
Agni said: O Śaṅkara, O Īśa, O Mahādeva, O life-giver of the universe, O Lord of living beings, O Great Brahman, O Consciousness—salutations be unto you! 27.
O you whose form is splendor, O three-eyed one, O bearer of the Gaṅgā, O three-eyed one;
O sustainer of the universe, O Lord of the Virāṭ, O essence of worldly existence, salutations to you! 28.

O Lord who is to be realized through devotion, O Master who transcends the sphere of existence and non-existence, O Bestower of fearlessness in this world, O Lord of beings, O Sovereign of worldly existence—salutations be unto You! 29.
O Great Lord, you are unperceivable even by those who know the truth of the Vedas and Vedāntas;
O Lord of all gods, Master of Speech, whose very form is speech, salutations, salutations to You! 30.

Homage be to you, who have extracted the life of beings deluded by the sport of the tiger of worldly existence, and who have arisen as the sun for the means to dispel the blinding darkness of saṃsāra. 31.
O you who, at the time of universal dissolution, have the fire of the destruction of existence as your forehead-mark;
O you whose form is your own will, manifesting the cycle of rebirth born of desire—homage be to you!
O you who are the form of time, who transcend all parts, O Lord of Desire and granter of desires, O Skeleton, born from the form of time, O God of Time, homage be to you! 33.
O fierce Lord adorned with supernatural powers, bestower of the fruit of the eight sovereignities, wearer of many forms, O Sthāṇu, O Viśvarūpa, let there be salutation to you! 34.
Salutations to the one who dwells on the peak of Kailāsa, adorned with masses of snow,
whose head has matted locks radiant with the Gaṅgā, and whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire.
Salutations again and again to you, whose limbs are covered by a tiger skin, who have a garland of severed heads around your neck, and who bear a skull-topped staff and a trident.
"O Lord, deluded by your illusory power, I wandered about, not recognizing you because I was arrogant with the pride of wealth;
O Lord of Gods, forgive this offense of mine, whether committed through speech, body, or mind. (37)
Skanda said: Then Maheśvara, having heard that supreme hymn from Agastya,
was greatly delighted at that time, his eyes wide with joy.
O Pot-born one, the one of great splendor, gladdened by the hymn of praise, spoke these words again to the fire for the sake of granting a boon to the ascetic. 39.
The Lord said: "O Brahmin, I have been praised by these excellent hymns issuing from your mouth, having beheld your asceticism, which is most difficult to perform even for the gods. (40)
"Now I shall grant a boon to you, who are both devoted and ascetic.
O knower of dharma, choose whatever boon you desire at this time."
Agni said:
"O Lord, if you grant me this supreme and unsurpassed boon, may I have constant devotion to you and worship you with unwavering steadfastness. (42)
"O Lord, I desire this alone as a boon: that there be firm devotion to the remembrance of you and to this supreme hymn of yours; grant me this through your grace. (43)
Rudra said:
"O you who are devoted to many forms of devotion, listen now as I grant this boon:
let there be great power for you, and let there be sovereignty and nobility."
"You shall become the witness of the world and its perpetual consumer of all things;
without you, every action of the worlds would be fruitless. (45)
Through your forms, this cause shall consume the world;
you are the consumer of oblations, the embodiment of sacrifice, and the accomplisher of all rites.
May you become the embodiment of all the gods, the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
you are established upon the ridge of Mount Meru between the east and the south.
"From this day forward, O Agni, you shall be my son and the lord of a quarter;
protect the direction eternally, for you are the eternal creator of all. (48)
He who, having become pure, always recites this divine hymn of praise to Agni, is liberated from all sins and goes to your world. 49.
Whether in suffering or in distress, or under the affliction of cruel and fierce planets, or when fear has arisen in battle—you protect that reciter. (50)
The wise person who constantly recites this captivating King of Hymns is liberated from all sins and is glorified in your world. 51.
Skanda said:
Having thus granted this great boon to the ascetic who was devoid of worldly attachments,
O Pot-born One, Mahādeva vanished into the sky.
Then all the hosts of gods, the groups of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
as well as the celestial rishis, the Siddhas, Nārada, and Bṛhaspati [approached].
Having gathered on the great peak, the mountain named Tejas,
they rejoiced upon seeing that ascetic who had obtained the boon.
The gods, headed by Bṛhaspati, joyfully sprinkled the Fire-god with the excellent water from the sacred bathing-place of Brahmajvālā.
O Brahmin, having thus been clothed with garments by the preceptor, who had likewise honored him with golden jars and purifying rites over which mantras had been recited; || 56 ||
Sounds resounded in the sky and the lords of the Gandharvas sang;
the goddesses scattered parched grain and rained down flowers. 57.
Then, O Pot-born one, the gods gave their wife named Svāhā to Agni; thereafter, Vahni married her according to the prescribed rites.
Then the gods, together with the Gandharvas, placing Agni as their presiding deity,
went swiftly from the middle of the east and south toward Mount Meru.
O Agastya, having established the sacred fire on that peak and duly awakened his grandson, the Lord of the World joyfully departed for the realm of Brahmā.
Having duly honored Agni again and again, the gods along with the Gandharvas departed each to their own respective abodes. (61)
O Pot-born One, he who bathes even once at Agnitīrtha attains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Agni.
From that time on, Vahni rejoiced in such a manner as would be the joy of Śakra himself;
and Yama, having heard of Śuci’s austerity, performed it as well with a resolute mind.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Siddhi of Agni, the Guardian of the Quarter," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 13.
Agastya said:
"O son of Rudra, it has been told to me that a difficult penance was performed by Yama.
At which sacred ford (tīrtha) or on which peak did he do so, and who is this mighty Yama?"
O Mahāsena, how did Yama come to dwell on that peak in former times?
I wish to hear all of this from you; please tell it to me.
Skanda said: That great lord previously mentioned to you, whose splendor is the mighty radiance of Rudra, has three divine offspring: Manu, Yama, and Śanaiścara.
He was a devotee of Śiva, all-knowing, and a master who had reached the further shore of all scriptures;
he was constantly devoted to all righteous duties and turned his back upon unrighteousness.
Restraint in all actions is therefore known as *yama*.
One who is free from dualities, free from longing, self-controlled, changeless, and always pure [is established in it]. || 5 ||
Therefore, Yama has been proclaimed by the worlds as one who possesses equal vision toward all living beings;
he is truthful, a knower of time, and is ordained over both dharma and adharma.
O Agastya, he was constantly devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu and intent upon the adoration of Śiva;
he was a proponent of non-duality, sweet-spoken, dedicated to sacrifice, and a generous giver;
likewise, he was devoted to the Sun and honored his guests.
O Sage, once during the day, Yama asked Ravi about the news he had heard from the mouth of the god regarding the austerity performed by Agni.
Yama said:
"O father, how was penance performed by the high-souled Agni?
I too have a firm desire to perform penance."
O witness of the world, O one of great splendor, grant me your permission;
for since perfection is attained through it, I shall not act without your command.
Sūrya said:
"I shall now relate that austerity which was performed by Agni.
Listen, my son, to this great knowledge from which the supreme is obtained. (11)
Having received the instruction from his father, he went to the Himalayas;
with his body smeared with ashes, he wore rudrākṣa beads.
Then the knower of dharma, Vaiśvānara, performed penance;
at the conclusion of his penance, having obtained a boon from the gods, he became a permanent guardian of the quarter.
"O child, you must perform such difficult penance as this, if you desire your own perfection, in the region to the south of the Himalayas. (14)
To the east of Nīlakaṇṭha and to the south of Umā’s pool is the place known as Siddhakūṭa; there, O son, those who perform austerities indeed dwell. 15.
One should mutter the great six-syllable mantra preceded by the syllable Om;
having duly installed the liṅga, one should worship the Lord with devotion. 16.
The Siddharasā is the best of rivers, and the Umākuṇḍodbhavā is a river;
having bathed at the Siddhatīrtha where these two join, one should proceed to the mountain Giri.
Having bathed there, one goes to heaven in one's own body; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed in Umākuṇḍa, a man becomes a perfected being (siddha) at that very moment.
Skanda said:
Having heard his father’s beneficial words, which were the most excellent among all speech,
the highly wise one was filled with joy, and the hair on all his limbs stood on end.
With a faltering voice, the wise one offered praise to the Radiant One;
placing his joined palms upon his head, he circumambulated him again and again.
Obeisance to the Sun, the unborn, the eye of the worlds;
obeisance be to You, whose nature is creation and sustenance, O Destroyer! 21.
Salutation to the one who is knowledge, whose form is knowledge, and who bestows knowledge; salutation to the eternal God, whose form is light, the Lord of lights. || 22 ||
Having thus praised his father again and again, that knower of dharma bowed his head to the god and departed for the peak of the Himalayas.
Then Yama, having arrived at Siddhatīrtha, the most excellent of waters,
frequented by the Siddhas, performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rite, O Agastya.
Then, having bathed and become pure, Yama smeared his body with sacred ash;
having applied a beautiful triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) on his forehead,
the wise one should wear Rudrākṣa beads on various parts of the body according to the prescribed rule.
He gave gifts to the sages according to the full extent of his wealth;
having bestowed those gifts, the son of Sūrya then ascended Mount Siddha.
There, on that peak of great merit, frequented by the world of the Siddhas, divine, filled with snow, and enchanting to all the gods; (27)
Seated upon a divine throne strewn with many jewels and produced from the elixir of accomplishment, he sat with his body straight, facing north.
Having meditated upon the mass of luminaries within his own lotus-heart possessed of filaments,
Yama indeed established a liṅga produced from vaidūrya gems.
On a divine, constructed altar, well-fashioned with five threads,
he then established it firmly with waters from sacred fords and various auspicious substances.
Endowed with single-minded devotion and focused intent, the knower of the mantra should worship with the finest perfumes, silk garments, incense, lamps, and likewise with food offerings.
Then the high-minded Yama worshipped Ādyeśa, who dwells within the cave of all beings, and indeed mentally recited the mantra.
Having placed the god Śaṅkara before him and gazing at his tip of the nose,
he remained for more than a hundred divine years with a single-pointed mind, fully concentrated.
Then, at the end of the rainy season, the Great All-pervading Lord appeared;
becoming light and possessing great splendor, illuminating the quarters with his brilliance,
he descended from the lotus to grant a boon to his devotee.
Beholding him, who was perfected through austerity, yet suffering and observing silence,
he assumed a divine form and revealed his own true self to him.
The omnipresent Mahādeva, whose form was clearly manifest and who was composed of all splendor, was delighted by the austerity of that silent sage.
Then he beheld the Lord of Beings, the supreme master of all splendors—
the three-eyed, four-armed one with the moon upon his forehead, bearing a skull.
Rudra, with a serene countenance, full of joy, and bearing a trident,
held a hand-drum and a garland, and wore a tiger-skin as an upper garment.
Having gazed upon the Lord of the gods, he bowed down to him with various prostrations;
the righteous-souled one, having performed a circumambulation, joyfully offered a hymn of praise.
Yama said:
Oṃ!
Salutations to the auspicious God, to the peaceful one, and to the Lord of Umā.
Salutations indeed to the one whose body is a mass of luminaries and whose form is splendor. 40.
Salutations indeed to the one who is beyond marks and yet possesses all marks, whose crown is the moon, who has three eyes, four arms, and holds a trident in his hand. 41.
Salutations again and again to the one who holds the skull-topped staff, the hand-drum, and the garland;
salutations to the one whose limbs are smeared with ashes, and salutations to the one who wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads. 42.
Salutation to Rudra of manifold forms, who possesses infinite forms;
salutation to him who is united with infinite power and who bestows infinite fruit. 43.
Salutations to you, the treasure-house of compassion; salutations to you who are the very form of compassion.
Salutations again and again to the self-controlled one, to the embodiment of generosity, and to the giver. 44.
Salutations again and again to the Lord of all beings, to the God who destroys hypocrisy, to Hara, to the primordial God of gods, to Śaṅkara. 45.
Salutations again and again to the one who is liberated from the bonds of the individual soul, who possesses a threefold form;
salutations indeed to the bestower of knowledge, the auspicious one, and the conqueror of death. 46.
Salutations indeed to the one of incomparable body, to the one whose form is the universe;
salutations again and again to the Lord of the Universe, to the Terrifying One who dwells within the body. 47.
Salutations again and again to Śarva, the blue-throated one, whose movement is beautiful with tawny eyes, who has shaken off the mire of impurity, and who is eternal.
Salutations to the one who wears a necklace of great serpent-kings, to the unborn one of immeasurable form, to the Supreme, the Highest Lord, to whom all bow down. 49.
O Lord of Gods, compassionate toward devotees, may my offense—this hymn born from the power of my speech—be forgiven by you for this embodied being who is devoid of devotion. 50.
Skanda said:
Having heard this hymn, the Great Lord, the God of gods,
together with Umā, beheld his joy upon observing his conduct.
Mahādeva spoke these words to him—his own devotee, who was alone and performing austerities—in order to grant him a boon at that time. 52.
Īśvara said:
"Choose a boon, my child, that is most desired by your heart;
O mighty-armed one, I shall grant you that supreme gift which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (53)
May you, at your pleasure, milk this cow of praise brought by you, bound with the rope of the Vedas and flowing with milk, which yields all desires as its calf. 54.
Yama said:
"O delighter of the worlds, O Lord of the three realms, grant me that most excellent boon today, as you have always done out of compassion for me. (55)
"Just as in the past the guardianship of the quarters was granted to Agni for all time, so too is my desire; O Unborn One, grant that to me. (56)
Īśvara said: "O devoted Yama, O highly wise one, let that which has now been spoken by you be granted as you desire; O son of Pūṣan, [accept] the guardianship of the quarters. (57)
"O noble one, stand constantly upon the peak on the southern ridge of Meru;
from this day forward, you shall be the guardian of that quarter. (58)
"Then people will say, 'This is the southern direction,' as the sacred tradition declares; furthermore, I shall grant you another boon that is the cause for the arising of worldly existence. (59)

For living beings, human birth is difficult to obtain; therefore, having reflected upon the good and evil deeds performed, as well as the words spoken true and false, you should inscribe them here. 60.
Therefore, they shall address you by the renowned name Citragupta;
then, having taken the living beings who are fit, subject them to your authority. 61.
"Having first deliberated upon merit and demerit, cast [the person] into heaven or hell;
and the people, as well as you, will again say, 'It was Time, the Ender.'"
"Take this staff and this noose with a steady mind; you are the punisher for the sake of disciplining the most wicked of men. (63)
Having bound living beings with the noose of the rope of desire, which is moistened by my māyā, they draw that Lord toward themselves from one side at the end. 64.
Having bound him on one side with your noose,
O Kāla, you will then drag him along with this staff, threatening him.
"However many living beings there are in the world—those still in the womb and those already born—you shall inflict torment upon them all, with the sole exception of my devotees. (66)
Upon seeing those whose bodies are smeared with ashes and adorned with rudrākṣas, as well as those wearing garlands of tulasī— my devotees and the devotees of Viṣṇu— close your eyes.
Furthermore, O Yama, I shall grant you another unsurpassed boon:
may you become the lord of the gods, asuras, humans, and the ancestors.
Skanda said:
Having thus granted that boon to his devotee, Hara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, vanished from sight after establishing the succession of the world's laws.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, were filled with intense joy upon gathering together and beholding the noble ascetic who had obtained the boon.
Then, having bestowed power upon him,
the gods further conferred the consecration (abhiṣeka) with golden jars filled with the water of that sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Then Brahmā, together with the gods, went toward the southern direction,
placing Yama at the forefront from Mount Meru amidst musical festivities and the finest hymns of praise;
having established the guardian of that quarter there, he then worshipped Yama.
Then Brahmā departed through the sky and the gods vanished;
from that day forward, this noble Yama became the guardian of the quarter.
On the great mountain Himavat, having obtained a boon from Kapālin and bathed three times at Yamatīrtha, he was liberated from all sins.
O Sage, the wise man who ascends Siddhakūṭa mountain even once shall enjoy happiness in the world of Śakra and thereafter become a guardian of the quarters.
Furthermore, O lord of brahmins, that high-minded one, having received his father’s command and performed ascetic penance,
surely practiced it even after hearing that the excellent Nairṛta had obtained a boon from Yama.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the World-Protector Yama," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 14 ||
Agastya said:
O Lord, who was that mighty Nairṛta who performed penance?
From whom did he indeed obtain his boon, and at which auspicious and supreme tīrtha?
If you have compassion for me, O master skilled in all matters, I wish to hear this; therefore, please show me your certain favor.
Skanda said: O Pot-born One, I shall now relate in its entirety that which was his conduct in former times;
out of affection for you, I will tell it all—listen now.
The wise son of Kaśyapa, known by the name Nairṛta, was a hero among all living beings, possessing the most exalted prowess. || 4 ||
Armed with claws, possessed of great splendor, endowed with great strength, and preeminent;
he was a night-stalker, violent by nature, a consumer of flesh, and a drinker of blood.
At one time, the mighty-armed [Kārttikeya], having approached where that best of the twice-born, Kaśyapa, was seated, questioned his father, the sage.
Having circumambulated him three times, Karbura bowed with devotion;
placing his joined palms upon his head, he offered praise from the depths of his heart.
Nairṛta said: Salutations to Janaka-deva, the progenitor of living beings;
salutations to the sage who is the creator of creation, maintenance, and destruction. (8)
Salutations indeed to Brahmā, who possesses all forms; salutations to the splendor of Brahman;
to the Lord of Yogins, whose self is purified; salutations to you, the radiance of Brahman.
"O father, best among the knowers of Brahman, I wish to hear from you in which sacred ford on a mountain peak Vaivasvata performed his austerities. (10)
Kaśyapa said: Listen, my son, for I shall indeed declare that which was asked of me— namely,
what was performed as penance by Vaivasvata and what was obtained from the wielder of the trident.
There was a wise son of Sūrya known by the name Vaivasvata;
he was the source of the arising of all living beings according to the standards of worldly dharma.
Having satisfied his father and being instructed by him, Nemi,
the son of Sūra, filled with joy, desired to perform austerities.
On the full moon day of Bhādrapada, conjoined with the constellation Pūrvabhādrapadā,
he took up his instructions and departed for the Himavat mountain.
Having bathed in the waters of Siddhatīrtha and taken refuge at Siddhakūṭa, he established the Lord according to the prescribed rites and chanted [the mantra] with a one-pointed mind. || 15 ||
Then Mahādeva granted him an unsurpassed boon;
having obtained the boon from Maheśāna, he became a guardian of the quarters—of this there is no doubt.
In the southern direction from Meru, he alone is the creator of all;
he alone is the sustainer of the ancestors and the ruler of living beings in due order.
At the end, there is no doubt that his world must be attained by those who live [righteously].
And you, my child, have a desire in your heart to perform penance;
having cast off the sixfold group [of internal enemies], remain steadfast with your senses fully conquered. 18.
Nairṛta said:
"To which peak should one go, and from where is the bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha) to be performed?
O dear one, how is it to be practiced, and who, moreover, is to be propitiated? (19)
"O best of sages, let instruction surely be given to me;
for we have heard that without a teacher's instruction, there is no action. (20)
Kaśyapa said:
On an excellent plateau of the Himavat, there is a lake named Mānas;
in ancient times, the Creator indeed created it for the welfare of all the worlds.
Whatever offerings to the gods (havya) and ancestors (kavya) the best of men perform there,
all that becomes inexhaustible, and they shall obtain their heart's desire at will.
Therefore, you too should perform your ablutions with great devotion;
O Karbura, listen now to the detailed procedure for performing penance.
Having bathed with the waters of a sacred ford, one should apply sacred ash as an ointment;
having placed Rudrākṣa beads upon one's limbs, one should joyfully mutter the mantra with a focused mind.
Having installed Rudra according to the prescribed rites, O son, one should praise him with the threefold hymns;
thus, O Karbura, you shall attain success through this practice. 25.
Agastya said:
"O Blessed One, since you are omniscient, I certainly wish to hear:
how did the Creator indeed create that divine lake in ancient times?"
O Lord, tell me: who among those gathered in that frost became liberated in that place known as Mānasarovar, which delivers one from the cycle of rebirth? 27.
Skanda said:
Brahmā joyfully created that [peak] with his mind, which is why it is called Śekhara;
it is thirty yojanas in width and likewise unfathomably vast.
Having invoked Gaṅgā, that Creator meditated upon the Supreme Śiva in his heart;
and she, Gaṅgā, whose life-sustaining waters are pure, appeared within the excavation. 29.
O Pot-born One, having beheld the auspicious water there,
the Creator was filled with joy and pronounced a blessing upon him for the welfare and liberation of the world.
Brahmā said:
"Stay forever in this lake, O Goddess whose form is water; salutations be unto you!
O auspicious Mother, bestower of boons, grant liberation through devotion to those who seek liberation. (31)
The man who bathes even once with devotion in the lake of the waters of your form shall not be born again in a womb; how much more so, then, for a living being? 32.
Skanda said:
Having thus joyfully bestowed his blessing upon him there,
Prajāpati performed austerities for a hundred divine years for the sake of the origin of all beings.
Then, having obtained power from the wielder of the trident, he first created the seven sages through his mind, and subsequently the four classes of living beings and the gods.
Once, at another time, while Agastya was established in Brahmanic austerity,
they reflected and in the past set their minds upon performing penance.
There, the seven sages performed intense penance with joy, each remaining properly apart and propitiating Rudra with acts of devotion. (36)
Those great sages simultaneously performed the ritual of pouring water upon the Gaṅgā;
there, the bow-wielding attendants of Śiva, whose nature is auspicious, were bathing together.
Then the highly meritorious Gaṅgā, being overwhelmed with anxiety, thought: "Why am I departing today? They will surely cast a curse upon me. 38.
Trembling repeatedly, Gaṅgā divided herself into seven parts;
wherever the noble ladies were stationed, she flowed separately to each of those places.
Then, having brought them down separately from the peaks of the mountains toward the presence of the sages,
they entered the lake as themselves.
Then, beholding her carrying seven streams, those great-souled ones rejoiced greatly and again bestowed blessings upon her.

The sages said: "O Noble Lady, since you have been detained by us for the purpose of performing our ablutions, from this day forward, may you become the bestower of the fruits of the seven [sacred] rivers. (42)
Therefore, for the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation, as well as good fortune,
a pleasing heart, valor, and sovereignty— these seven always yield fruit.
Skanda said:
Having thus bestowed blessings upon them with joy, O Agastya, those great sages remained there, devoted to asceticism and ever intent on the worship of Śiva. 44.
O noble one, at the end of a hundred years, a lake named Yuktā appeared by the grace of Śiva and the Goddess, for the welfare of living beings in the past. 45.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śukra, Śiva,
assuming the form of a swan— gentle and beautiful with fine feathers— indeed brought it forth into that lake.
With a red beak, red feet, and eyes that were yellowish-red,
Sugrīva, resembling the color of saffron, moved about with a pleasant voice.
Then the beautiful Haṃsī, born of the Noble One, moved about there;
likewise, the Goddess, in the form of a female swan, moved together with the wielder of the trident in the form of a male swan. 48.
In the form of a swan, the Lord of Gods wandered constantly with the goddess Haṃsī in that lake for a full thousand divine years.
Beholding the two swans moving through the clear waters and indeed feeding upon lotus stalks, Brahmā quickly rejoiced in his heart.
Then the lotus-born Brahmā reflected in his mind: "Who are these two swans that are of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, and who are they that wander here without them?"
The Śūlin (Śiva) made Manohara pure by assuming the form of a swan;
thinking "this is my lake," the unborn one indeed assumed the form of a swan.
Beholding the swans again with joy, Viṣṇu assumed the form of a swan;
beautiful and exceedingly gentle, he indeed moved about in that shape.
Having beheld that divine lake, Dharma assumed the form of a swan; he was celestial, gentle in appearance, white, and possessed of a beautiful neck. || 54 ||
Having pervaded that lake, they indeed sported there for a thousand divine years;
truly, one was eating lotus stalks while the other scratched him with its beak.
Rudra sported happily with Bhavānī in the lake,
while the pot-born Agastya, assuming the form of a swan, repeatedly surrounded them.
The Creator of the Universe, in the form of a swan, split the mountain peak;
with his strides, he leapt across the ocean filled with great waves.
Śaṅkara, in the form of a swan, pierced the peak from the southern side;
the divine river, intent on her sport, rose up with its excellent waters. 58.
In the form of a swan, Keśava split the peak on the northern side;
from its summit issued a very wide stream, full of water and flowing swiftly. || 59 ||
Then, from the peak of Avācī, Dharma himself indeed split it apart;
O Sage, a divine river, crowded with waves, surged forth.
Then, from that mountain peak, they issued forth as a fourth stream of water,
falling like blazing showers of wealth (vasu).
Beholding them fallen, Brahmā was greatly delighted;
he indeed assigned to them names that were appropriate to their forms.
Brahmā said:
"With a very steady wave, you have leaped from the mountain peak;
since you have attained the state of a male, O river, may you be my son forever."

O son, O hero, for all living beings and especially for those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas), you must certainly bestow the fruit of the fourfold aims of life, which destroys all sin. (64)
O daughter, that best of rivers flowed with gentle ease and playfulness;
for from the effort of Rudra, the hundred Rudras were born there perpetually, O Bhavānī. 65.
In the auspicious Tretā Yuga, you shall become the celestial river Ganges;
you will continuously accomplish the mental resolve of the descendants of Raghu.
Filled with water, that excellent river flowed forth extensively;
O daughter, since you were produced by the effort of Viṣṇu, be known henceforth as Viṣṇumatī.

O Goddess, you grant the heart’s desired objects of both worldly enjoyment and liberation to those who touch your waters; you especially bestow sovereign power upon those who have completed their ritual baths.
O best of rivers, at your first appearance, you who are garlanded with clear waves,
you flowed forth as the primordial one out of a desire to perform what is dear to Dharma.
O young girl, the fruit to be granted to those seeking liberation is union with me (matsāyujya);
you must certainly remove even their previously accumulated impurities. 70.
O daughter, beloved of me, whoever bathes here in my pool shall obtain the fruit arising from all sacrifices, having abandoned all sins.
Released from all sins merely by ascending the mountain,
a wise man who beholds the divine lake will certainly obtain the fulfillment of his heart's desires.
If anyone, by some stroke of fate, should bathe here with devotion,
even if he is incapable of performing worship or recitation, his merit and fruit shall be great.
Having crossed over the cycle of suffering and abandoned all births,
he shall go to the supreme state, leaving behind the great misery of dwelling in a womb.
Having abandoned that which exists as suffering within the eighty-four lakh species of birth for embodied beings, one should indeed go to the Supreme.
Skanda said: Having thus granted the boon to them, O Sage, Brahmā assumed the form of a swan and sported incessantly and eternally within that lake together with the swan-gods.
There, after some time, the gods came from heaven and performed penance,
