as did the Gandharvas, Guhyakas, Siddhas, Daityas, and Apsarases.
In the Kali age, this lake will not be abandoned by gods in the form of birds;
it is the golden mountain that is the breast of the earth and the mind-lake of Jambūdvīpa. 78.
Many there were liberated, having emerged from the cycle of suffering; by the touch of that water, they immediately abandoned birth through their good fortune. (79)
In ancient times, there was a certain barbarian hunter who made his living by destroying birds;
on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, he went to a lake to kill a swan.
Having stumbled into a lake, he stirred up the water with his feet;
emerging from the water with great effort, he, being free from sin, touched that water.
Then the Raudras, having mounted that celestial chariot (vimāna) which possessed a physical form,
led him to the most excellent city of Śiva, and a rain of flowers fell.
Having enjoyed happiness for ten kalpas, he fell from the abode of Śiva;
thereafter, he became a sovereign king on earth, a worshiper of Śiva.
O Sage, even that barbarian obtained that fruit through ignorance;
why then should a man endowed with knowledge not attain liberation from bathing? 84.
Then, having heard his father’s wholesome words, that best of Rākṣasas concentrated his mind on a single purpose and went quickly to Lake Mānasa.
Having arrived at that sacred bathing place, the high-minded one, with a single-pointed mind, bathed in the very pure water according to the prescribed ritual as instructed by his father.
Then, his limbs smeared with ashes, he wore rudrākṣa beads upon his body;
he gave gifts to the brahmins and ascended to the Brahmaśekhara mountain.
There, on that Niṣadha peak, inaccessible to all living beings, endowed with many minerals and well-mingled with many jewels, (he stood). 88.
Having duly installed a linga made of black iron and having bathed it with water from a sacred ford, he then performed worship with offerings of honor.
Seated upon a divine seat, facing the east with his body held straight,
he then gazed at the tip of his nose, his eyes slightly opened.
Then that hero, with single-minded focus, chanted with his intellect for more than a hundred divine years, meditating again and again. (91)
Then, at the end of the rainy season, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, Maheśvara appeared before Bhakti in order to grant her a boon.
The high-minded Karbura, possessed of great splendor and devoted to the worship of Rudra,
beheld that Mahādeva and composed a hymn of praise.

The son of Niṣadha said: I worship him, the Great Blue-throated One, the ocean of compassion; he who is auspicious, whose form is peaceful, whose body has the appearance of Śivā, who has entered half of Śivā’s body, who is born from a portion of Śivā, who is the beginning of Śiva, and whose limbs are Śiva. I worship him, I worship him! 94.
Obeisance to you whose form is knowledge, obeisance indeed to you whose form is subtle;
obeisance to the pure one who is the knowledge of knowledge, and obeisance to you who are exceedingly gross.
Homage to you, the god of even the gods, who possess divine form;
homage to you, the supreme, the highest lord, the most worthy of worship. 96.
Homage to you who are liberated from the higher and the lower, the one worthy of all worship;
homage again and again to the eternal one, whose form is eternal, and whose limbs are radiant. 97.
Salutations to you, the one worthy of worship even by those who are themselves worthy of worship, whose very self is the object of worship for the venerable;
salutations to you, the radiant one with blazing eyes, possessed of divine nature.
Salutations to You who are of the nature of power, who are peaceful, and who are the sole cause of purity;
salutations to You who are pure, whose form is pure, and who are the most supremely pure. 99.
Salutations indeed to Śambhu, who is the form of time, who is time itself, whose body is beautiful,
who dwells in the void, who is the means of valid cognition, and whose nature is the void.
Salutation to you, whose body is all mantras, the Death of Death;
salutation to you, the unborn, whose form is mantra, and whose body is pure. || 101 ||
Homage again and again to the immeasurable god Śaṅkara;
homage to you, the blazing-eyed, the essence, whose form is the very essence. 102.
Salutations again and again to the Primordial One, who possesses all forms and is infinite;
salutations again and again to the Non-terrible, the Terrible, and the Tatpuruṣa.
Skanda said: Having thus praised Mahādeva, the great hero, his hair standing on end, then bowed down again and again with words and thoughts.
O Pot-born one, having heard the hymn of the Lord of the Nairṛtas,
the omnipresent Rudra then rejoiced and granted him a boon.
Śarva said:
"Choose a boon, O knower of dharma, the most excellent of all boons;
I shall now grant you whatever you desire, O Rākṣasa. (106)
Concentrating your mind on a single point, you perform excellent austerity;
you are perfectly steadfast, devoted to me, non-violent, and have conquered your senses. (107)
"I am pleased with your asceticism, my child, and with your hymns that captivate all hearts. Know me as the granter of desires; considering this, choose a boon from me. || 108 ||
Nairṛta said:
"O omniscient one, if you are now pleased with me, however lowly;
O Śambhu, ocean of compassion, you surely show me mercy. (109)
"O Blessed One, O Lord, let such a status as the guardian of a quarter be granted to me, just as it was previously bestowed by you upon Daṇḍin. (110)
Śarva said:
"O mighty-armed one, I shall certainly grant you that which was requested by you;
for I am pleased with your severe asceticism as well as with your hymns of praise."
"So be it for you, O Great Hero, whatever is in your mind; from this day forth, may you be the Lord of the Quarters, protecting those who have arisen therefrom. (112)
Skanda said: Having thus granted the boon to that great-souled devotee,
the God, who is affectionate toward his devotees, then vanished from sight.
Then all the gods, headed by Bṛhaspati,
as well as Brahmā, Nārada, the seven ṛṣis, and others, arrived there.
O Sage, they bestowed the consecration upon him with auspicious golden jars,
filled with water from sacred fords and lifted up by the hands of the gods.
There the kettledrums resounded and shouts of victory arose;
showers of excellent flowers and showers of parched grain fell from the sky. 116.
Having consecrated him, the gods then went joyfully to the summit of Mount Meru;
having placed Nairṛta at their head there, Brahmā consecrated him as well.
Having placed him upon their shoulders, the gods, led by Viriñca and the lords of the intermediate directions, departed with respect as they had come.
Then, having heard that penance performed by the Nairṛta, the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) also undertook it.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Success through the Austerities of Nairṛta," in the Mānasarovar-māhātmya of the Himavat-khaṇḍa within the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 15.
Agastya said:
O Mahāsena, knower of the three periods of time, you are omniscient; of this there is no doubt.
Austerities, both difficult and great, have been performed by the high-souled Varuṇa.
Thus it has been said by you to me, and I wish to hear that;
who was this god Pracetas, and by whom was he instructed, O Lord? (2)
Skanda said:
Listen, O devotee, I shall recount all of his deeds to you;
for you are my devotee, O man of great wisdom, as instructed by Nārada. (3)
There was a son of Kaśyapa, renowned by the name Varuṇa;
he was high-souled, possessed of great splendor, and endowed with great strength and prowess.
He was always delighted by all dharmas, proficient in all branches of knowledge, a constant devotee of Viṣṇu, self-controlled, and ever intent on the worship of Śiva. || 5 ||
He was compassionate toward all beings, devoted to honoring guests,
truthful, most righteous, a master of his senses, and a great sage.
Once, O Sage, while Pāśī was seated in the midst of the assembly hall,
he beheld the sage Nārada arriving there from the sky.
Wandering indeed from the world of Brahmā, he beheld the Sage with his mass of matted hair,
who was playing the lute with great joy and repeatedly striking it.
He was constantly practicing the seven musical notes and endowed with the nine aesthetic sentiments;
he took great delight in song and rhythm, and wore a golden sacrificial thread.
He was one who sang the praises of Rudrayaśas, a slanderer fond of quarreling,
impartial toward all people in the world, and a clever informer of both what should and should not be told.
Seeing that he had arrived, O Sage, Varuṇa rose up;
having honored him with guest-offerings and hymns of praise, he seated the worthy guest upon a throne.
Having performed a circumambulation, Varuṇa bowed again and again;
and with devotion, he repeatedly asked the ascetic after his welfare.
Varuṇa said: "Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune! That this noble person, who was without a protector, should now find great protection because you have come here. (13)
Today my body has been purified, since today the ancestors joyfully partake of what has been offered;
thus, the merit performed in the past shall become fruitful this very day.
"I am indeed your servant, for whose sake I have come here;
O Noble One, I have been informed of the news—what shall I do? Let it be commanded. (15)
Nārada said:
"O best of men, son of Kaśyapa, you should not speak thus to me;
for you are true to your word, righteous-souled, and self-controlled toward all living beings. (16)
Devoted to Viṣṇu and having Śiva as your soul, you are equal to me, there is no doubt;
for you are always delighted in dharma and intent upon the worship of Śiva. 17.
He alone is indeed the best among men, worthy of worship by all the worlds;
he is to be honored by all beings, for he is the very embodiment of those two.
"O Nārada, this was previously told to me by Viṣṇu and likewise by Rudra: 'He who is my devotee is my own form; of this there is no doubt. (19)
O sage, whatever food or wealth is given with faith by those of excellent virtue to my devotee, I certainly accept that.
Thus was it described to me by Rudra and likewise by Viṣṇu;
from that time on, O wise Varuṇa, I have been possessed of devotion to them. 21.
I shall tell you the purpose of my coming; listen to it in detail.
On a delightful peak of the Himavat, penance was performed by Nairṛta.
Having concentrated his mind on a single point,
that great-souled one performed severe and most mighty asceticism for more than a hundred divine years.
The Lord, the Master of Waters, having arrived there, became pleased;
the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, granted him a great boon.
Likewise, [bestow upon him] the guardianship of the quarters and other great strength and prowess;
become the lord of the intermediate directions on Mount Meru, for he alone is indeed the destroyer and the creator.
"Having thus received this news, I have come into your presence;
for it is not otherwise that I speak to you, who are most righteous and devoted. (26)
Varuṇa said: "O best of sages, how wonderful and great is this, that the Rākṣasa has obtained the guardianship of a quarter of the world, as well as a strength that is supreme over all! (27)
How was it that the Blessed One was pleased by the power of asceticism of the practitioners, which has self-extraction as its cause, yet is described as asceticism performed for one's own sake? 28.
Nārada said:
Through austerity, dharma is obtained; through austerity, the human body is attained;
through austerity, prosperity is reached, and likewise, again, the body of a god.
When one practices with desirelessness, liberation is attained through austerity;
likewise, heaven and prosperity are attained through austerity. (30)
O son, likewise, the lordship over the earth is obtained through austerity;
through austerity everything is attained—there is nothing that is not exceedingly difficult to obtain. 31.
Through austerity, the Lord Rudra is brought under control, and likewise Viṣṇu; through austerity the entire world is brought under control—how much more so, then, insignificant mortals? 32.
If you have a desire, my child, perform difficult penance;
having made your resolve on a divine peak of the Himalayas, it shall be obtained.
Varuṇa said:
"O Nārada, I too have a desire to perform penance;
in what great sacred field (mahākṣetra) or in what holy ford (tīrtha), O Lord, shall I do so? (34)
O immensely wise one, O sage who knows all things, tell me directly what occurred previously, and the entire procedure for asceticism, O ascetic.
Nārada said:
On the beautiful western peak of the Himavat, known as Trikūṭa, there is a most desirable holy site situated between the Gaṅgā and the Sudhātaraṅgiṇī rivers. 36.
By bathing there, people go to heaven in their very bodies; of this there is no doubt.
In heaven, the gods honor that bathed one with offerings of worship.
"You are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, O great ascetic;
having bathed according to the rules at this supreme sacred ford, my child, you have arrived here together with your very body. (38)
Thus indeed do the gods constantly say in heaven regarding Varuṇa:
"O Pāśin, if you so desire, worship the Lord there. (39)
You too, having bathed there on Mount Trikūṭa, should then install the Liṅga; let it be consecrated according to your own desire.
Skanda said:
Having spoken thus, the wise Nārada vanished right there;
Varuṇa also went with joy to that Sudhātīrtha, where Dhruva was certainly present. 41.
He bathed there in that great, pure, and sin-removing holy ford,
which is difficult for living beings to attain, sacred, and the most excellent among all holy fords.
And according to the prescribed rite, the highly wise one, his body adorned with splendor,
again wore rudrākṣa beads while recollecting Rudra with his intellect.
Then, O Pot-born One, the wise one gave gifts to the Brahmins;
thereafter, the wielder of the noose ascended the great mountain known as Trikūṭa.
There, on that peak with its great summit, a most excellent place reaching to the clouds,
he joyfully performed the installation of a crystal linga.
Then, having sat upon a divine seat and facing the east,
he joyfully worshipped the Liṅga with waters from sacred fords and with offerings.
Thereafter, he chanted with firm resolve for more than a full hundred divine years;
at the end of that year, the Blessed Lord Rudra manifested from the sky.
O Sage, having beheld Śaṅkara in the form of light, the bestower of prosperity, Varuṇa (the wielder of the noose), his body with hair standing on end, then offered a hymn of praise to him.
Varuṇa said:
Oṃ! Salutation to the god Rudra; salutation to the lord of the Raudras.
And salutation to the one who performs the festival of Indra, whose form is the sacrificial fire-pan (kṛpīṭa). || 49 ||
Salutations to Hara and to Ugra, the bestower of the fruits of the desires of Kṛtānta;
salutations indeed to Kāleśvara, to Kāla, and to him who has transcended time (Kālātīta). || 50 ||
Salutations to the three-eyed one, to the formidable one, and salutations indeed to him whose hair is the sky;
salutations to the Lord Karbūreśvara, who grants the desires of the rākṣasas. 51.
Salutations to the unborn God, to Sthāṇvīśvara, to Śambhu;
salutations again and again to Īśāna, to the limb of Śiva, the eternal one.
Salutations indeed to the one worthy of the arghya offering, whose body is worshipful, and who bestows the world of saṃsāra;
salutations to the omniscient, the all-pervading Lord of the worlds. || 53 ||
O Lord, remover of all diseases, salutations to you for the sake of supreme liberation;
salutations to you, the auspicious one, whose body is auspicious, the sovereign lord of all beings. 54.
Salutations to Śiva, to Bharga, the bestower of the fruits of knowledge;
salutations indeed to the god whose source is the fire-drill, the Lord of Śakra.
Homage to the one whose form is auspicious, the destroyer of untimely death;
homage indeed to Rudra, the conqueror of death, who holds a trident in his hand. 56.
Salutations to the divine one of celestial form, the lord of the gods;
salutations indeed to the bestower of boons and fearlessness, whose body is peaceful.
Salutations to you who were bestowed by Śiva, who show the path to Śiva, and who are the god who carries the essence of worldly existence; O Śambhu, salutations to you eternally. 58.
Skanda said:
Having heard this supreme hymn, the best of praises, recited by Varuṇa, the wise Mahādeva felt great joy for his devotee. 59.
To grant a boon to his devotee, the Lord of Gods, who is affectionate toward his devotees and who dwells within the secret heart of all beings, spoke these words to him.
Śarva said:
"Choose a boon, O knower of dharma, Varuṇa, you who possess devotion to me!
Knowing me, my child, to be the giver of all things and to be affectionately disposed toward those who are deeply devoted to me. (61)
Summoned by your devotion and impelled here by your ascetic power,
I grant you now whatever boon you desire.
Varuṇa said:
"Oh, what fortune! Today the fruit of my own misfortune shall bear its result, since he whose body is composed of light has manifested his splendor."
O you who are saluted by all the gods, if you have affection for me,
O Great Lord, then give me that which was obtained from the Nairṛta.
Śarva said:
"The deed you have desired, performed by you whose soul is purified through austerity—let that be so;
this boon is granted to you, the most excellent of all boons."
"From this day forward, O Noble One, as you reside upon the eastern side of Mount Meru, you shall undoubtedly become the destroyer, the creator, and likewise the protector. (66)
Skanda said:
Having thus granted that boon to him, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings,
quickly vanished just as he had come from the sky.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas— Śakra, Agni, and Yama—
as well as Brahmā, the Rākṣasas, and hosts of Apsarases, arrived there.
There the sages beheld the high-souled Varuṇa, the ascetic,
who had obtained boons and was meditating as the great all-pervading Lord.
Then, having brought water from sacred fords, including that arising from the Sudhā-tīrtha,
he was consecrated by the noble ones with auspicious golden jars.

With praises and shouts of victory uttered by the gods from the mouths of deities and brahmins, with the sounds arising from various musical instruments, and with the deep resonance of flutes and cymbals; || 71 ||
Then Brahmā, reciting the Vedas, bestowed the consecration once again;
the seven sages, the preceptor, and the Siddhas joyfully remembered Manu.
Then, once more, the omnipresent Lord spoke these words from the sky: "O Varuṇa, become the lord of the waters today, just as my word commands."
Having heard these words from the radiant body situated in the sky, the gods again raised shouts of "Victory! while exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (74).
The Apsarases rained down showers of flowers and streams of parched grain;
the goddesses danced and sang, and the deities rejoiced there.
Then all the gods, placing the ascetic at their head,
went toward the western direction, O best of Brahmins, to Varuṇa with auspicious rites.
Having established him upon a peak of Meru, Brahmā assigned him his office;
thereafter, Brahmā as well as the celestial sages vanished from sight.
From that time on, Pāśī indeed became the creator, protector, and destroyer in the western quarter;
even the wind-god performed such fierce asceticism as is extremely difficult to practice.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Varuṇa’s Austerity," in the *Sudhātīrthamāhātmya* of the *Himavatkhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Skanda Purāṇa*. 16.
Agastya said: O Skanda, even though I have drunk the nectar-like essence of your words from the lotus of your mouth with the cup of my ears, I am not yet satiated, being afflicted by thirst. (1)
"O wielder of the spear, my mind yearns today for a drink once more, O Noble One, just as one afflicted by heat longs for water from your lips. (2)
Who is this Vāyu of great splendor, whose son is he that possesses such great strength? For what reason did he perform such severe austerity, and how did he obtain this most excellent boon?
O Mahāsena, in what place is the tīrtha that bestows manifold fruits?
Now I wish to hear this; tell it to me according to the rule.
Skanda said:
"Well asked, O highly fortunate one, regarding the account of Vāyu. Now I shall provide for you exactly as you have requested."
There was a great and virtuous lady named Aditi, the wife of the great sage Kaśyapa;
she was an ascetic woman, O wise one, who possessed many sons and lived in happiness.
In the great war between the gods and the asuras, the Lord of Śacī slew all her heroic sons; thereupon, she became overcome with grief.
Then that virtuous woman, out of envy toward the husband of Śacī— the slayer of her son—
performed ascetic penance with the intent of destroying Śakra, being motivated by that purpose.
Then that virtuous woman, emaciated by the death of her sons, gratified her husband Kaśyapa, who had returned from his vow of study, and chose a boon from him.
Diti said:
"O Blessed One, O Brahmin, knower of dharma, if you have affection for me, O Lord, I beg of you a splendid boon that shall be the cause of Indra's destruction. (10)
"O Brahmin, give me back that son of supreme prowess, who shall slay Śakra, the destroyer of my sons. (11)
Kaśyapa said: "So be it, O virtuous beloved; whatever you now desire shall be granted.
For there is nothing difficult to attain through asceticism, and the wish born of asceticism is fulfilled by asceticism itself. (12)
"O Goddess, O virtuous and devoted wife, a son shall be born to you who will indeed slay Śakra, provided that you observe this vow. (13)
"O Goddess, by virtue of your purity, you shall bear a child for a hundred autumns;
thereafter, you will give birth to a son capable of uprooting the three worlds."
Skanda said: Then Kaśyapa, having approached Diti and deposited the embryo within her, intended to produce the foremost of the gods for the sake of the host of deities. || 15 ||
The best of sages, the grandfather of all beings, went to the Himalaya, the greatest of mountains and a massive peak, for the sake of ascetic penance.
Then the highly virtuous Diti bore that seed—a fetus of such fierce energy that it was invincible to all living beings, including the gods. || 17 ||
She was pure at all times, devoted to all virtuous duties, auspicious,
intent upon her vows, true to her word among women, and one who had conquered her senses.
At that time, the sage Nārada, having taken up all the news and whatever deeds of hers had occurred, went to heaven from the presence of Ghaṭodbhava.
The wise one sang the glory of Rudra, repeatedly tuning his lute;
devoted to song and instrumental music, the steadfast one was a herald for all the worlds.
Then Sunāsīra beheld Nārada approaching,
playing upon his lute and singing the praises of Rudra’s glory.
Then Śakra rose from his throne and went before him;
having invited him to a seat, he caused him to sit down according to the prescribed rites.
Then Śakra honored the virtuous one with well-composed offerings;
having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, he questioned the great sage.
Śakra said: Welcome to you, O best of sages; is your body well? Is all well with every being in the worlds anywhere? (24)
"O Brahmaputra, best of the twice-born, you have come here for the purification of your body, since the celestial sage upon whom I depend has arrived. (25)
"The meeting of great souls leads to prosperity;
it is for prosperity that one should undertake a journey. Tell me this, O best of sages. (26)
Nārada said:
Listen, O Śakra, to the certain truth regarding the cause of my arrival:
the conduct of your stepmother Diti and her wondrously performed penance.
Your father was indeed gratified by her through various fasts accompanied by many observances; he was then entreated by her for a boon.
"O Lord, grant me that son who possesses great strength and prowess and will surely slay Śakra; he shall be the slayer of my sons. (29)
Kaśyapa also granted her a most wonderful boon;
Diti, remaining established in her vows and eager for that, conceived a fetus.
O Lord of the Gods, employ a stratagem if you desire your own welfare;
for as long as the obstacle has not yet arrived, remain diligent and wise.
Skanda said:
Having thus explained this to Śakra, the sage vanished.
And the lord of the gods, having heard those words spoken by the sage, [acted accordingly].
For the sake of his own security, O wise one, and for the destruction of his enemies.
Taking up his great thunderbolt, Śakra went to where Diti was staying,
intent on seeking her vulnerabilities and intent upon causing her to fall from righteousness.
O sage, he moved about there day and night with his identity concealed;
approaching her slowly and remaining hidden, he revealed himself in private.
Constantly intent on this, Śakra, ever filled with indignation, acted in this manner, wondering, "When might there be a lapse in her virtue? (35)
When one hundred years were lacking by one year, he perceived this deficiency:
that he had not washed his feet and had not touched water. (36)
Then, with a bewildered mind, Diti lay down upon her bed;
overcome by sleep, that virtuous and sweet-spoken woman was heavy with child.
Then the wielder of the thunderbolt beheld her, whose conduct and disposition were impure;
having entered her womb, the mighty Śakra deposited the embryo. (38)
Then, with his thunderbolt, he quickly cut it into seven pieces;
rent asunder by the vajra, that embryo wailed intensely.
Then the Bull spoke to him: "Do not weep in vain;
furthermore, the Bull cut that portion into seven parts, and each of those again into seven."
Then Śakra said to him: "You shall indeed be my friend, provided that you are released; otherwise, you shall not escape with your life. (41)
The embryo said: "Indeed, it is exactly as you say.
Then Śakra, having emerged, was satisfied with his heart's desires;
free from feverish anxiety, that wise one went to the charming Amarāvatī. 42.
Then, born from that womb, there arose a mighty wind,
the essence of the vigor of all things, which causes all the worlds to tremble.
He consists of forty-nine aspects; his body is composed entirely of splendor;
he dwells in the cave of the heart of all beings; and his prowess is supreme over all. 44.
Then, on the day of his birth, the quarters of the sky became exceedingly clear, and the gods were joyful in their hearts;
at that time, the sage went there with great delight.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Origin of Vāyu," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 17.
Skanda said:
O Sage, on a certain day while Vāyu was present in the midst of the assembly,
Nārada, the best of sages, arrived there by chance.
That illustrious one beheld Kalāpin with a lute in his hand,
singing a song in a beautiful voice and playing it again and again.
Then Vāyu, of great majesty, rose up from the surface of the assembly hall;
he went forth to meet the venerable sage, accompanied by his attendants and ministers.
Having joyfully honored the worshipful one with offerings worthy of guest-reception according to the prescribed rites,
the wise king bowed down and seated the sage upon a throne.
Then, being questioned by him regarding the news of the Pracetasas, Nārada,
the best of sages, described that entire matter to Vāyu.
Vāyu said:
O you who were born from Hiraṇyagarbha, O expert in all worldly affairs,
in which place, in which great field, would the perfection of penance be certain?
"I too have a firm desire to perform austerities;
therefore, O Brahmin, let it be instructed to me today, for I am indeed without a protector. (7)
Nārada said:
O Vāyu, oh, how most blessed you are! Your mind is truly wonderful;
such an intellect as that of this noble one is rare—what more can be ordained? 8.
On Himavat, the best of mountains, in the northwestern middle region,
stands the great and lofty crystal mountain from which the Brahma-river originates.
And at the confluence of those two, in that sacred ford (tīrtha), the most excellent among all sacred fords.
Having bathed there, one goes to heaven, freed from all sins;
liberated from such sins as the killing of a Brahmin, there is no doubt in this matter. || 11 ||
Whatever desire one may have, that very desire one certainly attains,
O great hero, if one performs a bath there at the Brahma-tīrtha.
In ancient times, Brahmā performed a bath for the sake of generating living beings;
having worshipped Śaṅkara there, he then brought forth creation.
Furthermore, whoever performs a bath at that highly meritorious sacred site immediately abandons rebirth and, through his devotions, attains the state of Brahman.
Having bathed there in that great sacred ford on the Crystal Mountain, perform austerities;
O Anila, smear your body with holy ashes and wear rudrākṣa beads.
Having duly installed that Maheśvara, the bestower of all things, as a liṅga, one who has conquered the senses and subdued anger should perform recitation at will. 16.
Skanda said: Having spoken thus, the sage Nārada— worthy of worship by the gods and the proclaimer of all news— then vanished from his sight.
Then, O Brahmin, Vāyu went to Himālaya, the best of mountains,
to the highly meritorious Brahma-tīrtha, which further destroys all sins.
Delighted, Vāyu beheld that which had been described by Nārada;
there the hero bathed at ease in the water and emerged from the depths with joy.
Then, the knower of mantras bathed again with sacred ashes over all his limbs,
wore rudrākṣa beads upon his body, and gave abundant gifts.
Then, O Sage, the one of immeasurable soul ascended that great mountain, a lordly peak of crystal, pure, stainless, and shining with the luster of silver.
Having duly installed a liṅga made of brass there,
he then worshipped the God who is saluted by all the asuras.
The knower of mantras, sitting with an upright body, free from all dualities, [should worship] with perfumes, flowers, lamps, and waters from sacred fords. || 23 ||
Then the all-pervading one, possessed of great strength and single-minded focus,
remained free from the six internal enemies for more than a hundred divine years, engaged in silent recitation.
Then the Lord Rudra appeared in his presence;
Vāyu revealed him [to him], and he offered a hymn of praise to the Great Soul.
Vāyu said:
Salutations to Bhava, to the one who is to be, to the multiformed, to the beautiful-formed;
salutations be to you, who have transcended time, who are time itself, and whose form is action.
Salutations be to You, whose body is a mass of splendors, whose self consists of all light, who are a portion of the light of lights, and whose form is luminosity. 27.
Salutations be to you, O Lord of All! You to whom all the gods bow down, yet you yourself never bow;
you who bestow everything, the Auspicious One (Śarva).
Salutation to you, the multiform Rudra, whose doubts have been liberated;
salutation be to you, the Great Lord, the self of awakening, whose body is pure. 29.
Salutations to you who are single yet of two forms, possessing many bodies;
salutations again and again to the God who is one-faced and two-faced.
Salutations to you, the many-faced Bharga, whose forehead is the lord of the stars;
salutations to you who possess the trident, whose form is Brahmā, and whose form is Viṣṇu.
Salutations to the gross and the subtle, to the one who possesses both a gross and a subtle body;
to the perceptible and the imperceptible, whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest.
Obeisance be to you, the Lord of Desire, the Desire itself, the Giver of Desires, the Lover, the One who possesses a fraction of the power of Kālarātri, and the Beloved of Desire. 33.
Salutations indeed to Īśāna, to Maheśa, to the eternal Tatpuruṣa,
to Hara, to Vāmadeva, and to Vyomakeśa.
Salutation indeed to Sadyojāta, to Raudra, and to Mahādeva;
salutation be to you, Aghora, Ghora, and Ghoradeha. 35.
Skanda said:
Having heard this hymn of praise, O wise one, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, was then highly pleased by Vāyu, the foremost of yogins. 36.
The god Śaṅkara said to Vāyu, who had performed great penance:
"Out of intense affection for my devotee, I have come to grant him a boon. (37)
Śarva said:
"O child, you have performed a most great and rigorous penance.
Therefore, you are blessed and have accomplished your purpose, for this was exceedingly difficult for all the worlds to perform. (38)
Summoned by you and impelled by your heart’s penance, I have come here;
I shall now grant you a boon that is very difficult for all the gods to obtain.
"O mighty-armed one, knowing me now to be the granter of desires, have no doubt;
whatever you desire, ask it of me today. (40)
Vāyu said:
"Oh, how great is my fortune now, since you are so exceedingly pleased with me!
What further service can be performed by me, your humble servant?"
Mahādeva, who consists of all splendor and is all-pervading, is beyond the range [of perception];
yet today he has become the object of my own meager vision. 42.
Now, let there be a special address to Your Majesty, who is worthy of worship by all the gods; what more remains to be done after this? 43.
If you grant me this, O God, who are compassionate toward all beings in the world,
I shall be eternally devoted to you and intent upon your worship.
May there be constant remembrance of your feet, likewise the utterance of your name, devotion to your salutation, and the hearing of your stories. 45.
Thus, O Mahādeva, you are entreated for nothing other than devotion and the true reality;
grant them, O Lord of the Universe, Knower of Devotion, who are affectionate toward your devotees. 46.
Śarva said:
"O Vāyu, if this indeed be your firm resolve now,
nevertheless I shall grant you a boon that is very difficult to obtain in the world."
Since the trees planted through austerities bear fruit with firm roots,
those trees will grant their fruits as happiness to the practitioners.
Are even those who possess branches capable of non-giving?
For austerity is the root of all things, yet the practice of austerity is most weighty. 49.
Through austerities one becomes a master, a destroyer, a creator, and a protector;
therefore, action is accomplished by the power of austerity—otherwise, what else could they do? (50)
Since you have indeed performed that which is extremely difficult for all the gods to accomplish, from this day forward, O Noble One, you shall be the constant life-breath of the world. 51.
"May all the worlds become as mere corpses without you;
may the worlds and the entire universe, with its moving and unmoving beings, be sustained by you. 52.
"Be invisible to mortals, for you shall take on my form; of this there is no doubt.
Constantly carrying all fragrances, flow with a strength that is supreme among all. (53)
O Vāyu, at the time of universal dissolution, I shall withdraw the entire world, including its inhabitants and all things moving and stationary, through your form; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, people say everywhere, "O Noble One, you are the destroyer.
There is no difference between me and you; our prowess is one and the same.
O Sadāgati, stay on the northwestern side of Meru;
from there, protect properly all beings, both moving and stationary, who dwell therein. 56.
In that regard, O Noble One, you shall be the destroyer and especially the protector;
and may you eternally be the creator. Go now, O Wind, as you please.
Skanda said:
Having been addressed in this manner and having granted a boon to Vāyu, the omnipresent Lord Ajā,
endowed with great splendor, quickly vanished from sight.
Then the gods along with the Gandharvas, Nārada, Bṛhaspati,
the Seven Sages, the Siddhas, Hāhā, Hūhū, and others likewise [arrived].
Brahmā, the foremost of the gods, Indra, Agni, Yama,
the Rākṣasa, and the wise Varuṇa arrived there filled with joy.
Then they beheld the most wonderful Vāyu, who had obtained boons—
resplendent, established in austerity, a devotee of Rudra, and whose very self was Śiva.
Then, O twice-born one, Brahmā, the refuge of all beings, beheld them and spoke these words to those ascetics for the sake of their consecration.
"O great-souled ones, bring the water originating from the Brahma-tīrtha;
I shall perform the consecration according to the command of Śiva. (63)
Then the gods, having brought together pure water from sacred fords,
O Brahmin, joyfully gave it to Brahmā, who took it in jars.
Having extracted the Vedas and standing facing north,
the Self-born Brahmā joyfully bestowed the consecration upon him with golden jars.
In heaven, all the hosts of gods performed a most wonderful musical performance;
there was likewise a shout of "Victory!", and showers of flowers rained down.
Multitudes of Apsarases danced to the accompaniment of songs and the playing of mṛdaṅga drums;
and the preceptor honored him with offerings of excellent sandalwood and worthy gifts.
Then, O brahmin, the hosts of gods and their circles of friends, their faces blooming with joy, brought that swift arrow and went to place it in the intermediate direction (Vidiśā). || 68 ||
O Brahmin, having then assigned each direction and its respective authority to the ascetic,
the great lord Brahmā vanished from his sight.
Then Kubera indeed performed penance on the Himalayas before Viśravas, having renounced his kingdom of gold, established Laṅkā, and fixed devotion to Rudra in his heart according to his desire. (70)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Success through Vāyu’s Austerities," in the *Brahmatīrthamāhātmya* of the *Himavatkhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Skanda Purāṇa*. 18.
Agastya said: On which peak did Kubera perform penance? This we have heard from you. Who was he, by whose command [did he act], O Skanda, and whose son was that one of great strength? (1)
O best among the knowers of Brahman, I wish to hear this from you;
O Lord, tell me all that deed which was performed by him. || 2 ||
Skanda said:
"The renowned one born from the mind of Brahmā is named Pulastya;
his son is known as Viśravas, and Kubera is his offspring."
O Sage, he who was born from the Guhyaka maiden, possessing great strength and prowess,
is that very one who became the lord of the Yakṣas, Ekākṣipiṅgala.
Constantly devoted to the worship of Rudra and intent on the adoration of Śiva,
he wore rudrākṣa beads, was well-bathed with sacred ashes, and was dedicated to the mantras of Rudra.
After some time had passed, he abandoned Laṅkā and arrived at the northern foot of the Himalayas,
where Gokarṇa and Śūlabhṛt reside.
While the city was being overrun by his younger brother Rāvaṇa, who was powerful and devoted to asceticism, the Yakṣa Sucintana remained indifferent. || 7 ||
Having bowed his head to his father, who had reached the further shore of many branches of knowledge,
he stood with palms joined in reverence and circumambulated him again and again.
There he questioned his father Viśravas regarding the fruit of asceticism,
as he was worshipping Mahārudra with perfectly steady meditation.
Kubera said:
"O dear one, you are omniscient, devoted, and skilled in all worldly affairs;
you are eternally intent upon all dharmas and compassionate toward all living beings."
Which dharma among all dharmas is prescribed here as the most excellent, by the mere performance of which the supreme goal is attained? (11)
Lanka has been overrun by force by the mighty Rāvaṇa;
O dear one, our prowess would not be sufficient to remain there.
Therefore, having come here, what indeed shall I, a wretched man, do?
Or rather, grant me refuge, for even Rudra is worshipped by you.
Viśravas said:
Listen, my son, I shall relate to you the life of your brother;
indeed, it was when you arrived here by means of the Puṣpaka chariot.
Then, beholding you standing upon the chariot like a great festival, Rāvaṇa became overwhelmed with grief and questioned his mother.
"Salutations to you, O virtuous mother! What radiant man has come here, accompanied by a celestial maiden and traveling in the Puṣpaka chariot? (16)
Having heard these words of her son,
she, full of affection for her son, spoke again to her son in his presence.
That elder brother of yours is indeed the world-renowned one named Kubera;
in former times, having propitiated Rudra, he worshipped Gokarneśa. || 18 ||
Then, being well-pleased, O son, Rudra joyfully gave him a divine vehicle named Puṣpaka, which moves at will and is auspicious.
"Kubera has arrived here by means of that vehicle; of this there is no doubt. O son, if you so desire, propitiate the fierce Śaṅkara. (20)
Then, having heard his mother’s words, Rāvaṇa was also delighted;
he propitiated the Lord of Gokarṇa and worshipped him again with joy.
Then that great-souled one again performed a great sacrifice;
repeatedly cutting off his own head, he offered it as the final oblation.
Then Rudra appeared; having first approached the Ten-faced one, he spoke these words to him: "O child, choose a boon for yourself."
Rāvaṇa chose a boon, and they quarreled with one another;
the proud ten-faced one said, "You choose! You choose! (24)
The Lord of Beings, who is affectionate toward all devotees, spoke again:
"O child, choose a boon now, whatever you desire."
Rāvaṇa said: "O Mahādeva, who are compassionate toward your devotees and the liberator from all suffering, if you indeed grant me this unsurpassed boon," (26)
"I now request from you, O auspicious one, devotion both before and after this, as well as the boon of invincibility and eternal divine vigor for me. (27)
O God, [it was frequented] by the gods, asuras, gandharvas, and kinnaras,
as well as by the hosts of yakṣas and especially by the vidyādharas.
O Śambhu, may I always possess invincibility and supreme prowess;
O All-pervading Lord, may all the planets forever become my servants. 29.
O Lord, O Śaṅkara, if you have compassion for me now and always, then grant me these very boons indeed. 30.

"O Great Lord, I do not beg for immunity from those who are vile; for what purpose would I seek it from those whose strength is like that of insects? Rather, [I seek it] from Tārkṣya, as if from sparrows. (31)
Śarva said:
"So be it for you, O great hero of noble vows, regarding that which you desire.
Furthermore, O devotee, I grant you that which is difficult even for gods and dānavas to obtain. (32)
May the Yuga increase by exactly fifty-four,
and may you rule the kingdom with full vigor for that same number of years.
Viśravas said:
Having thus granted him the boon, the powerful lord vanished with joy.
From that time forward, the proud Rāvaṇa held the worlds in utter contempt.
Go, O son of mighty arms, at your own will to perform austerities on the Himālaya, the best of mountains, upon the northern peak of that mountain. 35.
On the great peak rich in gold, joined with golden trees, filled with creepers of Jāmbūnada gold, and produced from the essence of Jāmbūnada; (36)
In that place, inaccessible to all beings, well-freed from the six classes [of enemies],
great, enchanting, and delightful, I shall establish the Lord.
And below that, in the great, pure tirtha worshipped by the gods, which grants all desires, auspicious, and free from all doubt; (38)
The Brahmaputra is the best of rivers, and the Svarṇarasā is the foremost of streams; at their confluence, O son, the Jñānatīrtha is proclaimed.
At that most meritorious tirtha, which was consecrated by Brahmā in ancient times,
one obtains the recollection of past births merely by touching its waters.
Whatever deed performed in a previous birth is known by people at that very moment, one should first thoroughly bathe there and then recite [the mantra] according to one's desire. 41.
One should smear the body with ashes, wear rudrākṣas while reciting the mantras, and, having worshipped the liṅga according to the rules, remain steady and with senses fully subdued. 42.
Skanda said: Having heard his father’s words, Kubera went quickly to the Jñāna-tīrtha on the Brahma-śikhara of the Himalayas to perform penance.
Having bathed there as prescribed by his father according to the ritual rules,
and having bestowed gifts, O Sage, he then installed a Liṅga upon that mountain.
For more than a full hundred divine years, he chanted as he pleased;
then, O Agastya, Kubera composed this hymn with firm resolve.
Kubera said:

Obeisance, obeisance to Him by whom, in the past, that which is difficult for even the gods to attain was bestowed upon Śakra—the guardianship of the quarters, sovereignty, and lordship over the deities—O auspicious one! (46)
Salutations indeed to that God, by whom security was bestowed once more upon Agni of fierce splendor, and who granted him lordship over the intermediate directions as his domain. 47.
Salutations to that God, by whom was bestowed upon Kāla a great and excellent strength, and indeed the lordship over the ancestors. 48.
Salutations indeed to that god, by whom the boon of supreme prowess—most exalted among gods and asuras—was granted once again to Nairṛta. 49.
Salutations indeed to that god, by whom the worship worthy of the gods was once again bestowed upon Varuṇa, as well as the supreme lordship over the waters. 50.
Salutation to that God, O mighty-armed one, by whom auspiciousness was indeed bestowed upon Vāyu, as well as sovereignty over living beings and the lordship of the quarters. 51.
Salutation to Bhadra, to Bharga; salutation to Śiva, the wielder of the trident;
salutation to Paśupati, to Śaṅkara; salutation, salutation!
Salutations to the one whose nature is light; salutations to the unperceivable embodied one;
salutations to the unborn Lord of the Mountain; and repeated salutations to Hara. 53.
Salutations to the Lord who is stainless, and to the splendor that is untainted;
salutations again and again to the eternal one whose body is bowed to by the worlds. 54.
Salutation indeed to that God, by whom one submerged in the dark ocean of worldly existence was effortlessly uplifted, and by whom one was delivered from birth and death. 55.
Skanda said: Then, O Brahmin, being greatly delighted by the hymns of the Guhyaka,
Mahādeva arrived and manifested himself in his presence.
Seeing the ascetic, who was self-controlled, free from possessiveness, and filled with devotion,
he spoke these words out of joy to grant a boon to his devotee.
Īśvara said: "O Guhyakeśvara, oh, how most blessed is your devotion toward me! It is constant, threefold, and joined with austerity. (58)
"O my devotee, accept from me whatever boon you desire, even if it be very difficult to obtain;
let your splendor be supreme among all, and let your prowess be such. (59)
Become the king of kings, O Bhava; become the lord of the northern quarter.
For by the grace of Meru, you shall indeed be the creator for those dwelling there. 60.
Furthermore, likewise become the guardian of my nine treasures;
and let fifty-two crores be accepted by you from me.
"From this day forward, O Noble One, may you be my constant companion;
for I, Kubera, who am devoted to what is dear, shall not leave you for even a moment."
Skanda said:
Having thus granted the boon, Rudra immediately summoned the gods and the sages to bestow the consecration upon her, who was devoted to her own master and beloved by him. 63.
Then the gods arrived, together with Brahmā and their priests,
as well as the ṛṣis, the siddhas, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
Having received the command of the Lord, the Grandfather of the worlds,
while reciting [the mantra], gave [the water] to him from vessels filled with the waters of sacred fords.
The sages, recollecting the Vyāhṛtis, likewise chanted mantras with auspicious golden jars;
and the hosts of gods likewise [honored him] with hymns of praise.
Then, having honored him with various divine sandal-pastes, the preceptor at that time gratified him with offerings and bestowed his blessings once again.
Then the kettledrums resounded, the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang, showers of flowers fell, and there was a roar of "Victory! in the sky.
Having established Kubera on the peak of Mount Meru in the northern direction, Rudra vanished; the gods then departed for their respective quarters.
O noble Brahmin, Maheshvara also, having initially become the lord of the directions by his own will,
performed on the peak of the Himalayas a severe penance that is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Success through Kubera’s Austerities," in the *Jñānatīrthamāhātmya* of the *Himavatkhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Agastya said:
"O Mahāsena, you are omniscient and proficient in all matters;
you are Rudra himself in the form of asceticism, the destroyer, the creator, and the protector. (1)
He who is the eternal bestower of boons upon the worlds and the granter of fruits to ascetics—how did that Blessed One, the creator of all beings, perform penance? || 2 ||
Mahādeva is the embodiment of light, the great omnipresent one whose form is will;
the eternal god, free from modification, is perceived as a mass of splendor.
Since the deities obtain their desired fruits while remaining unperceived by all the worlds, O Noble One, how could he have obtained any fruit? 4.
He alone is the enjoyer and he alone is the object of enjoyment; for he alone is the sacrifice itself.
He alone is the oblation, the clarified butter, the sacrificial material, and indeed the sacrificer. (5)
He is the Hotṛ priest, the bearer of oblations, as well as the mantra; he alone is the Veda and that which is to be recited.
He alone is the witness of the world, the noble one, the refuge of all gods, and the all-pervading Lord.
"Thus has a doubt arisen in me upon hearing this marvel concerning you, O Lord. Cut it away for me, O General; you are surely one of pleasant speech to us. (7)
Skanda said:
"The conduct of the radiant gods is most wonderful;
O twice-born one, no doubt has been raised regarding this by the sages in the past."
For the protection of the Dharma and for the stabilization of the worlds, you are the embodiment of Dharma and the performer of penance; as the all-pervading Lord, you should practice the Dharma.
The earth, together with its mountains and oceans, is established by Dharma;
and Truth is established by Dharma, while the cloud that bestows life comes from Dharma.
Through dharma one attains fortune; through dharma one obtains progeny;
through dharma one lives long, and the full lifespan of a man is attained.
One should gladden the mind through dharma; happiness is obtained through dharma.
Whatever desire exists within one's heart, that is attained through dharma. 12.
Greed and delusion, as well as anger, pride, and envy,
along with suffering, affliction, and poverty, are obtained through unrighteousness.
Therefore, in order to bring about both the existent and the non-existent, he whose nature is both existent and non-existent,
who is devoted and whose essence is the welfare of all the worlds, performed austerities.
Agastya said:
In what place and at what sacred ford did that all-pervading Lord himself perform penance;
whom did Hara, the one of great splendor who embodies all the gods, propitiate?
I desire to hear this from you, the son of the Omniscient One;
if you have compassion for me, O Lord, speak to me, for you are possessed of glory.
Skanda said:
There are eleven Rudras who are portions of the Effulgent One;
among them, Īśāna, the most excellent portion, performed penance. (17)
In the middle between the eastern and northern directions is Tejocala, most beautiful;
and below that is the great tīrtha, the best among all excellent tīrthas. || 18 ||
O Sage, there is the highly meritorious Citrā river, as well as another called Vahnitejas;
likewise, there is the meritorious Bhasmapaṅkā at their confluence.
It is renowned as Bhasmatīrtha, which bestows the fruit of all holy fords;
having bathed there, people go to heaven in their physical bodies—of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed and recited the Rudra hymns, one is glorified in the world of Rudra;
he who beholds the Bhasma-tīrtha is liberated from all sins. || 21 ||
O Sage, even a mortal obtains that fruit which is gained by bathing at the three and a half crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) originating in Jambūdvīpa. || 22 ||
A mortal obtains that fruit which is granted by all sacred fords merely by bathing once at the excellent confluence of Bhasmatīrtha. 23.
Agastya said: O Mahāsena, you have described the Bhasma-tīrtha as supremely purifying and the source of the fruits of all holy places; how does that Bhasma-tīrtha come to be?
O Guha, how did that illustrious Lord Īśāna, who is the soul of the three gods, full of splendor, and eternally dwelling within the hearts of all beings, perform penance? 25.
Skanda said: And when Īśāna performed his ablution with ashes upon that mountain, a most excellent and meritorious river was born from the ashes of his body. 26.
Then, O wise one, that very pure stream falling from the mountain peak became famous as Bhasmapaṅkā, flowing toward the confluence of those two rivers. || 27 ||
O Brahmin, where Maheśāna bathed— desirable to all the gods— there that high-minded one ascended the mountain of splendor.
On its peak, which was greatly purified, produced from all kinds of jewels,
possessed a golden ground, and was enchanting to all the gods.
Inaccessible to the gods and beings, adorned with much frost,
with elevated plateaus made of jewels, and as brilliantly radiant as the sun and moon.
There, having seated himself upon a divine throne and facing north,
the Lord meditated upon the auspicious Brahman, which is both supreme and non-supreme, and is the primordial source of all that is supreme and non-supreme.
That great lord chanted for more than a full hundred divine years;
then, O sage, at the conclusion of the chanting, the gods became agitated with anxiety.
The gods said:
"Knowing that in former times Śakra encountered a great and terrible crisis without him,
and realizing now for certain that Rudra is not present here in this place," 33.
Having arrived here with their minds overflowing with joy, those Daityas will once again wage war and plunder Amarāvatī.
Indra said:
"O immortals, let us all go to where Mādhava resides;
let the news of Śambhu and of our ascetic penance be reported to him. (35)
And having heard that news which has been reported by us,
we shall indeed act in such a manner as Viṣṇu shall command.
Bṛhaspati said:
"Well spoken, O Śakra! What you have said is beneficial for us, there is no doubt;
it has been constantly present in my heart from before."
"Go, O high-souled ones, to where that one whose banner is Garuḍa resides;
let us deliberate there, for we must remain there without delay. (38)
Skanda said:
Having heard their speech thus addressed with joy,
and considering it to be for his own welfare, O sage, they went to where Hari was.
Then all the gods bowed to Viṣṇu, the eternal Brahman;
having circumambulated him as was fitting, they honored him with hymns and offerings.
Viṣṇu said:
"Welcome, O gods! May there be constant welfare for you—now, in your kingdoms, in your bodies, and likewise in your wealth."
"O consumers of oblations, tell me truly before me why you have come here together, preceded by your preceptor."
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Viṣṇu, we have now been welcomed through your grace;
I shall relate to you the news concerning us who are exceedingly terrified."
On the Himalaya, the best of mountains, Rudra has been chanting for a long time, thinking, "The Dānavas will attack Amarāvatī. || 44 ||
"O Mahāviṣṇu, it is our firm resolve that we cannot remain there without Rudra; therefore, O Lord, come here and rouse Rudra. 45.
Skanda said:
Having heard these words fallen from the mouth of Viṣṇu, the son of Aṅgiras—
which were approved by the gods and likewise for the welfare of all the worlds— (46)
Having reflected upon that task, Viṣṇu then summoned Brahmā;
thereafter, O wise one, he consulted with Brahmā at that time.
Having summoned all the gods, as well as the Moon, the Sun, and Nārada,
Viṣṇu, accompanied by the celestial sage Aṅgiras, went to the Himālaya.
O Sage, where that all-pervading Rudra, who embodies all the gods, was performing his penance,
there he beheld the omnipresent Maheśa established in austerity.
The god, consisting of all light, possessed the radiance of ten million suns and the brilliance of ten million moons, illuminating the ten directions.
Having beheld him once more, the Self-born, overcome by a certain fear, consulted with the gods and spoke these words, O Sage.
Brahmā said: "O Viṣṇu, alas! How can we approach the Unborn One while he is engaged in ascetic penance? Truly, O Viṣṇu, I have spoken the truth; [this cannot be] without his very grace."
O Vaikuṇṭha, we gods have truly become dissolved into this mass of splendor of the one of great and fierce majesty;
for we shall surely go into his presence. 53.
"Just as moths do not hesitate to enter a flame, so too we all stand in doubt; what should be done after this? 54.
Skanda said:
Having heard these words spoken for their benefit by Brahmā,
the gods became unable even to go into his presence.

O Brahmin, even the Sun, with his exceedingly fierce rays, was unable to approach him; his body trembling repeatedly, he was described by the best of gods as "the Unborn" (Aja) after consulting the gods and following the words of the lotus-born Brahmā, and thus went into the presence of Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Consultation of the Gods," in the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, concerning the emergence of Rudra’s asceticism.
Agastya said:
"O son of Śiva, you have told me that this is the first portion of the Lord;
we have heard that Mahādeva possesses fierce splendor and is the witness of the world. (1)
How was it that the sun, possessed of great splendor and being a deity whose very nature consists of unbearable radiance, was unable to proceed into his presence? || 2 ||
Skanda said:
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the gods, led by Bṛhaspati, then gladdened him, O wise one, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (3).
Having summoned the god Pūṣan, they spoke with reverence to him,
after all the gods had deliberated, regarding the immediate need for Hari’s manifestation.
The gods said:
"O Primordial God of great splendor, you who have compassion for all beings!
You are the creator of all creatures; there is no doubt that you possess the energy of Rudra. (5)
"Go, O Sūrya, to the presence of Mahādeva Rudra.
Having gone there, the God who is established in asceticism should be saluted by you according to your desire. (6)
Sūrya said: "O gods, you have surely prepared yourselves for my destruction! Who, other than a fool, would seek his own destruction by pursuing me? (7)
He whose splendor is utterly unbearable, whose fire is of terrible aspect,
and of whom I am but a partial manifestation, while he himself is born from a ten-millionth part of that [supreme] being.
O Lord, by whose opening and closing of his eyes the dissolution and creation of the world occur, it is not possible for me to go into the presence of him while he is engaged in penance. 9.
Aṅgiras said:
O Himāṃśu, great hero, have compassion for us, for the sake of the welfare of the gods, and for the protection of the abode of the deities. 10.
O Candra, go to their presence for the destruction of those who fear us,
and let their ferocity be pacified by your own cool rays.
Candra said: "O Guru, salutations to you! It is not possible for me to go there, into the presence of the high-souled Rudra himself, who is engaged in severe penance."
Whether they be wrathful or free from anger, who goes into their presence without first having received the command of Maheśa? This was declared previously. 13.
If one who is devoted in such a manner goes to the presence of Śambhu without reflecting on His command, he attains the supreme state. 14.
Indra said:
"O Dahanāgni, you are radiant and an emanation of Rudra, of this there is no doubt;
therefore, bring about the welfare of the gods and especially of the kingdoms. (15)
The body exists for the benefit of others and for the protection of dharma;
the self is a cow of plenty that grants all desires, yet it remains for but a moment—of this there is no doubt. (16)
For this very reason, they are sought after for the benefit of the three worlds by the wise;
go to the presence of Rudra and report this news to him. 17.
Agni said:
O King of the Gods, O one of great wisdom, O benefactor of the worlds!
Everything that has been spoken by you to me is indeed the truth. (18)
The wise first examine what is possible and what is impossible before undertaking an action;
O Śakra, virtuous people certainly do not perform a task that is impossible.
The universe is created by means of her wills and likewise protected;
she withdraws the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, leaving nothing behind.
He by whose eye-fire the universe is surely reduced to ashes will likewise reduce me to ashes; neither he nor I am capable [of resisting him]. Salutations to you! 21.
Nārada said:
He was self-controlled in character, pure, virtuous, and always devoted to all duties;
he was a benefactor to others, godlike, truthful, and had conquered his senses.
O Varuṇa, you alone are indeed capable, being the essence of all qualities and flavors;
O Lord of the Waters, go certainly to the presence of Rudra.
O Lord Pāśin, go to the presence of that powerful and unbearable sharpness of the Lord, and with your own life-giving portions, pacify his splendor. 24.
"Noble-born, endowed with virtuous conduct, and always devoted to the duty of giving—go quickly, for you are pleasing and have been a constant devotee of Rudra. (25)
Varuṇa said: "O Brahmin, it is not possible even for me to go into his presence, O noble one, in order to pacify that ascetic of fierce splendor. (26)
O twice-born one, the life of that person who, being incapable, promises a task he cannot perform, serves only as a mockery to the world.
Just as a child might desire to grasp the orb of the moon situated in the sky, such shall be my power for the sake of mocking him. 28.
Therefore, O wise lord of sages, one who stands firm in discernment does not perform what cannot be accomplished by the non-Self, for his mind is afraid of such censures. 29.
Skanda said: Then, O Brahmin, having heard what was spoken, the gods together with Śakra went swiftly to where the Creator was, accompanied by four immortals.
O Pot-born one, they then related all those words spoken in distress by those dwellers of heaven,
as well as their actions, to the Creator.
Then Lokeśa also went there and related the current account to Viṣṇu,
who possesses all forms and knows the three periods of time.
Brahmā said: And in this regard, even those gods became unable to go near him; having seen the power of Rudra, they were seized by terror and trembled. (33)
O Lord, even while remaining there, those gods became effortless;
O Viṣṇu, let an effort be made—what further should be done after this? 34.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Grandfather, we shall go together with the gods to the presence of the high-souled Rudra there, and a hymn of praise shall be performed by us simultaneously."
Having heard this hymn, Mahādeva will certainly become pacified;
likewise, the high-souled lords of the worlds are pacified by hymns and by praises.
Dharma is attained through praises; one obtains the fruit through hymn alone.
Therefore, this hymn is composed, by which fear is destroyed.
Skanda said:
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, the life-sustainer of all living beings, Brahmā and all the other gods exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (38).
Having first circumambulated Upendra according to the prescribed rite,
they bowed down with their joined palms placed upon their heads, praising him with joy.
Then Brahmā and the other foremost gods, overcome with a slight fear, approached him slowly and praised Rudra.
The gods said:
Oṃ!
Salutations to Rudra, to the fierce one; salutations to you who possess a terrible form.
Salutations to you, the unborn one of fierce splendor, who possesses a body of terrible power.
Salutations again and again to the one who is devoid of qualities yet possesses portions of qualities, to the immutable light,
to the self of the five elements, and to the portion of truth.
Salutation to the one whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, to the consciousness that is pure awareness,
to the ether-like one whose body is space, and to the one whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire.
Salutations be unto you, the god whose mouth is Aurva, whose head is the sky, who dwells upon the earth, whose ears are the quarters of space, and whose belly is the ocean. 44.
Salutation to the one known as Bhujaṅga, whose nature is the ego;
salutation to the one with cloud-like hair, the formidable one, whose seed is the lotus. || 45 ||
Salutation to him whose body is hairy like a tree, whose navel is Mount Sumeru;
salutation to the source of the Grandfather’s creation, who devours all beings. 46.
Salutation to that God, the heart-essence, who is indeed the Pradhāna and Puruṣa; who is non-dual, incomprehensible, the primordial, and the cause. 47.
Salutations to the one who is to be meditated upon, who is well-conceived, whose nature is both conceivable and inconceivable;
may you protect us who are overwhelmed and scorched by your intense splendors. 48.
May you protect us in this unfathomable, shoreless ocean of worldly existence which is composed of illusion.
O Lord, lover of your devotees, may you constantly embrace your servants with your grace; and may you evermore protect us, who dwell in ignorance, by covering us with your shadow. 49.
Skanda said:
Then, having heard that hymn falling from the mouths of all the gods,
he who is easily pleased was gratified by those divine praises and his own powers.
Śaṅkara spoke to them with a voice faltering with joy;
withdrawing his own splendors, he became serene of countenance. (51)
Īśāna said:
"O gods, sages, and devotees, you have come here into my presence and have joyfully offered this hymn of praise to me in accordance with the truth. (52)
Therefore, O children, I am well-pleased with your praises;
what service may I perform for you? Tell me now.
The gods said:
"Every boon has indeed been granted to us; nothing remains here.
By your grace, we have all become deities. (54)
"O Lord, without you we are unable to remain in heaven;
for we know this secret of yours: that the abode of the gods would be empty [without you]. (55)
"The Daityas will attack; therefore, terrified, we have come here.
For this reason, we shall indeed consecrate you as our lord this very day."
Skanda said: O Brahmin, having brought the waters of the sacred fords drawn up in golden jars, Viṣṇu joyfully performed the consecration of the Supreme Self.
Brahmā, reciting the Vedas, joyfully bestowed the consecration upon him once more;
and the sun, of great splendor, gave him brilliance with its own blazing radiance.
Candra performed the consecration with jars rich in nectar and endowed with medicinal herbs;
Śakra performed the consecration with water drawn from jeweled pitchers.
Vahni gave [the power] to Maheśa with water from a jar filled with splendor;
likewise, Pāśī gave it to him with the waters of all the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Vāyu again gave him fragrant and cool waters;
the Seven Sages then performed his ablution with water consecrated by the recollection of the Gāyatrī mantra.
Nārada also joyfully gave him the cry of victory while reciting mantras; and those who had previously failed in their rites performed his consecration with purifying substances.
The wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu provided the bath with auspicious streams of milk;
likewise, the gods and other Gandharvas presented him with offerings.
Then, reciting the mantras for that Lord, the preceptor joyfully worshipped the All-pervading One with perfumes, flowers, and divine garments.
Then there fell a profuse shower of flowers and parched grain,
cast down from heaven by the arms of celestial nymphs, originating in the sky.
A wonderful cry of victory arose and kettledrums resounded loudly;
there, celestial women sang the glory of Rudra with their whole being.
And there the Apsarases danced to the sounds of drums and cymbals;
then Viṣṇu spoke to the Lord for the welfare of all the worlds.
Viṣṇu said: "O Lord of Beings, stay in the middle between the eastern and northern directions on the peak of Mount Meru; from there, protect the worlds situated therein constantly."
"O Omniscient One, from this day forward, be for all time the guardian of the quarters;
then the worlds will constantly call you Īśāna. (69)
Skanda said:
Having promised him this, he went to where Viṣṇu was,
situated above in the midst of the quarters, for the sake of protecting the world.
Even today, Hara protects the entire world in happiness;
therefore, living beings constantly call the Lord of the Twice-born "Viśveśāna" (the Lord of the Universe). 71.
From that time forth, the guardians of the quarters, Dhruva, Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, Nara—the subduer of the wicked—and King Bhagīratha, who was his very self, performed severe penance within the wheel. 72.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Consecration of Īśāna," in the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
Who was this Dhruva, the great hero whose every desire was supreme?
O Skanda, how did he perform his penance—was he a human or even a god?
In what place and at what sacred ford was he instructed by whom, O Lord?
I wish to hear this; tell it to me, O son of Śaṅkara. (2)
Skanda said:
There was indeed Uttānapāda, who was honored by all social classes;
his son was the mighty-armed one, renowned by the name Dhruva. || 3 ||
And his father, Uttānapāda, having placed his beloved elder brother on his lap and seeing him seated in the assembly, [was filled with joy]. (4)
Dhruva became indifferent there; having gone to his mother’s presence, he then reported her lack of regard for him and that news to her.
Then, having become indifferent in mind and repeatedly remembering his own lack of respect, he asked his mother about the news regarding her words.
Dhruva said:
"Having placed my brother on his lap in the midst of the assembly, my father sat there;
even while looking at me, he abandoned all joy and shone equally with him. (7)
"O mother, tell me how my father’s beloved brother might become [my friend];
my father, though a knower of dharma, never shows affection toward me. (8)
Skanda said: Having heard those words of her son, which were indeed full of contempt, his mother then pacified her son with gentle speech.
Sunīti said: "O son, do not grieve; whatever was done in a previous birth—whether sorrow or happiness, my child—all that is obtained here."
By destiny, one obtains all that: the body of a king with the limbs of a Brahmin, and the fourfold physical form consisting of a human body with the limbs of a god.
Action performed in a previous birth is indeed destiny; of this there is no doubt.
Having understood this through his own mind in this world, the wise man is not deluded by it.
Therefore, austerity is the root; austerity alone is most weighty.
By austerity everything is obtained, whatever one desires, at that very moment.
Skanda said:
O Brahmin, having heard his mother's words, he became intent on asceticism;
though disregarding his father, he was quickly filled with joy. 14.
Then, O Sage, the son of Uttānapāda went alone to a desolate forest to perform penance, having abandoned hunger and thirst. (15)
There, in that forest thick with trees and frequented by lions and tigers,
Dhruva beheld the Seven Sages in a place inhabited by all kinds of creatures.
With palms joined in reverence, Dhruva paid homage to those brahmins,
having properly circumambulated them again and again with hymns of praise.
The Seven Sages said: "Who are you, O child, so firm of soul, who has surely come here to this forest that is inaccessible to humans and inhabited by various creatures? (18)
"O tender child, no fear whatsoever exists for you;
tell me, O boy, why you have come here running away from a tiger or a deer. (19)
Dhruva said:
"O best of the twice-born, I am not fleeing from tigers, lions, or other beasts;
I have come here by chance because of the humiliation I suffered at the hands of my father. (20)
"I am the son of the lord Uttānapāda and of Prajāpati;
having come here as a neutral observer, I am known by the name Dhruva. (21)
"Having abandoned me, his eldest son, and having placed him upon his lap, my father stands in the midst of the assembly; therefore, I am filled with detachment."
Therefore, I have come here with the desire to perform severe penance;
O great sages, it is the truth that I no longer wish to live here.
My mind is intent upon describing the beauty of the Lord’s sandals;
if you have compassion for me, please grant me your instruction. (24)
This body, agitated by pleasure and pain, remains for but a moment;
yet it is through this that liberation, which destroys the ocean of suffering, is attained. (25)
The Seven Sages said: "Oh, how wonderful and great is the deed of this boy! For one who possesses such great intelligence, what could possibly be difficult to attain? (26)
"My child, you are still very young, yet you are intent on performing austerities.
For if you were truly capable of practicing penance, your body would be like that of one standing in the midst of fire."
On the great peak of the Himalayas, the highest of all with its beautiful summit, one should fix the mind in single-pointed concentration and recite the Rudra-mantra. (28)
O child, having first bathed according to the prescribed rites at Kāmatīrtha— the most great, most pure, and the best among many excellent tīrthas— and then at Sarvonnata, you may proceed.
Skanda said:
Having heard the words of the sages and being instructed by the ṛṣis,
Dhruva, the great yogi, went to Himālaya, the best of mountains.
Filled with joy to perform austerity, having abandoned both the pleasant and the unpleasant, he was freed from the cloak of delusion and clothed in the cloak of knowledge. || 31 ||
In the south-eastern direction from the Himavat, in a place most beautiful with many caves,
flows the excellent Brahmaputra river and the supreme river Kāmadhārā.
O wise one, at the confluence of those two, Kāmatīrtha is proclaimed;
having bathed there, people go to heaven, even if they were previously burdened by sins.
At that highly meritorious tirtha, praised by Brahmā as the bestower of boons,
the sin committed over seven lifetimes is destroyed in an instant by bathing.
There, Dhruva bathed properly at Kāmatīrtha according to his desire;
he smeared his body with ashes and indeed wore Rudrākṣa beads.
Then Dhruva surely went to that mountain of all-elevated peaks,
which was inaccessible to all living beings and adorned with abundant snow.
Seated there upon that peak with his body straight and perfectly motionless,
he chanted prayers for thousands of mortal years, remaining entirely still.
And, O Sage, with his hair standing on end, that great-souled one, overflowing with devotion, praised Maheśāna Rudra with words consisting of His names, uttered with a faltering voice. (38)
Dhruva said:
Oṃ!
Salutations to Śiva, the auspicious one, who possesses a benevolent form and is the embodiment of splendor.
Salutation to the one whose body is a mass of splendors, the lord of lights.
Salutations again and again to the giver of worldly existence, to the god who is the essence of all, to the wielder of the trident, to the stainless one, to Rudra, the lord of all beings. 40.
Salutations again and again to the one whose body is the sky, the primordial one, the beginningless one, the one with matted hair; to Rudra, the creator of beings, the benefactor Śaṅkara. 41.
Salutations again and again to the skin, which is of the nature of touch and consists of the red portion;
salutations indeed to the flesh, which is of the nature of the individual soul (jīva), and to that which is of the nature of fat. 42.
Salutations to the one whose form consists of sinews and bones, who takes the form of the three channels;
salutations to the sense of smell residing in the nose, and to taste which perceives flavors. 43.
Salutation to the one who possesses eyes and vision, to the ear and hearing;
salutation to the one who is the form of life for all living beings, whose very self is designated as the individual soul (jīva).
Salutations to Bhīma, who is the form of the earth and whose embodiment is water;
salutations to Ugra, who is the form of fire and whose embodiment is wind. 45.
Salutations to you, the inner-dwelling deity whose form is the intellect;
salutations indeed to you whose forms are the mind, the consciousness, and the ego.
Salutations to Śambhu, who is consciousness, discernment, and the very form of knowledge;
salutations to Bharga, who is Śakti and the creator of the worlds. 47.
Save me, O God, Lord of Beings, from the ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra; O All-pervading One, save me who have fallen blind into a deep well of the blinding darkness of ignorance. 48.
Skanda said:
O Sage, having heard this hymn of praise from Dhruva with such devotion,
Lord Rudra was exceedingly pleased by that eulogy, his devotion, and his excellent austerities.
Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, the Great All-pervading Lord appeared;
beholding him with joy, O Sage, he spoke these words.
Īśvara said:
"O child, a most wonderful and severe penance has been performed by you!
Having abandoned the state of duality, you have remained devoid of all objects of enjoyment. (51)
Such was the boy Dhruva who propitiated Śṛṅga.
"O child, having become motionless in this solitary place, Brahmaśekhara," [52]
Therefore, I now grant you this boon which is eternal and immovable;
listen to me with one-pointed mind and full concentration regarding that which is certain.
"Since you have come here and performed penance because of your disregard for your father, therefore, by my grace, may you become glorious and supreme over all. (54)
From this day forward, you are noble, floating above all the worlds;
remain there, perfectly immovable, upon that great place on the peak of Mount Meru.
Then people will say: "He is known as Dhruvaloka;
while all worlds move swiftly, O Dhruva, you remain immovable. (56)
Skanda said:
Having thus granted the boon, Rudra then vanished;
Brahmā, approaching him, joyfully conferred upon him the consecration. 57.
Then Brahmā, accompanied by throngs of Apsarases exulting in song and instrumental music, brought Dhruva on a chariot that moves at will.
Then Brahmā established Dhruva, the highest of all, upon the great peak of Sumeru, the abode of the gods, at its very summit.
Brahmā too performed severe penance, by which they quickly incurred the curse of the goddess;
for having committed an offense while in the secret place of the goddess, they consequently became trees.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Attainment of Dhruva’s Penance," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 22 ||
Agastya said:
How did the goddess, who is compassionate toward all beings, bestow a curse upon all the gods? And how were those limbs of yours reduced to trees? (1)
I desire to hear this; tell me, O son of Śaṅkara!
Who is that goddess of great splendor, and what is her supreme majesty?
