O Mahāsena, in what field of great merit does she reside constantly? And what, in particular, is the name of that sacred ford (tīrtha)? || 3 ||
Skanda said:
Listen, O Pot-born one; with a single-minded and concentrated mind, I shall relate to you that divine event as it occurred in the past, concerning which you have questioned me. 4.
The Brahmaputra is the best of rivers, and the Kāmadhārā is the foremost of streams;
between these two stands the great mountain whose peak is named Nīlācala. 5.
It is renowned as Kāmakṣetra, the most excellent among all sacred fields;
in that greatly purified field, which bestows the fruits of all desires.
There was a wise and great goddess, renowned by the name Kāmākhyā,
who was formerly praised by Brahmā while she resided within the eye of Viṣṇu.
That Māyā is the eternal Yoginī, served by millions of Yoginīs;
whatever they desire with devotion, they obtain that very thing from her. 8.
O wise one, on a certain day Maheśvara departed from heaven,
leaving behind his attendants and the gods for the field of desire in the netherworld (rasātala).
Then Hara, established in joy, together with her who is named Kāmā,
knowing that place to be a secluded retreat, O Goddess, the Lord attained great delight.
O Sage, the Lord became unable to abandon that place;
deluded by Kāmākhyā, the God did not move anywhere else. 11.
Once, having learned during the day that Rudra was not present in heaven, that great sage Nārada, who is fond of quarreling, [set out]. || 12 ||
He went quickly to where Hiraṇyakaśipu,
the great hero and lord of the Dānavas, was stationed in the midst of the assembly hall, filled with joy.
Seated upon a golden lion-throne and surrounded by all the Daityas,
he listened to various accounts falling from the mouths of his own spies.
He was constantly served by songs celebrating the glory of Rudra, by the sounds of mṛdaṅga drums and rhythmic clapping,
and by dances imbued with the nine aesthetic sentiments.
At that time, Hiraṇyakaśipu beheld the noble sage descending from the sky with joy as he approached from the heavens.
He was singing with great joy the fame of the Lord,
lute in hand, endowed with the musical notes, wearing a garland, and possessing a sweet voice.
Seeing that Nārada had indeed arrived near the assembly hall,
Hiraṇyakaśipu quickly went out to meet him along with his attendants.
Then the lord of the Daityas, having honored the sage with various offerings of worship, bowed down; O Brahmin, he then brought him forward and seated him upon his own throne.
He first inquired after Nārada’s welfare and his recent activities, and then said again:
"Welcome, O best of sages! Tell me quickly, what shall we do? (20)
Nārada said:
"O child, I have not come here by mere chance, but out of affection for you,
having brought some news from heaven and from here at this present time."
Listen, O Daitya, I shall relate what has occurred regarding heaven and the earth;
all the gods are filled with terror because of fear of you, without a doubt. (22)
O child, Mahādeva went to where Kāmākhyā resides;
there, the great Lord rejoiced for a very long time in a secluded place.
Then all the gods in heaven reflected:
"Now all the asuras will plunder us; this is certain, there is no doubt. (24)
"Without Rudra, the gods will certainly not ascend to heaven;
O gods, where else shall we go now, for our own sake? (25)
Thus the gods would undoubtedly become agitated with anxiety;
know this to be the truth, for I am departing—may it be well with you. (26)
Skanda said: Then, after the sage had departed, the wise Hiraṇyakaśipu,
having heard that news from Nārada, was filled with great joy.
He summoned all the Daityas—young, old, and those of middle age;
thereupon, the enemies of the gods belonging to his lineage quickly assembled.
Then, having summoned those great-souled and mighty heroes of the assembly who were of three different ages, he had them seated in order.
The heroic Hiraṇyakaśipu consulted with the Asuras,
along with his aged ministers and those counselors skilled in counsel.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O noble Daityas, you whose prowess is supreme among all,
listen to my report concerning the vulnerabilities of the inhabitants of heaven."
Afflicted by our power, the gods became terrified;
they were certain that we would invade heaven.
Having abandoned heaven, Mahādeva went elsewhere to the surface of the earth,
to where Kāmākhyā resides, served by hosts of yoginīs.
"Now these great portents have arisen," they prophesy;
"how is it that the gods remain here, overwhelmed, without Rudra? (34)
Thus it was told to me by the wise Nārada, and especially by my spies;
tell me, what should be done? (35)
Skanda said: O Sage, having heard these words of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Daityas deliberated from nearby, both individually and together with their ministers.
The high-minded and wise Anuhrāda, a great hero skilled in all forms of policy, spoke first in the midst of the assembly.
Anuhrāda said:
"The ignorant man who undertakes an action without knowing his own power is indeed blameworthy; he should be recognized as one who is mocked by all the world. (38)
O best of Daityas, a wise person always undertakes a task after first considering his own power, so that he may not suffer humiliation. (39)
Prahlāda said: "What has been spoken by Anuhrāda is undoubtedly for our benefit—that place where indeed the gods, who strike fear into all enemies, reside. (40)
Where Śakra dwells, surrounded by all his hosts of troops;
where the guardians of the quarters stand as protectors, and where likewise are those whose weapons are their curses.
There the sun wanders, whose radiance is unbearable;
there the moon of bright rays wanders, whose coolness is unbearable.
Where Viṣṇu, of great splendor, the slayer of enemies whose banner bears Garuḍa,
formerly tore asunder our strength and army with his seat.
In that matter, O father, tell us how victory may be obtained by us;
if Hari were not there, it could certainly be achieved. (44)
Saṃhrāda said:
Viṣṇu alone is to be honored, for he is not inferior; Viṣṇu alone is the most excellent.
Viṣṇu and Rudra are not distinct; as is Viṣṇu, so is Hara. || 45 ||
If, at the outset, two gods are honored equally by one who is respected yet harsh, they shall indeed become the protectors of the worlds; therefore, they must never be treated with contempt. 46.
"Thinking that Rudra does not exist, they are now fighting with the gods;
O dear one, there would be doubt regarding victory in this matter for us in the third heaven. (47)
Nikumbha said:
"O dear one, that by which the rising up against others who are established and powerful is carried out by those endowed with only slight strength," 48.
The humiliation of such a person has been declared by those expert in many sciences of policy;
therefore, the illustrious king should rouse him by means of those endowed with great power. 49.
He who knows his own strengths and weaknesses is wise;
therefore, a lord should employ his army against enemies according to strategic principles. 50.
O dear one, having acquired even slight advantages, a wise king endowed with a fourfold army should engage in battle with his powerful enemies through the application of political strategy.
Bali said:
"One should make peace with an enemy at the proper time, and one should fight with adversaries at the proper time;
for victory is attained at the proper time, while defeat occurs even at the improper time. (52)
He who fights with his enemies without knowing the proper time and the improper time perishes before long, even if he be great.
One understands the action [performed] at the proper time and shall obtain victory in the three worlds;
therefore, having first deliberated upon the time, action is undertaken by the wise. (54)
Hiraṇyākṣa said:
"If even from one [of you] there exists fear in your hearts, how is it that the Daityas are engaged with their enemies by means of many heroes? (55)
Even when attacked by those with great strength,
O child, he disregards even the lowly, even if they are of inferior strength, provided they have weapons in their hands.
One should never fight, even against many who are base;
it has been heard that a black cobra was struck down by ants.
"O Danujas, if there is indeed fear of Viṣṇu for you, it shall certainly be so;
I myself will surely fight with him in battle, of this there is no doubt. (58)
Vipracitti said:
"Aha! What a great marvel it is that you, though wise, do not perceive the supreme vulnerability; what will you accomplish with your ritual acts?"
All the deities tremble now that Maheśvara has been provoked; agitated by anxiety, they wonder, "How indeed shall we remain in heaven? (60)
And at this time, O Asuras, it pleases our hearts that today we set forth for the journey that shall crush all our enemies. 61.
At this time, the Daityas will have a great vulnerability;
one must fight with firm resolve, never at a time of supreme prosperity.
Māyā said: "O Daityas, what has been spoken by Vipracitti is the truth; there is no doubt.
Let us depart this very moment for our prosperity and for our own victory."
O best of Daityas, if there exists in your hearts the desire to rule over Amarāvatī in heaven without any thorns in your side, [then act accordingly]. 64.
"O Lord Hiraṇyakaśipu, let the armies be summoned today;
let everyone now prepare for battle."
"O best of Daityas, do not remain for a long time after having summoned all the soldiers; proceed with your fourfold forces."
Skanda said:
O Brahmin, having heard these words of others and of Maya,
and considering them to be true, that wise one then desired the kingdom of heaven.
At that very moment, Hiraṇyakaśipu summoned his army from all those who had arrived,
including both children and the elderly.
Then the wise Hiraṇyakaśipu joyfully issued commands to the Daitya Vipracitti, as well as to his other ministers.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O Daityas, put on your excellent armor;
now take up your choice weapons as well as your missiles."
Likewise, let the drivers of the elephants, horses, buffaloes,
donkeys, and camels certainly fasten their armor.
Having mastered all the arts, you have fashioned for me this perfectly constructed and well-crafted chariot, the best of all chariots, which moves at will and is adorned with many wonders.
Having fashioned many various weapons and missiles in great numbers, he also created the noose of illusion, the spear, the veil of invisibility, and the swift-moving [missile].
Skanda said:
O lord of brahmins, having now heard the words of the king of the Daityas,
Maya then brought minerals there for the sake of his craft.
Having forcibly seized that divine chariot, which moved at will and blazed like fire,
Maya indeed fashioned it with various mechanical devices and with a richly variegated hue adorned with refined gold.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Consultation of the Daityas," in the Himavat-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 23 ||
Agastya said:
O Skanda, how did that best of Daityas construct a divine chariot? Of what nature was the vehicle of Maya for the battle against the enemies of the gods?
If you have compassion for me now, O Skanda, I wish to hear this; tell it to me, O Lord, as it truly is.
Skanda said: Maya fashioned a divine chariot made of Jāmbūnada gold, beautiful in every limb, bright, and inlaid with rubies.
It was a firm sixteen-wheeled chariot, possessing a beautiful pole made of illusion,
endowed with the sound of thunderclouds, and drawn by a thousand serpents.
O Sage, it is half a yojana in height and half that in width; it is accompanied by subordinate peaks and contains many mountain summits.
Abounding in rubies and corals, adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli,
and beautifully graced by emeralds resembling topaz gems.
Furthermore, it was adorned with five-colored banners made of every kind of jewel,
and it was intensely radiant, encircled by the fashioned faces of various creatures.
Resembling the radiance of the sun, beautifully adorned with various colors,
it was furnished with many wonderful paintings and featured the faces of animals engaged in various movements and postures.
In the front part, it was brilliantly adorned with an owl-emblem,
shining with splendors and decorated with a network of tiny bells.
He was skilled in the art of driving with reins as his hands, expert in managing subordinates, knowledgeable of the proper time, and possessed of great wisdom; he was joined by such a charioteer.
O Sage, it was equipped with various weapons and missiles, inspiring fear in enemies,
endowed with many illusions, capable of moving at will, and exceedingly beautiful.
O lord of brahmins, having thus constructed that supreme chariot, Maya then first presented it to the lord of the Daityas— a vehicle that brings fear to all the worlds.
Beholding that divine chariot, he rejoiced together with the gods and asuras;
the lord of the Danavas bestowed his own bracelet upon him in the assembly hall.
Then the Daitya, equipped with armor adorned with many variegated designs and set with diamonds and lapis lazuli, was fully armored.
Then, having performed the rites of atonement and given gifts to the twice-born, Hiraṇyakaśipu quickly mounted that chariot.
Then, that best among speakers comforted the charioteer with sweet words and spoke these further words to him.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O charioteer, listen certainly to my words;
you must protect me whenever I am again situated in danger. (17)
Having drawn the chariot away from that such-like encounter with one another,
since you were situated in a perilous position, you must be protected by me once again.
Knowing this rule, whoever indeed [employs it] against another in a great battle immediately attains victory and does not encounter distress. (19)
Skanda said:
O Sage, having heard the sweet words of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
he joyfully accepted them and paid homage to that Lord.
Then, having duly received the command of his lord, O Ghaṭotbhava,
the charioteer urged on the elephants and the drivers of the chariots.
Then, having once again properly readied that excellent chariot,
he gave that same kind of divine vehicle to Hiraṇyākṣa at that time.
It was made of gold, possessed great brilliance, and was exquisitely adorned with all kinds of jewels;
it had a horse as its mount, was exceedingly lofty, and was equipped with every weapon and missile.
O brahmin, Maya then gave Prahlāda a divine chariot that swiftly struck fear into his enemies and was resplendent with flags and banners.
It was fashioned from a combination of silver and gold, adorned with many variegated patterns, inlaid with rubies and corals, and exceedingly beautiful.
Furthermore, he gave to Saṃhrāda a supreme banner with a serpent-staff, adorned with flags and featuring the faces of deer that appeared to move about.
Furthermore, he fashioned for him an excellent chariot made of silver,
variegated with dark-blue gems and adorned with every kind of jewel.
He gave to Anuhrāda a chariot with the emblem of a cock's head raised aloft, adorned with many-colored banners,
possessing eight wheels, and shining with a brilliant luster.
Having gathered many elements, he fashioned a supreme chariot—
eight-wheeled, richly wrought of iron, and filled with various lights.
Maya gave to Nikumbha a chariot equipped with a network of tinkling bells, adorned with crow-emblems and banners,
and furnished with many weapons and missiles.
Maya, having forcibly fashioned a divine chariot made of iron,
equipped it with a golden lattice and provided it with a white banner.
Furthermore, he gave to Kālakāya a buffalo as a vehicle, which was dark in body and resplendent with uplifted banners that shone like white clouds.
It was divine, made of Jāmbūnada gold, resembling molten gold,
joined with faces of bulls and lions, and exquisitely fashioned from various jewels.
And Maya gave to Bāli a palace with windows latticed with jewels, adorned with vulture-emblemed banners and flags, and equipped with various weapons and missiles.
A splendid chariot made of eight metals, adorned with gold,
embellished with lapis lazuli and rubies, and most wonderful to behold.
He gave to Vipracitti a terrible vehicle drawn by buffaloes, which was accompanied by the sound of iron bells and struck fear into his enemies.
Having honored that most wonderful, divine chariot, which was exceedingly variegated, made of Jāmbūnada gold, covered with a golden lattice, and adorned with the tinkling sound of small bells; 37.
Maya gave to Bāṇa a most terrible chariot with variegated banners, drawn by many donkeys,
and filled with various weapons and missiles.
Having thus given the chariots to them,
the artisan then himself ascended that unsurpassed chariot.
Having equipped themselves and mounted their chariots, the best of the Daityas went forth,
accompanied by an army of thirty koṭis of chariots and consisting of the fourfold forces.
Having first performed auspicious rites for his welfare and having bestowed wealth as gifts upon the brahmins, that noble and wise one indeed dispatched all the Danujas toward the battle.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Departure of the Daityas," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 24.
Skanda said: Nārada also went to heaven, where Vāsava dwells,
playing the lute with great delight and singing with sweet tones.
Filled with joy, skilled in debate, all-pervasive, and fond of quarreling,
he immediately reported that news to Śakra.
Nārada said:
O King of the Gods, O highly wise one, O Lord, listen now with an undivided mind to this account from me for the benefit of all the gods.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, having girded himself with armor and mounted his chariot,
set out from that region accompanied by a vast army.
Surrounded on all sides by an army of thirty crores of chariots, he will come here for battle today; let him see it for himself.
O thousand-eyed one, knowing that Śaṅkara does not exist along with you,
may you prepare yourself with your armies for the welfare of heaven.
Skanda said:
Having heard these words of his, he was somewhat seized with fear;
he then summoned all the gods, led by Bṛhaspati.
The Protector of the World (Viṣṇu) then consoled them all with sweet words for the sake of guarding heaven, and summoned Viśvakarman. || 8 ||
Then Śakra, having first summoned Viśvakarman with great honor, commanded him to prepare a chariot. 9.
Śakra said: "O Viśvakarman, O highly wise one, skilled in all crafts! A great battle between the gods and the asuras will take place here."
Accompanied by an army of thirty million chariots, Hiraṇyakaśipu will come here and wage a great battle with me.
Therefore, let many celestial chariots be constructed by you now— numerous, exceedingly sturdy, and fit to be the dwelling places for tumultuous battles.
Skanda said: Having heard these words spoken with great respect by Indra, the wise Viśvakarman, who knew the proper rites, was filled with joy.
Having gathered all the elements, he fashioned a supreme vehicle, beautiful in its various parts and enriched with gold, silver, and jewels. 14.
There was a massive iron wheel, broad and with an iron hub,
along with a parasol made of Jāmbūnada gold and adorned with every kind of jewel.
Adorned with a network of small bells producing a great sound like that of bell-metal,
and joined with banners of five colors, it was the supreme Vajra-banner.
That most wonderful celestial chariot was fashioned of gold, adorned with lattices of jewels and windows, and yoked to Airāvata.

O Sage, Viśvakarman gave to Śakra a vehicle that was inlaid with various jewels, richly equipped with weapons and missiles, capable of moving at will, adorned with canopies of coral and pearls, and radiant for battle.
Then Śakra, beholding that most wonderful celestial chariot,
was filled with joy and, unfastening a necklace from his own neck, gave it to him.
Having girded himself with armor, Indra ascended his firm celestial chariot;
thereafter, he fed the twice-born and bestowed abundant gifts upon them.
Having received the benedictions of the Brahmins and having been saluted by them,
Śakra was then greatly delighted and comforted his charioteer once more.
Then, a supreme vehicle fashioned quickly from Jāmbūnada gold appeared,
its silver latticed windows radiant with the faces of animals depicted in various postures and movements.
Furthermore, he gave to Jayanta a divine chariot, equipped with a beautiful umbrella and banners, crowded with many weapons and missiles, and drawn by elephants and steeds.
The Creator of the Universe fashioned a divine vehicle, composed of all splendors, exquisitely constructed, consisting of various jewels, and blazing with the light of gems.
O wise one, he has now given to the Sun a chariot drawn by seven horses, blazing with fierce splendor and endowed with a jeweled parasol.
Furthermore, Viśvakarman fashioned that most excellent of all vehicles, adorned with many silver parts and embellished with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
The Creator of All gave to Soma a chariot with the luster of silver, possessing the brilliance of the moon, equipped with a parasol, and drawn by swans; it was endowed with a most lovely splendor.
Then the Creator of All fashioned again a vehicle made of copper,
inlaid with all kinds of jewels and adorned with gold and silver.
He gave to Jātavedas a divine palace consisting of red splendor, with windows made of topaz,
which was unbearable for all the worlds.
Then Viśvakarman again fashioned a divine, very firm aerial chariot made of iron, adorned with silver and gold ornaments.
O Sage, Bhīṣma, who was borne by a buffalo and resembled a heap of crushed collyrium, equipped with banners and flags, was delivered to Vaivasvata.
Furthermore, the Creator fashioned a great golden vehicle,
as well as the mouths of living beings, which were beautiful with their various gestures and movements.
He gave to Nairṛta a firm, great, and heavy chariot with eight wheels, drawn by donkeys, well-constructed,
and studded with various jewels.
Furthermore, Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned a vehicle made of all kinds of jewels,
which was filled with the various movements and gestures of aquatic creatures depicted on its faces.
He joyfully gave to Varuṇa a chariot made of beautiful Jāmbūnada gold, endowed with hundreds of divine weapons and equipped with a network of tinkling bells.
Having fashioned a supreme, divine vehicle made of gold, which moves at will, possesses the beauty of jewels, and is endowed with various splendors; 36.
Furthermore, he gave to Vāyu a beautiful eight-wheeled chariot, richly adorned with artificial silver ornaments and equipped with banners and flags.
Then, having fashioned another Puṣpaka chariot with Jāmbūnada gold and silver, it was exceedingly brilliant and inlaid with various jewels.
Furthermore, he gave to Kubera a vehicle that moved at will, possessed great beauty, was adorned with networks of tinkling bells, and featured raised banners and standards.
Then Viśvakarman himself ascended that divine vehicle, which was composed of all elements and filled with many jewels.
Then Indra commanded the gods throughout the ten directions:
"O immortals, you must protect your own city in due order."
First, the preceptor performed the rite for prosperity and then indeed dispatched them with force;
having equipped the army and formed a battle array, he went forth from the city with his chariots.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Departure of the Armies of the Gods and Asuras," in the Himavatkhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 25 ||
Skanda said: At that time, all the Asuras ascended chariots, horses, camels, and likewise other elephants, and marched toward Triviṣṭapa.
Then the lord of the Daityas beheld the city protected by Indra,
which was graced by the noble Nandana grove produced from the Pārijāta tree.
Having established a military array in all directions and being well-protected by the guardians of the quarters,
it was filled with golden palaces and crowded with golden trees.
Then Hiraṇyakaśipu, with joy, summoned all the chariot-warriors and commanded the Daityas according to their fitness and in due order.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O mighty-armed Prahlāda,
first fight with Jayanta from Amarāvatī, who is surrounded by ten million chariots."
"O child, let Anuhrāda fight from the south-eastern direction;
and you, O dear one, accompanied by Vahni, shall go forth with ten million chariots."
Let Saṃhrāda, together with Kāla, fight from the south;
taking ten million chariots, then lead him away.
"O hero Nikumbha, fight equally with the Nairṛta, taking with you an army of ten million chariots and surrounded by your troops. || 8 ||
"O hero Kālaka, take ten million chariots and, surrounded by your army, engage in battle with Varuṇa from the western side. || 9 ||
"O hero Bala, together with Vayu, you must fight them,
taking ten million chariots and surrounded by a vast army."
Do not despise that Vāyu, who brings fear to all living beings;
for you, my child, are a great hero with supreme and exalted prowess.
"O Vipracitti, let Kubera fight together with you;
taking ten million chariots, go forth toward the north accompanied by your forces."
O hero, surrounded by a vast army and taking with me ten million chariots, I fought alongside Viśvakarman.
O Hiraṇyākṣa, we shall remain here demonstrating our resolve;
when the armies flee, it is then that we shall fight.
Skanda said:
Then, O sage, the Daityas arrived for battle at that time, having received the command of their lord and saluting the Lord of Asuras. 15.
Then, having returned to their respective abodes, the Daityas, filled with joy,
let out a most terrifying roar that struck fear into all living beings.
Then, O Brahmin, the gods also raised a most wonderful roar upon seeing all the Danujas, and thereafter let out a lion's roar.
Then, O steadfast one, a roar arose from both armies,
terrifying to all living beings, like that at the end of a Yuga.
Furthermore, there were the sounds of kettledrums, tabors, clay drums, and drums born of water,
as well as ḍhakkās, dundubhis, and cymbals.
O wise one, there was indeed the trumpeting of elephants and horses,
as well as the sound of bowstrings, chariot wheels, and the tumultuous clamor arising from the heroes.
Then those great heroic Daityas, fighting on foot, engaged in battle on all sides with the gods who were likewise great warriors.
The gods and the Daityas went against one another with arrows, swords, battle-axes,
maces, spears, nooses, iron clubs, and likewise with javelins.
Then,
O wise one, the foot-soldiers of both armies fell everywhere upon the battlefield like trees struck by harsh blows.
The outskirts of the city then shone with floods of blood arising from wounds;
covered by that, Bhima appeared like the single ocean at the end of an aeon.
Their fallen bodies, covered by great waves and likewise by floods of blood, appeared like mountains shrouded with only their peaks remaining visible.
Then Jayanta, at the outset, certainly showered volleys of arrows marked with his own name upon the army of the Daityas.
O Brahmin, at that time Prahlāda also crushed the army of the gods on all sides with nets of exceedingly sharp arrows marked with his own name.
Then Jayanta also, swiftly taking his bow in the midst of the enemies of the gods,
rushed forward in battle out of anger.
He struck the chariot-warriors on all sides with sharp arrows;
he rained down showers of shafts and afflicted the foot-soldiers and the car-warriors alike. 29.
Then, with razor-edged arrows and broad-headed shafts, he indeed severed the heads of heroes fighting together— chariot-warriors as well as foot-soldiers.
Drawing his bow with an arrow back to his ear and aiming at the heart-center of Prahlāda, he struck him.
With ten arrows each, he struck down the horses and chariot-drivers;
and with five each, he slew all the foot-soldiers.
Then he quickly cut down the banners standing at the front of the chariots;
looking here and there, he struck them repeatedly with his arrows.
Prahlāda did not waver in battle, even though he was being severely afflicted by arrows;
having overcome the pain for a moment, like a lordly elephant struck by goads.
Then the exceedingly powerful Prahlāda also beheld that army shattered and fleeing in terror from the battlefield.
And beholding Jayanta stationed in the midst of the army,
crushing his own forces with fury, the asura was overcome with delusion.
Having summoned all his armies, he spoke these words:
"O great heroes, O Daityas! There can be no success in flight. (37)
Indeed, O Lord of the Daityas, you must certainly fight with me, placing our duty (dharma) foremost so that great fame may be obtained. 38.
Skanda said: Then, having quickly heard the words of Prahlāda, the Dānavas were filled with joy and went forth once more for battle to where the son of Indra was.
Taking up their bows, the heroes rushed forward simultaneously;
he discharged showers of arrows, and the ten directions became enveloped in darkness.
At that time, he tormented the gods with showers of arrows, as well as with weapons,
blows from many missiles and arms, iron clubs, and slings.
Then the army of the gods was afflicted by those weapons and missiles,
like a herd of cattle in the darkness of winter by falling rain.
For Prahlāda, out of great rage, took up his bow with an arrow,
drew it back to his ear, and bit his lip firmly.
Aiming for the middle of his chest, he pierced Jayanta with ten arrows,
and springing up, he let out a roar at Jayanta’s heart.
Again, piercing them with ten arrows at a time, he let out a roar;
he struck the chariot-warriors, the charioteers, the horses, the foot-soldiers, and likewise the elephants.
With his arrows, he cut down the celestial banners standing upon the chariots,
as well as the mounts of the celestial vehicles, their feet, and likewise their hands.
Then he said to the charioteer: "O charioteer, drive the chariot to wherever the array of the gods stands. 47.
Furthermore, afflicting both the gods and the foot-soldiers with the rims of his chariot wheels,
he struck them with sharp arrows while displaying himself throughout the ten directions.
Then those armies, being tormented and seeing the enraged Prahlāda, fled toward the interior of the city, like herds of deer upon seeing a lion. 49.
Then Vahni, having gone into the midst of the enemies of the gods in his chariot,
discharged nets of arrows like the rays [of light] at the end of an eon.
Having drawn it back as far as his ear and aimed at the space between her breasts,
he leapt up, struck, and let out a roar like a blazing fire.
Having pierced the charioteer with ten arrows and the horses with twenty,
he further cut down the standard with three arrows and the parasol with another three.
And with five sharp arrows, he cut asunder the beautiful bow, as well as the string and the arrows indeed discharged by Anuhrāda. 53.
O Sage, the Fire-god pierced other chariot-warriors with ten arrows each,
and having struck their charioteers with five, he plunged them into the region of the heart.
He struck the foot soldiers with six arrows each without delay,
and likewise, having sighted the warriors before him, he struck them with ten arrows each.
Unable to stand before the fire of unbearable brilliance, those enemies of the gods,
afflicted by the nets of his arrows, were no longer able to remain stationed upon their chariots.
Abandoning the battlefield in fear, scorched by the fire-like luster [of his weapons], their bodies pulverized by his arrows, they fled in the ten directions. 57.
O sage, the Daityas—charioteers with banners and likewise foot-soldiers—trembled upon seeing him, like deer beholding a rutting elephant. 58.
Then, O Brahmin, Anuhrāda did not waver in that great battle,
even though he was being struck on his limbs individually by those moving through the air.
Having crossed over for a moment, he beheld his own fourfold army fleeing, having abandoned the battle at that time. (60)
Beholding his great army terrified and torn apart by the fire-arrows,
Anuhrada challenged them with hand-gestures.
The great chariot-warrior Anuhrāda spoke these words to them:
"Ho there, O Daityas, great warriors! Desist from this flight!"
"Born of the Daitya lineage, you heroes should be destroyers of sin;
why then have you fled, abandoning the field of battle? (63)
"O great heroes known by our name, renowned throughout the three worlds, place the dharma of the Daityas before you and fight indeed with me! (64)
O wise one, having heard these words of Anuhrāda, the warriors immediately turned back and went to where the lord of the asuras was stationed.
Once again those Daityas fought with one another in that great battle;
rushing at each other's troops, they could no longer distinguish their own from the enemy.
Then, O Brahmin, Anuhrāda, overwhelmed by anger,
took up his bow with an arrow and spoke quickly to the charioteer.
O charioteer, O mighty-armed one, urge the horses forward quickly;
take the chariot directly to where the sun is stationed.
Taking the command, the charioteer also swiftly urged the horses to where the Brahmin’s chariot had led the chariot of Agni at that time. 69.
Drawing the beautiful bow with an arrow up to his ear,
he pressed his lips together with his teeth and slightly bent his slender body.
Then Anuhrāda, out of anger, swiftly struck the chest of Jātavedas— who had been deceived by a trick— aiming for the space between his breasts.
Furthermore, he struck ten arrows each into the hands and feet of Jātavedas,
and ten into the region of his head.
With five sharp arrows he cut through the two quivers, the bow, and the standard;
with five more, he pierced the charioteer and the horses.
Taking up the Vāruṇa weapon, he rained it down upon him;
thereupon, O Pot-born One, even the hero Agni became devoid of power.
With ten arrows each, he struck down other chariot-warriors;
with six each, the foot-soldiers; and with four each, the charioteers.
With thirty and twenty [arrows] respectively, he struck the elephants and horses;
leaping up with light-handedness, he let out a roar.
Then the charioteer drove the vehicle back toward the city;
seeing it had retreated, his armies pursued it. || 77 ||
Then, people quickly reported that news to Śakra;
for the two charioteers of Jayanta and Vaiśvānara had been driven out of the city and slain.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Flowing Away of Water from the Chariots of Jayanta and Agni," in the Devāsura-yuddha section of the Himavat-khaṇḍa within the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 26.
Skanda said:
Once again there was a great battle, tumultuous and hair-raising;
with weapons, missiles, and projectiles, O Brahmin, it was as terrifying as the end of an eon. 1.
The battle between those two, Citra and Saṃhrādakāla, was great;
then, even though it was day, it became as if night due to the showers of weapons and missiles.
O Brahmin, a tumultuous battle took place between those two, Kāla and Saṃhāda, as they sought to slay one another, terrifying the armies.
Then, with many millions of sharp arrows whetted on stone, which had golden shafts and were discharged from all sides by both of them, [the battle raged].
Those two chariots, having entered the midst of the battle, shone intensely, like two golden-peaked mountains at night covered with fireflies. || 5 ||
Then he said to the charioteer regarding the departure of the chariot:
"O charioteer, it is time; bring the chariot quickly to his presence."
"I shall slay Saṃhrāda, the enemy of the gods, with my sharp arrows.
Having heard Kāla's words, the charioteer drove the chariot forward.
Then, O wise one, the charioteer and the steeds of the chariot quickly urged them forward with effort to where Saṃhrāda was stationed.
Filled with indignation, Kāla quickly struck Saṃhrāda in the chest with twenty arrows drawn back to his ear.
And then, with five more arrows, he struck Saṃhrāda,
aiming at his vital points— the hands, feet, and forehead.
Then, with ten by ten [arrows], he likewise cut down the horses and the charioteer;
with three by three, he severed the banner, the bow, the arrows, and the quivers.
He pierced the chariot-warriors violently with six sharp arrows each,
and furthermore, he struck the foot-soldiers and others with five arrows each.
With two arrows at a time, he likewise cut down the banners along with their pennants,
as well as those standing at the head of the armies and those positioned at the front of the chariots.
With his arrows, Kāla severed the heads of those Danujas;
he repeatedly cut down tens of thousands of foot soldiers as they fought. || 14 ||
He struck the Daityas who were fighting again and again,
using thousands of crores upon crores of arrows and lances.
Then, O sage, those Daitya armies,
overwhelmed by the arrows of Time and trembling again and again, fled in all directions.
And Saṃhrāda, the great hero, was quickly overwhelmed with fury upon seeing the army terrified and torn apart by his Kāla-arrows. || 17 ||
Making a clanging sound, the enraged one, having swept the excellent seat,
summoned his entire army and commanded his charioteer.
"O charioteer, lead the chariot now to where that Kāla is.
Thereupon, the charioteer quickly urged on the horses and the chariot to that place. 19.
Then Saṃhrāda spoke to Kāla, the destroyer of the world,
making it heard by all the gods, his own troops, and others as well.
Saṃhrāda said:
"The word 'Kāla' is renowned to you as the very time of death for those who have died; however, it is not the time for those who sustain life, for you are certainly not capable of reckoning that."
"You are not capable [of acting as] Time for those living beings who sustain their lives;
Time alone is able to reckon the times of those engaged in action, but not at an improper time."
"Fight, O King of the Dead, if you have any manliness left in you! Show me your prowess now, and I shall show you mine at the end. (23)
"Having slain many Daityas on all sides in battle, you, who are powerful, do not grieve over the lowly ones who have been killed; fight today if you are indeed strong. (24)
"By slaying you now with as many [strokes] as there were of those who have been slain, I shall rescue my preceptor by means of my own mantra. (25)
Kāla said:
"O fool, you do not boast for long; show your manliness today!
For those who are truly brave do not boast, but rather demonstrate their own prowess."
"O fool, having slain you along with your lineage, Purandara will certainly rule the kingdom, making the three worlds free of thorns. (27)
Skanda said:
O wise one, having heard these words from the midst of Kāla’s army,
the Daitya, filled with indignation, bit his lower lip violently.
Drawing his bow up to his ear and fixing a hundred arrows upon it, he aimed at Kāla with the bowstring and discharged those many shafts.
O sage, he violently struck Kāla with arrows resembling Time itself,
piercing thousands of them into all of Kāla's vital organs.
With ten arrows at a time, he struck down the horses with great swiftness of hand;
having pierced the charioteer with ten, he cut down the standard with two.
With arrows drawn back to his ear, shot by thirties, thirties, and likewise twenties,
he struck the chariot-warriors, the combatants, and the mounts.
Then, seeing that the charioteer had driven the vehicle away from the battlefield toward a nearby spot, having been distressed and moved swiftly; || 33 ||
Then, being tormented by his arrows, they fled from the battle toward the city of Devasenā; seeing this, Yama withdrew his vehicle.
Then the Daitya Saṃhrāda, leaping here and there,
discharged showers of arrows and again let out lion-like roars.
Then there occurred a great, tumultuous, and hair-raising battle between Bhīṣma and the gods and asuras, as well as between Nikumbha and the Yātudhānas.
With tomaras, bhindipālas, prāsas, and likewise with iron clubs,
fists, arrows, and swords, those two struck one another.
Then, O Brahmin, Nairṛta, that great chariot-warrior, having strung his mighty bow,
swiftly went into the midst of the Asuras on his chariot.
Then he released showers of arrows on all sides;
all the directions became shrouded in darkness as the sky was being covered. (39)
In that great battle, the mounts became effortless under the showers of arrows,
like the nights during the rainy season in the dark fortnight of winter.
Taking up many arrows, that son of Nirṛti buried them in Nikumbha’s body;
they shone constantly upon his armor like leeches.
Having struck the charioteer with arrows, as well as the horses and others,
he cut through his bowstring along with the arrow and the bow itself.
Then the son of Nirṛti crushed all the foot soldiers and chariot-warriors with his arrows,
as well as the horses, elephants, and camels, each separately.
And the Daitya armies, their spirits terrified, fled here and there, O Brahmin;
abandoning the battlefield, they were tormented by the hosts of Nairṛtas.
Then Nikumbha also,
beholding the army terrified and fleeing like an ocean with its embankment breached, was filled with indignation.
Then the great car-warrior Nikumbha, too, surrounded by his troops,
went swiftly with his bow to where the Nairṛta stood.
Having encountered him in battle with his chariot, he struck down Patañjikā;
then, filled with rage, he spoke to the cannibal, making his words heard by the entire army.
Nikumbha said: "O dull-witted son of Nikasha, you who are always devoted to base conduct, a night-stalker who constantly drinks the blood of living beings and consumes their flesh. (48)
"You are deformed by your fighting with claws, and your body is censured by the world;
joined with these contemptible traits, you are base—of this there is no doubt. (49)
"Now, O wretch, show us your prowess!
Today I shall slay you and satisfy the Lord of the Danujas. (50)
Skanda said:
Having spoken thus, that high-souled and mighty Nikumbha took up his bow with an arrow and once again made the twang of the string resound.
Drawing the bowstring with the arrow firmly to his ear, he discharged sharp arrows that were eager to drink the blood of the Rakshasa. || 52 ||
He swiftly struck down the charioteer and cut the standard with three arrows;
with floods of gold-tufted shafts, he also destroyed the parasol and the chariot-steeds.
Then, having quickly bitten his lower lip, he slew even more chariot-warriors and foot soldiers who were fierce in battle with many arrows.
Then, seeing the chariot-warrior wounded in battle,
the charioteer quickly drove the noble, gold-adorned chariot away.
Beholding the aerial chariot of the Nairṛtas standing there,
the divine armies fled toward the city of Amarāvatī.
Then the messenger, having gone there with haste, reported that news to the assembly:
how indeed the Nairṛta had been defeated in battle and the conduct of the Asuras toward Indra. || 57 ||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Departure and Return of Kāla and Nairṛta," in the Devāsura-saṃgrāma section of the Himavat-khaṇḍa within the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. 27.
Skanda said: O Brahmin, there was once again a great battle, terrifying to both gods and asuras, between Pāśika and Ālaka, each desiring to slay the other.
The gods and the Danavas alike discharged showers of arrows,
so that all the directions became blinded by darkness as if by a cloudy night.
With maces, sharp iron clubs, javelins, axes,
and spears, as well as gold-feathered arrows, the gods and the asuras struck one another.
Filled with indignation, the great hero Pracetās quickly commanded his charioteer to prepare the chariot for departure into battle.
"O charioteer, O mighty-armed one, urge the horses forward now;
quickly take my vehicle to where Kālaka stands. (5)
Having heard that command of Pracetas,
the charioteer then drove the vehicle, which was as dark as Time itself, swiftly from nearby.
Then, having fixed his arrows to the bow drawn back to his ear,
he swiftly discharged those shafts marked with gold.
Then Pāśī, aiming at that great asura Kālaka,
simultaneously struck him with thousands of sharp arrows.
Then, having quickly bound the gods with nooses,
Pracetas slew hundreds and thousands of them with his sword at the forefront of the battle.
And he struck down the chariot-warriors and the foremost combatants who were eager for battle at his front,
first binding them with nooses and then slaying them with sharp axes.
Then those Daityas, both chariot-warriors and foot-soldiers,
fled upon seeing him, who resembled Time itself, as the destroyer of the Daitya army.
All the Danujas, their bodies pierced by his arrows and overcome with fear, abandoned the battle and fled trembling in the ten directions. || 12 ||
Then the powerful Daitya named Kālaka beheld his own troops fleeing and spoke thus to his son: 13.
"O Sūta, you who are mighty-armed and skilled in all forms of combat, I shall now fight there together with Pracetas. (14)
"O great hero, O wise one, lead the chariot to where Pracetās stands;
urge my horses on quickly, for I cannot endure this improper act for long. (15)
O Brahmin, having heard these words spoken by Kālaka,
he urged on the horses of the chariot, which was adorned with a banner and decorated with gold.
He quickly brought him there where the lord of waters stood;
and then the wrathful Kālaka beheld the lord of aquatic creatures.
Drawing [his bow] back to his ear and aiming at the space between Varuṇa’s breasts, the hero struck him violently with thousands of arrows.
Furthermore, taking up thousands of arrows, Kālaka pierced the bodies of the wise ones, making them appear as if they were rivers of blood.
Then he quickly struck the charioteer with thirty arrows,
cut down the standard with two, and [struck] the mounts with thirty each.
Furthermore, with hundreds upon hundreds of sharp arrows, he struck down foot soldiers and chariot-warriors alike, and let out a lion’s roar.
O Sage, seeing that the son of Pracetas was covered with many wounds from arrows, the charioteer quickly drove away the Varuna vehicle.
Seeing that the vehicle had been driven away from the battlefield by the wise one,
the army of the gods, trembling with fear, fled toward Amarāvatī.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, Bali and Vāyu fought each other most fiercely;
their impatient armies also engaged one another, desiring victory over the opponent.
Those armies of gods and asuras released a rain of arrows,
until the intermediate quarters of the sky were rendered blind by the downpours, like the month of Nabhas.
Then Vayu, of great splendor, taking the bow along with the arrow,
commanded the charioteer to set out with the chariot.
O illustrious charioteer, urge on my horses and lead my chariot now to that place where Bali stands for battle.
Drive my chariot properly and protect these horses;
O you who are skilled in battle, having ascertained the relative strength and weakness of both ourselves and our enemies. (28)
Skanda said: Having heard these words of Vāyu, the charioteer urged on the horses and brought the vehicle to that place where Bali, the king of the Daityas, was located.
There, in the battle, he beheld Bali seated upon his golden chariot,
discharging fierce arrows and shafts that came to rest upon his head.
Then Vāyu, overcome with rage, took up ten thousand arrows;
quickly making his bow into a circle with those shafts, he struck him. 31.
Indeed, Vāyu blew away the gold-winged arrows from Baleri’s body, and his [Vāyu's] winds drank his blood. 32.
Then, O sage, he deeply pierced the horses with fifty arrows,
and furthermore, he swiftly struck the charioteer with twenty-five.
With two [arrows] he cut down the raised standard together with its banner;
then with two more he severed the arrow held in his hand and the bow.
O Brahmin, with a hundred feathered shafts he indeed struck down chariot-warriors;
furthermore, with fifty he slew warriors, and with half that number, foot-soldiers.
Some with swords, others with spears, battle-axes, arrows,
slings, and maces, the gods struck down the Dānavas.
Then the armies of the Daityas fled in the ten directions,
wounded by the arrows of Vāyu, their bodies trembling and overcome with fear.
Both Bali and the charioteer, pierced by arrows and enduring the pain like cows in the month of Bhādrapada under heavy rain, were freed from their agony in an instant.
Then Bali, beholding his own army fleeing—
terrified, pierced by arrows, and like a river whose banks have been breached— [proceeded].
Then the exceedingly powerful Bali spoke again these words to his troops, who were trembling with fear, employing the principles of statecraft: 40.
Bali said:
"O Daityas, you who stand in unrighteousness and have turned your backs on the duty of battle!
Turn back, turn back! From where has this fear come upon you?"
Having abandoned our duty and resorted to cowardice, fie upon your manliness, for you have fled in fear! 42.
"Since our master's affairs cannot be accomplished through flight, how can we wish to abandon Hiraṇyakaśipu? (43)
"Adopting the dharma of the Daityas, fight indeed with me!
O you of great strength, let us attain success; let it come to pass! || 44 ||
Skanda said:

Then, having heard the words of Bali, which were endowed with the fourfold principles of policy, O Brahmin, they returned from all directions to where he was staying, from whichever direction each had come. 45.
Then, O King, the Daityas were filled with great joy by those words full of statesmanship;
looking at him, they honored him while exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (46)
Then, O Brahmin, Bali, surrounded by all the Daityas, went there in his chariot to fight, consoling his charioteer as he proceeded toward the charioteer [of the enemy]. 47.
The gods and the daityas fought, each desiring the other's destruction;
then, they came to recognize their own kin from the enemies among themselves. 48.
Covering one another with nets of arrows,
they then struck each other with nooses, javelins, swords, spears, and iron clubs.
Then Bāli, possessed of great splendor and skilled in combat, fought with Vāyu;
he even rendered the wind to his left.
Biting his lip with his teeth as he drew back arrows up to his ear,
Bali struck Vāyu violently with thousands of shafts.
He struck at all the armor with thousands of arrows having shafts made of gold, and he let out a lion's roar like the wind.
With a hundred [arrows], he then struck the chariots, horses, and the charioteer;
and aiming separately, he cut down the standard with two [arrows]. (53)
Furthermore, O steadfast one, he swiftly and furiously struck down the leaders of the chariot-warriors with five hundred each, and their subordinates with a thousand.
Moving swiftly in all directions, he crushed the chariots with their deep-set wheels and the foot-soldiers of the gods as he roamed about.
Then, seeing the chariot-warrior covered in wounds, the charioteer, filled with fear, drove the vehicle away from the battlefield. || 56 ||
Beholding that obstruction of the wind, those hosts of gods fled in terror from their vehicle and now toward the kingdom of Śakra.
Then, O wise one, the army quickly went and reported the news and the activities of the Danuja to Purandara, who was nearby, concerning that which had been done for the sake of summoning him. 58.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Carriage-Procession of Varuṇa and Anila," in the Devāsura-saṃgrāma section of the Himavat-khaṇḍa within the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Skanda said: Then, O Brahmin, there occurred a great and tumultuous battle between Vipracitti and Kubera, which struck fear into both gods and demons. 1.
Chariot-warriors fought with chariot-warriors, foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers,
and elephants again with elephants, as they battled one another.
The gods and asuras showered volleys of arrows upon one another intensely;
the quarters of the sky became shrouded in darkness, like nights filled with rain.
The gods and the Daityas struck one another with various terrifying weapons—arrows, swords, maces, and nooses—failing to distinguish between their own kin and their enemies. || 4 ||
Then there arose a roar that made the three worlds tremble—a tumultuous clamor of "Seize them! and "Kill them!", along with cries of "Alas! Alas! (5).
The terrifying sound arising from the rims of chariot wheels, as well as the neighing of horses, and likewise the cries of elephants, buffaloes, donkeys, and camels; || 6 ||
Then the wise Kumbhakarṇa, quickly taking up his bow,
spoke there to the charioteer in sweet and conciliatory tones.
"O charioteer, you who are highly wise, drive my horses incessantly;
lead the vehicle quickly to where Vipracitti is."
Then, having heard the Yakṣa’s pleasant words,
the charioteer urged on the horses of the celestial chariot and drove the vehicle to that place.
And the immensely powerful Kubera beheld the army of his enemies,
slaughtering all the gods with nets of arrows here and there.
Then Kubera, the lord of the Guhyakas, overcome with anger,
drew [his bow] back to his ear and struck with arrows of sharp points.
O Sage, he then drove into his limbs, aiming at all the vital points, arrows with shafts made of gold and furnished with beautiful feathers.
In the battle, the Lord of Wealth pierced Sūta with thousands of arrows and struck down the charioteers individually;
he also severed the banner of Vipracitti with two shafts.
Furthermore, he swiftly struck down thousands of chariot-warriors eager for battle,
as well as hundreds upon hundreds of foot soldiers.
Overcome with rage, Vipracitti emerged from his affliction in an instant;
in the midst of the battle, he spoke to his charioteer, making himself heard by both his own men and his enemies.
Vipracitti said:
"O charioteer, wise one skilled in battle, urge on the drivers of the chariot!
Quickly lead my chariot to that place where the Yakṣa stands. (16)
Today I shall indeed slay him along with his charioteer,
as well as Kubera, the celestial hosts, and their mounts at this very moment.
Skanda said: Then, having heard the roar uttered by Vipracitti, the charioteer,
skilled in setting out on journeys and filled with joy, drove the chariot forward at that time.
O Sage, where the descendant of Pulastya stood, he quickly brought that chariot,
which was skilled in battle and capable of displaying the celestial army.
Then he beheld the descendant of Pulastya discharging many arrows;
thereupon, his soul impelled by wrath, he took up his great bow.
Making his great bow into a circle, Vipracitti, with light-handed skill, pierced Kubera in an instant with ten thousand arrows.
Furthermore, taking up another hundred thousand sharp-pointed arrows,
he then swiftly struck them into the heart of the high-souled Kubera.
For with ten thousand he slew ten thousand chariot-warriors;
with two thousand he killed individual combatants, and with thousands he struck down the chariot-drivers.
O Brahmin, he swiftly slew a thousand charioteers of the five [armies] and,
with two [arrows], cut down the banner and the bow of Kubera.
Then the divine host there blazed forth on all sides;
it vomited intense blood from the wounds of its mouths, nostrils, and ears.
And the Daitya armies, beholding the celestial soldiers pierced by the arrows of Vipracitti and drenched in streams of blood, fled away. || 26 ||
And the charioteer of Kubera, having momentarily set aside his own pain and seeing that wound, indeed drove the vehicle away from the battlefield.
O sage, having seen the chariot, I then drove it away from Kubera;
those divine armies fled in terror toward the city.
Once again, there was a great battle between Maya and Viśvakarman;
there, those two masters of illusion engaged each other in a battle of illusions.
Desiring to slay one another, they first rained down a shower of arrows,
so that all the directions became blinded like nights during the dark fortnight.
Then the armies struck one another with weapons and missiles,
with swords, and with gold-feathered arrows having the plumage of herons and vultures.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, the master of great illusion and expert in all forms of magic,
leapt into the sky together with his chariot and his weapons.
Then, standing in the sky, Viśvasṛj showered down rains of arrows with iron tips, fletched with the feathers of peacocks and herons.
Then those troops of Maya fled in the ten directions,
their limbs mangled by the falling arrows, terrified and tormented.
Then, O Brahmin, seeing his own army afflicted by the illusory arrows and beholding the master of illusion stationed in the sky, Maya became enraged.
Maya quickly leapt up and, stationed upon his chariot, remained unobserved in the sky;
he then surely rained down showers of stones upon the army of the gods.
Furthermore, by means of his illusory power,
the asura Maya simultaneously rained down mountain peaks, boulders from the slopes, and trees.
Then the divine army, afflicted by the blows of rocks, trees, and arrows, abandoned the battle there and fled, overcome with fear.
Then those two heroes, both experts in various magical illusions,
fought in many ways within the vault of the sky, as if they were made of Viśvakarman’s own craftsmanship.
Those two high-souled ones, each leading a hundred thousand troops, moved about stationed in the sky;
they struck one another with many weapons and missiles.
Then, leaping from their vehicle, those two heroes fell upon the earth,
embracing one another and not letting go of each other.
Then they fought with one another once more in hand-to-hand combat;
striking again and again, they struck each other with palms and fists.
They fought a mace-duel that caused all beings to tremble,
as sparks produced by the blows of their maces illuminated the quarters of the sky.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ, by means of his power of illusion (māyā), fashioned a mind that was similar to him;
with that [mind], he engaged in battle against those whose prowess was equal to his own.
O Brahmin, the person born of illusion indeed fought with Māya;
then a great and fierce battle took place upon the surface of the earth. 45.
Then, O Sage, Viśvakarman went to heaven and ascended a celestial vehicle made of various jewels, situated in the sky and exceedingly brilliant.
Then, in that battle, Viśvakarman quickly rained down a shower of fire and thereafter a shower of stones upon the Daitya army from all sides.
O Brahmin, the Creator of the Universe swiftly rained down a shower of arrows, a similar shower of weapons,
a shower of trees, and again a shower of dust.
Then the Daityas fell, vomiting blood from the wounds on their faces,
being struck from all sides by showers of stones consisting of weapons and missiles.
Then Maya, having recognized that the man was indeed born of illusion (māyā),
abandoned the fight with him and reflected upon the appropriate course of action.
Moreover, O Brahmin, at that time, having created through my own power of illusion (māyā) a man who was my very likeness,
I caused him to fight with him as an equal.
Maya, whose body was composed of illusion, leapt into the sky;
there in the firmament, he beheld Tvaṣṭṛ seated upon his vehicle.
While [Maya] was causing the Daitya armies to be struck down on all sides by showers of rocks, he too, filled with rage, quickly mounted his chariot there. || 53 ||
He rained down showers of arrows like locusts during a famine,
as well as a fierce shower of stones and a heavy rain of dust on all sides.
Then Maya swiftly rained [weapons] upon the divine army;
thereafter, the illusionist Maya deluded them in battle by means of his magic power.
With songs and the beating of mṛdaṅga drums, he caused Tvaṣṭṛ to dance;
and seeing Tvaṣṭṛ dancing and singing, the Moon,
having manifested him as possessed by his own illusory power (māyā), showered him with nectar.
Then, O Pot-born One, having been drenched by the showers of nectar from Tvaṣṭṛ,
he performed great deeds in the battle and returned from the field to the city.
Then the messenger spoke of the progress in the slaying of Vṛtra and the events occurring on the battlefield,
as well as Tvaṣṭṛ’s defeat in combat and how he was now bewildered by the illusion that was causing him to dance.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Retreat of Viśvakarman," in the Devāsura-saṃgrāma section of the Himavat-khaṇḍa within the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 29 ||
